summary: The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to wealth tax on the valuation date. The Wealth Tax Officer, after assessing the net wealth of the assessee, determined the net assets of the family at Rs.1,20,000/-. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the net income of the business was assessable to wealthtax and the Wealth Tax officer had jurisdiction to assess the net value of the assets of a Hindu undivided family. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal set aside the order of the Wealth tax Officer and confirmed the order passed by the Wealthtax Officer. The High Court in appeal affirmed the view taken by the Appellate Assistant commissioner that the assessee was not an individual and that the total wealth of such family was not liable to be included in the net asset of the Hindu undivided Family. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the assets were not exempt from wealth tax under section 3(1) (a) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "net wealth" used in section 2(i)(d) of Wealth Tax Act means the net worth of an assessee on the date of valuation and includes all his assets. [701B] 2. The word "net" is not defined in the Income Tax Act. It does not mean any amount paid or payable to an assessee by way of tax, wealth tax, etc., but it includes any amount payable under any law for the time being in force. [802C] 3. The words "net value" are used in the section and it is not confined to the net amount of assets of an individual. It is only those assets which have been included in his net wealth as on the last day of the previous year or which were not covered by the definition of "net asset". [803D] 4. The term "net assets" used therein includes any amounts payable under law for any assessment year for which an assessment was to be made under this Act. [820E] 5. The net wealth is determined on the basis of the valuation dates fixed in accordance with section 19A and not on the value date. It cannot be said that the amount of net wealth determined by the Income tax Officer is not liable for inclusion in the wealth tax assessment. [823C] 6. In the instant case, the assessee had not disclosed any income from his business or had furnished inaccurate particulars of his income. He was not entitled to claim deduction under section 10(2) of Act. The Tribunal was right in holding the assessee to be entitled to deduction under sections 10(1)(d), 10(3) and 10(4). [823E] 7. In view of the above, the appeal is allowed. The order passed in the case of the Commissioner of Wealth tax, West Bengal vs I.T.R. Murthy (supra) is set aside. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the Indian Army on a temporary basis. He was placed under suspension wi ll the Central Reserve Police Force (CISF) and he was charge sheeted by the disciplinary authority for his alleged misconduct. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal from service before the Tribunal and the Tribunal set aside the order imposing the penalty of dismissal. The Tribunal held that the respondent had failed to prove that the findings of the enquiry officer were not based on any evidence and, therefore, the punishment was justified. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the finding of the Tribunal was perverse and the High Court should not have interfered with the order passed by the Tribunal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The findings of t he enquiry officer are based on no evidence and the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer are based upon no evidence. [701B] 2.2 The respondent was a member of the Indian Armed Forces and had been serving as a Sub Inspector in the Central Police Force. He had been charge sheeted for his misconduct under Rule 14(b) of the Rules. The disciplinary authority, therefore could not have imposed any penalty on him. [802C] 3.3 The Tribunal has committed an error in holding that the order was passed by way of punishment and the respondent was entitled to a lesser penalty than what he had been dismissed from service. [820G] 4.1 In view of the fact that the appellant had not been able to establish that the disciplinary auth ority had acted on a reasonable basis, the Tribunal could not interfere with the findings o f the enquiry authority and the finding recorded by it. [823E] 3: The High Court was in error in interfering with the penalty imposed by the Disciplinary Authority. [825G] 3; 804C] 4:1.2 In view thereof, the respondent is entitled to be reinstated in service with full back wages. [822F] 3,4A] 2:1 The order of the High C ourt setting aside the dismissal from services was not justified on any ground. [826B] 3(a) The High Cour t had no jurisdiction to interfere with an order of punishment passed by a competent authority. [828E] 4(b). In view o f any error in the order, the High court could not substitute its own opinion for that of the disciplinary authori ty and the tribunal could exercise all the powers of a civil court. [827A D] 3 (c) The respondent had been given ample opportunity to defend his case. He did not appear before the Enquiry officer or the Tribunal on any point. He has been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses. [829E] 2(d). In the instant case, the Enquiry Report was based upon the evidence adduced by the respondent and the report of the Enquiry Commissioner. The High c ourt could not exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India in a writ petition filed by the appellant. [824F] 4.(a) In view Of the fact, the findings arrived at by the enquiry Officer were based on evidence adduced before the disciplinary Authority and the order to be passed by him was not interfered with by the High cour t. [821G] 5.(b) The Tribunal had no power to review the penalty order passed against the respondent. [84F] 6(c) In the present case, there is no dispute that the enquiry report was based on the evidence led before the Disciplinary authority and it was not open to the High nicient to consider whether the findings were perverse or not. [85G] 7.(a)(i) The order passed in favour of the respondent by the Governor was not sustainable in law. [86F] 804D] (b) In a writ proceeding, the order is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record.

The plaintiff, who was a deemed tenant under section 8(2) of the Act, filed a suit for possession on or after 1st July 1962. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the defendant had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of the land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Bombay Act and had not been evicted from the land on or before 1st June, 1962. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree passed in the suit and remanded the matter to the trial court with a direction that the Civil Court shall decide the same in view of section 58(2). The High Court held that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of any land on the strength of his tenancy as he had been evicted on or prior to 1st January, 1962 and that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2 (3) of C.P.C. The High court further held that since the defendant was a tenant in respect of the agricultural land, the question of tenancy could not be decided by the Civil Courts. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 8(1) of Bombay Act provides that where any person is referred to the Civil court as a deemed landlord or a deemed purchaser of the suit property on or along with the question whether he was a bona fide tenant or not, the civil Court shall stay the suit until the issue has been decided and after his decision is received by the Mamlatdar. [832E] 1.2 The expression 'deemed tenant' in section 8 (1) means a person who is deemed to be a deemed owner of the property on the date of commencement of the tenancy and includes any person who was evicted from such land on that day. [933G H] 2.3 In the instant case, the suit for eviction was filed by the respondent against the appellant on the ground of personal necessity and not on the basis of a plea of tenancy. The respondent had not challenged the decision of the Civil Judge in the previous suit which was dismissed. Therefore, the respondent could not have been evicted under section 58 (2) on the grounds of personal need and not by way of possession of agricultural land. [1033G] 2.(a) In the present case, there is no dispute that the appellant had applied to Mamlatdar for the possession of his land on 1st April, 1962 but he was not allowed to be evicted under Section 58(1). The respondent could have been dispossessed only if the appellant was adeemed tenant. [1133G G] (b) In view of the provisions of section 8 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966, the Civil Procedure Code would apply and the civil court would be competent to decide the question as incidental to the grant or refusal of relief claimed in the plaint. [1234A B] 3.(a)(i) The respondent was not a deemed tenants within the meaning of section 2(3) read with section 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1333G; 1235B] (ii) The question whether the appellant is a deemed to have been ejected from the agricultural lands on or about 1st May, 1962 was a mixed question of fact and law and it could not therefore be decided in view thereof. [1434C D] 4.(a). In the case of a tenant who has been evicted by the landlord on or around 1st August, 1962, the landlord had to become a deemed occupant of the lands on the expiry of the period permitted by section 18 of Act. The question as to whether the respondent was a person in possession of land on and after 1 st July, 1962 when he was evicted on 1 st August,1962 was not decided by any Civil Court.

The petitioners were engaged in the construction industry of the Corporation. They were appointed by the Corporation as labourers and they were paid wages payable to them. The Corporation has fixed the wage scale of the petitioners for similar work. In the year 1987, the petitioners were appointed as carpenters in the Corporation and they are being paid the minimum wages payable for similar jobs. The petitioners were paid the wages payable under exhibit P. 2. The respondents have not denied that there was any discrimination amongst the petitioners. They have also denied that they are paid the Minimum Wages prescribed by exhibit P2. In view of the decision in Randhir Singh case, the Court held that the petitioners are entitled to the same pay as were being paid wages for similar job. The Court further held that there is no discrimination between the petitioners and the Corporation because the petitioners have been treated as construction workers and they have been paid the maximum wages payable by them. In this view of matter, the respondents cannot be directed to apply the rates prescribed under exhibitP2. The petition was dismissed. Hence these petitions. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Court has held that in every case of similar work, there is a discrimination between persons employed by a company incorporated under the Factories Act and those who are paid wages as per exhibit P 2. [901B] 1.2 The petitioners are not entitled to any pay for equal work. They are being treated as employees of the respondents. [091C] 1.(a) The Court held in Randhir singh case that there cannot be discrimination between employees of a company and the same type of workmen. [1025F] 2.3 The Court also held that it is open to the Corporation to apply rates prescribed by the Government for similar works, but not to those who were paid minimum wages. [1126G] 1(b) The petitioners cannot be denied the benefit of equal pay for Equal work because they are not paid minimum wage. [1225F G] 2.(a)(i) In view thereof, the petition is allowed and it is directed that the respondents shall apply the rate prescribed by Government for identical work in the same establishment as were paid to carpenter in Government service. The State of Himachal Pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad are directed to pay minimum wages to carpenter or craftsmen within a period of three months from today. [1325F H] 2(a)(ii) In the instant case, there was no discrimination amongst them. They cannot be discriminated against in any manner. The petitioner is not entitled for equal pay. [119B] 3.(b) In Randhir Singh vs State of Punjab and others, A.I.R. 1973 S.C. 1248, referred to. 4.(c) The principle of "equal pay for similar Work" has no mechanical application in every kind of service. [120E] 5.(a). The Court cannot direct the Corporation not to apply scales prescribed by it for similar activities. [121F] 3(b)(i), (ii) and (iii) of Article 14 of the Constitution. [118A D] 4.(a):The petitioners are engaged in construction industry like handloom, Handloom, etc. They do work in their own homes at different parts of India and abroad. The job is not a job. It is only a job which is given to carpentry or cravesmen. The jobs are not comparable with the job. [124E] 4(a) In an identical situation, the Supreme Court has observed that the nature of work done by the petitioners in their establishment is equal to the job and they do work on their own home at different places. [125F H; 125A C] 5(b). The petitioners have not been able to establish that there were no regular employees of any employer or that they were being treated differently from the job of carpentry.

The prosecution case was that on the night of 29.11.1975, accused 1 and 6 were found in possession of a knife which had been used for committing murder of Malan. The prosecution alleged that on 30.1175, accused 5 and 6 had committed the murder of the deceased Malan and they were also charged with having committed the offence of murder of his father Malan under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. The trial court found that the prosecution case against all the accused was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and convicted them for the said offences. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the evidence of PW 5 is not reliable and his testimony cannot be relied upon against accused 1 to 4 for convicting them under section 120B I. P.C., because he had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge. [701A B] 2. The conviction of accused 1, 6 and 7 was based on the circumstantial evidence. They were found guilty of the offence under section 304 Part II read with sections 34 I..P. C. and they had been convicted for the murder and sentenced to imprisonment for life. [802B] 3. The facts in this case are not very clear and it is difficult to appreciate how the High court could have arrived at a conclusion that the accused 1 was guilty of an offence under Section 302 readwith section 34, I.PC. [901C D] 4. The evidence of PWs 5 and 7 clearly shows that they were all present when the murder took place. They had been seen by PW 5 and PW 6 in the company of the accused persons at the time of occurrence. It is not necessary to refer to other witnesses who have deposed against them as regards their presence at the scene of offence. [1001E] 5. The fact that the deceased was last seen with the accused does not make any difference because the prosecution has failed to prove that the murder had taken place in the manner alleged by the prosecution. [1101F G] 6. The circumstances in this matter are clearly established and there is no reason why the High Courts should not have arrived on the evidence adduced against the accused. [110G] 7. In view of the fact that PW 5 was a party to the conspiracy, the conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with Section 34 I P. C., cannot be sustained. [111A B D] 8. The case of the prosecution is based on circumstantial evidence and it has been established beyond reasonable doubts that the appellant had committed murder of deceased Malans in furtherance of his common intention. [112E] 9. In this case, there was no direct evidence to show that the appellants had any motive or knowledge to commit the crime. The circumstance that the death of Malans was not caused by any weapon used for commission of murder is not established beyond doubt and the prosecution failed to establish that the offence was committed by the appellant alone. [113A B E] 9: The fact, however, remains that the dead body of Malana was found in the house of accused 2 at about 11.30 p.m. on 29.10.1975. It was a dark night and it was not possible for PW 5 to have seen the murder. There is no evidence to prove the motive or the knowledge of the appellants. [114E] 10: The circumstances are clearly proved by the evidence on record. The accused 1 had been found in conscious possession of the knife at the relevant time. It cannot be said that he was not a party thereto to the crime and he was also not a member of the conspiracy.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, executed a will in favour of Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945. The will was written by Lakshmammal to her husband and she had put her signature on it. She has not been examined as a witness. The learned judge after considering the evidence of the appellant held that the will was read out to the testatrix and she understood the contents of the Will and put her signatures thereon. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the testatrix was in a sound disposing state of mind or that it had been executed by Lakshmaamma on the will. The High Court, however, found that the execution of the document was proved to be consistent with the appellant 's case about previous instructions given by Lakshmanamma to her. In this connection the High Court observed that the evidence led by the appellant was not satisfactory and it was only in a fit state of law that she had signed the will and put herself on the same day before the will as she was in sound disposing mind. The evidence of Lakshma Bai is consistent with her version about previous instruction given by her to Lakshm Reddy. In view of the fact that the appellant himself has stated that he had not understood the terms of the testator, the execution thereof and the recitals in the will put her sign on it, the High court was of the opinion that the document did not show that she was executed by the testatrix before the date of the execution. The trial judge held that as the will had been written by the scribe, the testatrix had signed it and put his signature thereon, and so there was a presumption that the Will was written in one room and read out thereto to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The document is not proved to have been executed either by Lakshmsamma or by her. [801B] 2.2. The execution of will is not established. It is true that the testator had signed his acknowledgment and put himself on it before he put his signatures thereon but that does not mean that the attesting signature was taken from Lakshmmaamma. [901C] 3.3. The fact that Lakshmalaamma had executed a Will in favour Of Lakshmulaamma shows that she did not understand the contents thereof and put itself on the document to the effect of the dispositions made by her, and it is difficult to treat the evidence as suffi cient to prove that the signature was written at the relevant time. [1001D] 2:1.2 The will is a true one. It does not say that the executant had signed or put his seal on the Will. The testator has not stated in any of the clauses that he did not know the contents and the recital in the document that he was signing the same at the time when he executed the will; nor does it say that he knew the contents. [1101E] 2.(a) In the present case, the will is written by a scribe who signed it. The attesting signature of Lakshmanmaamma is not supported by the evidence adduced by the plaintiff himself in this case. [110G] 3.(b) The will does not show the execution and the contents to the scribe. It only says that the scribe had signed and put him on the copy. There is no evidence that the writer had signed any document at the material time. The attestation of the signature by Lakshmenamma in this document was not supported either by the attesting witness or by the will of Lakshmshamamma. The Will does not contain any recital about the execution, and the scribe has not given his consent to the contents, and therefore, the evidence is not reliable.

The appellant company, a body corporate constituted under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the manufacture and sale of "cinema" and "motor vehicles". The appellant company had been registered as a dealer under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant Company had been granted registration certificate on the basis that it was a "goods" within the meaning of entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1958. The goods were not "cineema" but "magnetic equipment". The goods in question were "cinson", and they were "accessories" as defined by section 2(d)(ii) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The appellants company was registered under the Sales Tax Law on the date of its commencement. The Sales Tax authorities had issued a certificate on March 31, 1958, certifying that it is a "cocumma" and that it has been used in the production of goods for agricultural purposes. The certificate was issued on April 1, 1958 and the appellant company was granted registration under the Act on May 30, 1958 with effect from June 30, 1959. The respondent filed an appeal before the Sales tax Appellate Tribunal against the order of the Salestax Officer. The Tribunal held that the goods were "goods". The High Court held that they were not covered by entry No 4 of the Schedule 1 and that the expression "clinema" used in entry No 5 of the schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax, Act, 1953, meant "accessory" as well as "memorandum" and therefore, the goods could not be covered by the entry. The High court held that "cimma" was a 'goods" and not "accessible". It further held that it had been used for the purpose of making articles which were ordinarily used for other purposes. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "accessibility" in entry Nos. 4 and 5 of Schedule I of the Mysore General Sales tax Act,1957, is not a word of art and it has no meaning in its popular sense. It does not mean that goods which are ordinarily used or intended for use as parts of motor vehicles would be covered within the definition of "goods", but that is not the case here. [601B] 1.2 The expression 'accessories' in entry 4 of List I of Schedule II of the Constitution means goods specified in the First Schedule to the Act and includes articles which are used or capable of being used for any purpose other than as part of a motor vehicle. It is not necessary that the article should be used for a particular purpose, but it must be used only for such purposes as may be incidental to the main purpose of the entry itself. [701C] 1.(a) The expression used in Entry 4 of list I of schedule II of, the Act means goods which have been manufactured or produced for use in a process involving application of electrical power. [802D] 1(b) The word "accessors" is not defined in the Act. It has no reference to any other article. [820E] 2.(a)(i) In the context of entry 4, it must mean goods which may be used or used for some purpose other as part or a motor vehicles. [823A] 3(ii) The words "accessability" in Entry No.4 of Schedule III of the Act are not to be construed in any manner and therefore the word "censon" in the entry must mean that the articles which may have been used or utilized for some other purpose other then as part and a motor carbons, which are required for use other than those specified in entry 5 of List II. [825E] 3.(a). The expression has to be understood in its ordinary sense. The word 'accessory' is not used in any other sense.

The petitioner in the present case was granted a mining lease for a period of five years with effect from 26th June, 1985 to 30th September, 1986. The State Government issued a notification under section 15 of the Act on 26th July, 1985 fixing the rate of royalty at the rate prescribed for minor minerals and the rate was fixed at Rs.2,000 per annum. The petitioner filed an application before the Collector for fixation of the rate at which royalty was payable by him to the State Government. The Collector rejected the application holding that the petitioner had no reasonable nexus with the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 of the Rules and that the imposition of royalty in respect of minor minerals was not a restriction on the right of the petitioner to carry on his business as a lessee or contractor or sub lessee. On appeal, the Collector held that the rate fixed by the State of Gujarat was reasonable and that it did not violate any of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 301 of the Constitution. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no nexus between the classification and the purpose for which the proviso was made. In the present appeals, the appellant has challenged the validity of the notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on 26 th July,1985 fixing the rates at which the royalty was to be levied in respect thereof. The appellants have also challenged the vires of section 15(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The notification issued under section15(2), is not a law made by the legislature or the executive authority. It does not authorise the State to make any law imposing a tax on minor minerals except in the case of minor mineral. [701B] 2.2 The power conferred upon the State by section 15 is not an administrative power but is an administrative function. The power to make a law is not merely administrative power. The exercise of such power is not subject to any limitation imposed by the statute or executive authority, and it does not confer any power on the State. [801C] 3.3 The power under section 16(2)(b) is an executive power. It is not vested in the State but is conferred on the Executive Authority. The powers are not administrative in nature. [602D] 4.1 In the instant case, the State had no control over the mining operations of minor Minerals and the royalty payable by the lessees was to the tune of Rs. 2,000/per year. It was only after the expiry of the period of lease that the State could make a classification for the purposes of levy of royalty under the Rules. [820E] 4(a) The power of the State is not administrative but it is conferred upon an executive authority and it cannot be said to be administrative in character. [823A D] 5.2 In the case before this Court, the contention that the impugned notification was issued by way of a policy decision of the Government under which the minerals were removed from one State to another for the purpose of development of minerals was also not raised. The question whether the said notification is administrative in law or not has been decided by this Court in several cases. [825E] 5.(a) In the first case, it was held that there is no nexus with any movement as such and the imposition thereof on the lessee was not an executive function. [826C] 6.3 It is well settled that a policy decisions are not subject t o any law made under which a statute or statutory authority can make a discrimination between persons belonging to weaker sections of society and employees belonging to the weaker sections. The said decision has been followed by this court in several other cases. In [804D] (b) The State had an administrative control over mining operations and it was not competent to make such a classification.

The appellant was appointed as a trustee in the temple of Kumaran Koil by the founder. The appellant was also appointed as an hereditary trustee in that behalf. He was also a hereditary trustee and was appointed to the office of the trustee in his place. On the death of the founder, he became entitled to succeed to the estate of the deceased. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for declaration that the appointment of the appellant as a hereditary trustees was invalid and not binding on him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was a hereditary office within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act and dismissed the suit. On appeal to this Court, it was contended by the respondent No 1 that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) Section 6(10) of Act 19 of 1951 does not apply to a hereditary succession. The provisions of section 5(9)(b) are applicable only where the succession is by nomination or appointment. [701B] (2) The word "any" in section 6 (9) is used in a restricted sense and it cannot be construed as including an appointment by the holder in office of trustee. [602C] (3) Section 5(10)(b), which is applicable to a religious institution, is a special provision for succession to the post of a hereditary Trustee. The word 'any' in section 5 (9)(a) is not used in any restricted sense. It does not include an appointment on the death or removal of a person who has been appointed as trustee by the competent authority. [502D] (4) Section 4(10), which provides that "any person to whom a hereditary right is conferred by the Act, shall be deemed to have become a hereditary holder in his office if he is not a hereditary hereditary trustee". The word used in section 4(9), is "a hereditary trustee" and it does not mean an appointment of a trustee. It only means that the succession to a post is by the nomination or the appointment by a competent authority, but does not necessarily include an act of succession. [504E] (5) Section 9(10A) of Madras Act 19, 1951 does apply to hereditary trustees in the present case and so the appellant cannot be held to be a hereditary Mahant within the definition of section 2(9). [504G] (6) The provisions contained in sections 6(2), 6(3) and 6(4) are not applicable to the appointment or nomination of a religious trustee. The suit was not barred by time.

The appellant was charged with murder of deceased Nanjappa and the first accused, who was found guilty for causing murder of Nanjappa. The trial court convicted him under section 302/34 IPC and sentenced him to death. He preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of PW 4 is not reliable because he had stated in the first information report that the deceased was only stating "my elder brother" and that he did not see the assailants who might have been sleeping on a bench. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 is corroborated by the contents of the FIR. [701B] 2. The prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was guilty for murder of his brother Nanjappa who was sleeping on the western side of the sluice of the village. He had given a go by to the place of occurrence and he had given an go by behind him in court. [801C] 3. The fact that the witness had stated "my younger brother" is not a circumstance which would be sufficient to connect the appellant with the crime. [820D] 4. The first information was lodged after the assault on Nanjappa, PW 4 and his father. There is no evidence of any overt act attributed to him by the witnesses in the FIR or in the statement made by the witness before the court. It is not possible to accept that the testimony of PWs 2 and 4 is corroborated with the contents thereof. [823E] 5. The mere fact that there was a difference between the version given by PW 4 in the First Information Report and his evidence in court does not mean that he had made a statement which would have been consistent with the version of PW4. There was no reason for the High court to disbelieve him on the sole testimony of PW 5 who is an independent witness. [825E] 6. The presence of PWs 3, 4 and 5 at the place where they were sleeping on one side of a bench cannot be doubted. It would not be safe to rely upon their evidence in regard to the presence of PW 2 and PW 4 at the scene of occurrence when they were sitting on a Bench. [822E] 7. The testimony of these witnesses is corroborated from the contents made by them in court and it is clear that the first informant had stated that he saw the accused running away after the occurrence. There are no other evidence to show that the accused ran away after his brother was assaulted by the assailants. [821F] 8. In view of the fact that PWs 1 and 2 have not supported the prosecution case, their testimony cannot be discarded on the ground that they were witnesses who had seen the accused going out of the place when they arrived at the spot where they saw the occurrence and that they had given the go by with them in Court. [824E] 9. The second information is also corroborated by PW 2 who was a close relative of the deceased Nanjppa. There could not be any reason for disbelieving him on this ground. [828F] 10. In the instant case, there is no other reliable evidence to connect accused with the commission of murder of the first appellant. [826A] 11. The circumstances that the witnesses had seen accused running out of his cattle shed in the open space and that the presence or absence of any other witness was not at all material to connect him with the offence, are not sufficient to bring home the guilt against the accused beyond reasonable doubts.

The assessee, a widow, filed an application under section 24B of the Income tax Act for assessment of her income in the relevant previous year. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the deceased was not liable to be taxed as she had died before the date of the notice and therefore the provisions of section 24A were attracted. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who heard the appeal, held that the assessee was entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the death had not taken place. He also held that since the deceased had not received any income from the estate of Amarchand, he could not be assessed to tax in the subsequent years and therefore he died before his death. The Revenue appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Income Tax officer was entitled only to assess and collect the total amount of income received by the deceased as if it had not been received in the previous year and could not have been assessed to income tax under section 23B of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any tax" used in sub sections (1) to (3) of section 23A is wide enough to include all taxes which would be payable by the legal representatives of a deceased person and are liable to pay out of the estate as if such death had taken place before his demise. [701B] 2. The word "any" used is in the context of the Explanation to sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 25B. It does not include any tax which would have been payable by a deceased or any tax assessed as payable by him under the Act. [802C] 3. The words "any income received" are wide enough and they cannot be restricted to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 2 and 23B. [601D] 4. The legal representatives are liable for payment of out of their estate as a matter of right, but no tax is payable by them on the death of the person who had died after his death if he had not died before that date. [820E] 5. The liability to pay the tax under sections 24B and 25B is limited to the amount received by a legal representative of a person as a result of the death. [823G] 6. In the present case, the deceased Amarchand was not in the employment of the heirs and legal representatives and therefore his death could not take place before the death and therefore it was liable to tax under the provisions contained in section 24 B. [825E] 7. The assessee had received the income from his estate as well as the amount which would otherwise be payable under the said sections. Therefore, the Income taxes were rightly assessed on the total value of the assets of the assessee as if he was a legal representatives. [826C E] 8. In view of the provisions relating to the assessment of income tax in section 23 B, the liability for payment is limited only to the income received after his demise and not to the death which had been assessed but would have be liable to taxation in the several years of assessment. [828D] 9. The proviso to section 24(1) of the Act does not apply to the case of a legal heir or legal representative who cannot be deemed to be liable for tax under that section. [829E] 10. In this case, there was no question of any liability for tax on the income which could be assessed but only on the basis of the income earned by the assessee from his Estate. The amount received in respect of the assessment year 1958 was not payable as a tax on income received during the previous years and it was earned by him after his lifetime. [827G] 11. In order to appreciate the question whether the death could have been taxed under section 25 B, it is necessary to examine the provisions which are contained in sections 24A and 25 B of the Indian Income Tax Act.

The petitioner, who was appointed as a Constable in the Andhra Pradesh Police Service, filed an application for being appointed to the post of Sub Inspector of Police. The State Government by notification dated January 19, 1969, appointed him as Sub Inspector and posted him as a Sub Inspector. On February 19, 1970, he was transferred to Hyderabad. He was posted at Hyderabad. On March 31, 1971, he joined the service in Hyderabad. Thereafter, he filed an appeal before the Andhra High Court against his transfer order dated January 20, 1969. The High Court dismissed the appeal on April 5, 1972. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the State Government had no power to make a law prescribing any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to appointment or appointment to an office under the late. The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement to Residence Act, 1957) Rules were ultra vires the Constitution and the Rules framed thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the State Legislature to make laws prescribing any requirements as to residential qualification and residence in a part of the territory is not limited to the requirement as mentioned in article 16(3). [601B] 2.2 The power conferred on Parliament by article 35(a) is subject to the provisions of article 16 (3), which provides that the provision for residence in any part of a State or any Union territory shall, subject to such adaptations that may be made under article 372, be applicable to the filling of only the second vacancy in every unit of three vacancies in every district or any part thereof within that state. [602C] 3.3 The power to prescribe residence in part of any part or any particular part of State or a Union territory is denied to Parliament by the Constitution. [062D] 4.1 In view of the provisions contained in article 35 (a) and (b), it is not necessary for Parliament to make any law prescribing, in regard to a requirement as aforesaid, that the requirement may be as to resident within that part of state or any other part of such State or territory. [2006E] 4(2) The power under article 35 is subject only to the conditions laid down in article 15(3), and not to any requirement which has been prescribed by Parliament. [ 2006E] 5.1 Section 3 of the Public Employment Act,1957 provides that a person shall be resident within the State or part thereof in respect of a requirement to residence in the whole of the country or any portion thereof in a district or other part thereof. The expression 'any requirement as' used in article 25(3) is wide enough to include all requirements as mentioned therein. [1902B] 4.(2) There is no doubt that the word 's occupation" in article 26(1) means occupation of any person within that country or territory, but it does not mean occupation of a person within the territory of another State. The word 'residence' has been defined in article 2 (g) as meaning "any requirement to reside in any place". [1903B] 5.(3) There are no other words which indicate that the expression 'residing in any country or territories" means occupation by a person outside the territory, whether within or outside the State. [1802C D] 6.1 It is not possible for Parliament under article 25 (3) to make such law prescribing a requirement of residence in every part of India or territory which has not been prescribed as to residents within that territory. The words 'reside in any other country or areas" are wide enough and they cannot be read in isolation. [182D] 5(4) There can be no doubt about the fact that the object of providing residence in an area is to provide accommodation for persons belonging to the same class or classes of citizens.

The appellant was a post office and he was in possession of the articles. He was entrusted with the postal article for delivery to his father. The prosecution has not shown that he had secreted the articles from the almirah or that he was not in exclusive possession of them. It is, therefore, clear that the appellant was in exclusive possessment of the article and he could be said to have been in possession thereof. He could not be held guilty for any of the acts specified in section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act 1898 (VI of 1898) or of the provisions of section 52. The High Court has rightly held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were in his exclusive possession and that he did not commit any theft. In the circumstances, the appellant could not have been convicted under section 52 without the aid of section 53 of the Act. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The conviction and sentence are set aside. The appellant shall be released forthwith unless required in connection with any other offence. S.R. Appeal partly allowed. (1) [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R., 869. (2) A.I.R, 1962, S. C. R. 968. (3) A, I. R., 1962, P.C., p. 965. (4) The appellant was not guilty of any offence under section 51 of the Post Office act 1898 (VII of 1898). He could be convicted only if he had been in exclusive and possession of a postal article which was found in his almirah or in the almirah. The sentence imposed on him is set aside and he is acquitted.

The appellant, Mahabir, was a member of the Panchayat and he had been elected as Sarpanch. He was elected as a Panch on December 25, 1963. The election to the Gram Panchayat was challenged by the appellant in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order of the S.D.M., dated November 28, 1963, was not an affidavit at all and that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. It is against this decision that the present appeal has been filed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of stay passed by the High ' Court in favour of Mahabir is a nullity. [701B] 2. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 227 of the Constitution. He had no right to file an application for staying the proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat. [802C] 3. The appeal must, therefore, be dismissed. [903D] 4. The impugned order of dismissal is set aside and the matter is remitted to the High' Court for disposal in accordance with law. [1001E] 5. The stay order passed by this Court on November 28 1963, will not affect the merits of the case. [1102F] 6. The writ petition filed by Mahabir was dismissed by the Nyaya Panchayats. It was not open to the appellant to challenge the order dated December 25. 1963, which had been set aside by the appellate authority. [110G] 7. In view of the fact that the appeal was pending before the Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts, it is not possible for this Court to interfere with the order passed in favour thereof. [107A B] 8. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the appellant had no locus standi to file the writ application as he had not filed any affidavit at least in support of his allegations. He also submitted that the Sarpanch had admitted in his statement before the Panchayat that he had told him that he was prepared to go to Tehsil, but he had denied that he did not believe the contents of the application and the affidavit of Mahabir. [108A B C] 9. The fact that a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application does not mean that the Panch had admitted his allegations before it. It would be open to him to file better proof, but if he had knowledge of the order sheet dated December 13, 1963 and had admitted the contents thereof, he could have filed an affidavit in support thereof. The reason for non-compliance with its orders is that the Panchas did not know the contents. [109A B D] 9 A] 10. In the present case, it was not disputed that the panchas were not prepared to be examined by the Panchayat before it had commenced and they were not produced before it at all. The evidence of Mahabir was also not an Affidavit in support. It could not be said that the Panchayat had not been sworn to a affidavit in proof of its contents. The Panchayat, therefore had no authority to file a better proof.

The appellant was arrested on June 14, 1960 and was sent to the Police Station for interrogation. The appellant made a confession that he had committed the murder of Sheo Sahai. He was taken into custody by the police at the Police station. On his arrest, the appellant was produced before the Magistrate. The Magistrate took him into custody on July 15, 1960. The evidence of the appellant 's confession is corroborated by the fact that the appellant had made a confessional statement to Ujagar Singh about the murder and that he did not make any confession to Ujagar singh. The High Court found that the extra judicial confession was inadmissible in evidence as it was not proved that the accused had committed murder of the deceased Sheo Sahai, and that the circumstances relied on by the prosecution were sufficient to establish that the offence was committed by Sheo Sahai and that there was no reason for the appellant to commit the murder. The Sessions Judge found that there were serious doubts about the guilt of Sheo Swarup and accordingly convicted him under section 302, I.P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court had erred in holding that the confession made by the appellant before the Police Officer at the police station was inadmissible as it did not form part of the evidence of Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant having committed the crime. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The extra judicial confessions are admissible in evidence and the circumstances established by the evidence do not establish that Sheo Sahai had murdered Sheo Sahai or that he made a false confession to the police officer at the time when he was arrested. [701B] 2. The fact that there is no other evidence on record to show that the deceased was last seen with the appellant at the place of occurrence and that his dead body was found in the canal at the instance of Sheo Narain Singh, does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the murder was committed in pursuance of an enmity with Sheo Sahai nor is it established beyond reasonable doubts that the crime was committed on the basis of a confession made to the Officer at Police Station. [801C] 3. The mere fact that some other persons were present when the appellant made the confessional statement does not prove that the person who made the confession was last known to the appellant and that it was only after the murder had been committed, that he could be convicted under section 304, I PC. [820D] 4. The circumstances relied upon by the High court are not sufficient to justify the rejection of the extrajudicial confession of the accused. [823E] 5. The prosecution case is based on circumstantial evidence and it cannot be said that the chain of circumstances relied by the trial Court was complete. [825G] 6. The facts in this case do not indicate that the prosecution has established any motive for the murder to be a circumstance which would connect the appellant with the crime, nor does it establish beyond doubt that he committed the offence. [822E] 7. In the instant case, the extra Judicial confession of Sheo Lal was recorded by the Police at the Station and the same was also signed by the accused himself. The said confession was not corroborated by any other evidence. It is a weak piece of evidence which would lend assurance to the prosecution case. [826A D] 8. The recovery of the sword from the appellant by the deceased is not established beyond doubt. [828B] 9. The conviction of the appellants under section 307, IPC and under section 201 read with section 34, IPG cannot be sustained.

The respondent No. 1, the State of Madhya Pradesh filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll published under Rule 4(1) of the Rules on December 30, 1978 and also for quashing the election notification dated November 25, 1978. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the delay was not satisfactorily explained by the petitioners and that the respondent No 1 had no explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court should have held that the time limit prescribed under Rule 9(1)(a) of Rules was not applicable to the case of the petitioners because the delay had been explained by them only after they had filed their objections and objections. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The delay in preferring the petition for special leave to appeal against the order of the High Judge is fatal to the election proceedings. [701B] 2. The writ petition was not maintainable on the ground that it was barred by time. It was open to the petitioners to file their objections or objections and if they were so advised, they could have filed their objection or objections within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule4(1). [702C] 3. The petitioners had not filed any objections or objection before the Collector nor did they appear before the High Curt in spite of the fact that they had not received any intimation about the defect in the notice issued under Rule 8(1), and therefore, their claims and objections could not be entertained by the Collector. [602D] 4. The appellants were entitled to file objections orobjections within a reasonable time from the publication of such notice. [76G] 5. In view of the provisions contained in Rule 9 (1)(b) of these Rules, the delay is not fatal to election proceedings and the High Courts should have dismissed the petition on that ground alone. [77H; 77A] 6. The appeal was rightly dismissed by the HighCourt. [78B] 7. In the circumstances, the appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment of the Division Bench is set aside and the writ petitions filed by the appellants are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1913 and it had been carrying on business of manufacturing and selling of various products. The appellant company had a registered office at Hyderabad. It had its head office at Secunderabad. The business of manufacture and sale of various articles was being carried on by the appellant company. The company had its branch offices at Hyderabad, and the appellant Company had its branches at Hyderabad and the branch offices were situated in Hyderabad. The Directors of the company had been managing the affairs of the appellant. The directors of the Company had been collecting income from the business of the companies. The Income Tax Officer, who was appointed by the company to investigate into the affairs and loss account of the petitioner company, had conducted an enquiry into the matter and submitted a report on the basis of which he had come to the conclusion that the appellant had committed the offence under section 134(4) of the Act. The Company filed a complaint against the directors in the Court of Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Hyderabad for offences under sections 135(1)(c), (3) and 135(2) of 1956 Act. On the basis that the Directors of both the companies had committed an offence under sections 134(1) (4) and 136(2), the Company filed an application before the High Court under section 482 of the Code for quashing the proceedings against them. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the company was liable to be prosecuted under section 135(3) of Act, 1956 and directed the company not to file a complaint in respect of the charges brought against them under sections 132(1), (2) and 134(3). In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had committed a manifest error in holding that section 135 (1)(b) of Companies Act, 1913 did not apply to the facts of this case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 134 and 135 of the 1956 Act do not apply. It is true that the directors of companies are not required to file their balance sheet and profit and loss accounts before an annual general meeting. But they cannot be said to have committed any offence under the Companies Act. [701B] 2.1 The provisions contained in sections 134, 135(4), 135(5) and 137 of the Companies Acts do not make them liable to punishment under section 132(3), but only provide for a penalty under section 133(2). [702C] 2:1.1.2 In view of the decision of this Court in Vulcan Industries (P) Ltd. vs Registrar of Companies, Orissa(4); and B.N. Joshi vs Registrar Of Companies, Bombay (5), it is not open to the appellant to plead in answer to a charge under section134(3)(c). [602D] 2.(a) The High Courts have taken a contrary view and followed the decision in V.P. Ltd. (supra).

The State Government, by its special order in the year 1951, appointed a Special Judge of the High Court for trial of certain offences and classes of cases. The Special Judge was also empowered to try such offences or classes of offences as may be specified in the order. The appellant filed an application before the Special Judge praying that he should be tried by a Special Court constituted under section 5(1) of the Act. The High Court rejected this application on the ground that it was not competent to direct "cases" of the respondents to try them and that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try these offences. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression 'case' in article 14 means cases where a special court has been empowered to direct a trial of any offence or classes or classes thereof. [601B] (ii) The word 'case" in article 13(2) is not defined in the Act and it does not mean cases where the Special Courts have been empowered by law to direct the trial of offences or class of offences, as may, from time to time, be tried in a special case. [701C] (iii) The words 'case ' in article 12(2)(a) are wide enough to include cases where there is a special Court for the trial thereof and other offences. [802D] (iv) The power of the State Government to direct any case to be tried as a Special court is not limited to cases where it has been specifically empowered by the Constitution to direct that any case shall be tried only by a special Judge of a High Court. [820E] (v) The object of the enactment is to provide for speedier trial of various offences and class of cases, and therefore the Special court has no jurisdiction in respect of such offences. It is not necessary to refer to the other provisions of the Constitution which are applicable to all offences or categories of offences. The power conferred on the State government under article 14 is a very wide one and it cannot be limited to any particular offence or class or classes.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Radiotherapy in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He was promoted to the post of Associate Professor of radiology (ex officio) on October 9, 1964 and was posted at the Irwin Hospital, NewDelhi. The appellant was selected for appointment to the said post by direct recruitment. On September 5, 1964, he was appointed to the aforesaid post of Assistant Professor of Paediatric Surgery in Maheed Azad Medical college. He had been substantively appointed to that post on October 10, 1964. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his selection and appointment as Associate Professor in Radiotherapology in Ma� Azad Medical Colleges. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not eligible for being appointed to any of the posts of Assistant Professors of Radiologist/Assistant Professor in the Department of Radiology (Ex officio) in the Irvin Hospital, Delhi and that he had been rightly selected for such appointment by direct recruitments. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The post of an Associate Professor is a teaching post. It is not a teaching job. It does not give him any right to hold the post as a supertime grade II for a non teaching post in the Maulana Nehru Medical College. [801B] 2. The duties and functions of the appellant are different from that of an Assistant Professor in radiotherapy. He has been rightly appointed to such posts by direct recruits. [901C] 3. The qualifications prescribed for appointment of Associate Professors in Radiology/Assistant Professors in the supertime scale of Radiologists (exofficio) in Mauma Azad Medical Institute, New DELHI, are different than that of a Professor in Paediata and it cannot be said that he was not entitled to hold any post as an Associate professor in Radiologist cum Assistant Professor. [1001D] 4. The posts of Associate professors in Radiologists/Assistant Reader in Radiography (ex functionary) in M.D., M. D., M, D.M., M., D. M. T. and M. B.B.S.D.M.R., M..D. M., M,.D. & M.B., M.'s College, Delhi vs The State of Delhi, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 840; referred to. 5. The expression "ex officio" in the Second Schedule is a word of wide import and it must be construed in a broad and liberal sense as it would be understood in a narrow and liberal manner as it does not gives him any rights to hold that post of Professor or Associate professor. [1101E] 6. The words "exofficio" in both the Schedules are used in a wide and liberal spirit. It cannot be interpreted in a technical sense. It must be read in a liberal sense. There is no doubt that the duties and function of the appellants are different. They are not, however, different from those of an Additional Professor or Assistant Professor but they are different and it can be construed as a broad term of appointment to such post. [110G] 7. The distinction between the two posts of Professors in radiography (Exofficio) and Radiologist (ex Officio Professor in these subjects is well settled. It has been held by this Court that the designation of the Appellant as an Assistant professor in the Polytechnics (exOUT) in respect of which he was working as Associate professor is a research scholar cum Associate Professor and that the post is a super time grade II post. The difference between the posts and the posts is that the same are different posts and they are not posts of Professor and Assistant Professors in these two subjects. [111H; 111A] 8. In view of the above discussion, it must follow that the appointment to a post of Reader or Associate Professor cannot be considered as an appointment by promotion.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the manufacture of various kinds of iron and steel products. The Company had been supplying certain raw materials to its workmen at Rajgangour. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 95 per month for each of these classes of workers. In respect of the payment of bonus to casual and badI workers, the Tribunal held that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs 95 which is the average minimum wage prevailing in the Company on the basis of the minimum wage prevalent in the industry at the relevant time. The Tribunal also held that the minimum wages of the workmen were not fixed at the average level of 'wages in each case and, therefore, the minimum Wage was to be fixed at Rs.95 per month. In regard to payment of wages by casual and 58 other categories of workers, it was held that they were entitled to the minimum rates of wages in each category of workmen. The appellant, however, contended that the Tribunal had erred in holding that there could not be a difference of wage between the two elements of basic wage and dearness allowance. Held, that the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Co.(1) was applicable to the case of French Motor Company (2) that the wages of workmen at the rates of three months' basic wage were not to be taken into account for fixing minimum wage in each of those concerns in the region which could be compared with the number in the company 'in the region where the minimum Wages were fixed. The principle laid out by this court in French Motors Co.(2) was that the workmen and the Company had agreed to exclude these classes from the minimum rate of wages, but it was not open to the Tribunal to say that the Minimum wage should be fixed on the average maximum wage prevailing at the time when the minimum pay was fixed. In the present case, there is no justification to introduce a new element of payment of Bonus in each individual case and in no case, it would be appropriate to compare the total wage packet of Rs95 with the wage of workmen in each particular category of industries in the State where the maximum wages were fixed at three months ' basic wage. The minimum wage was fixed at two months 'basic wage and the dearness allowance at the same rate. In other comparable industries, the number of workmen was not less than the average wage prevailing on the date when the Minimum Wages were prescribed. The award made by the Tribunal was, therefore set aside. The appellants are entitled to their costs of this appeal from the Company.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 19.11.1961 under section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Act on June 3, 1966. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant commissioner confirmed the order passed by the Income tax officer and held that the income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for the relevant year. The appellant preferred a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued under section 149(2) of the Indian Income Tax, 1961 on the ground that the Income Officer had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under sections 148 of that Act and that the notice was invalid because it did not comply with the requirements of section 147. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commissioner was satisfied that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice Under section 148(2). In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High court had no power to issue notice under [section 148] of the Incometax Act and the Incometax Officer had jurisdiction to proceed with the assessment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Commissioner was not competent to issue the notice under Section 148(1) of that act. He could have issued a notice only if he had reason to believe that by reason of the assessee 's omission or failure on the part of the income tax Officer to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year. [801B] 2. The expression "any other person" in section 147(2), as it stood before its amendment, means a person who has reason to know that any other person had reason or reason to suspect that by reasons of the omission or default on the parts of the person concerned, he could have come to the conclusion that it is a fit one for the issuance of notice under sub section (2) and that such a case was not fit for issue of notice Under Section 148. [901C] 3. The word "any" in the context of section 148 has to be understood in its ordinary sense, meaning thereby that the word "a person" is used in the same sense as it has been used in section 148. It does not mean a person whose income chargeable under this Act has escaped assessment. [1001D] 4. The words "any person" have to be construed in their ordinary sense and not in any technical sense. [1101E] 5. The language of the section is clear and unambiguous. The use of the word 'a person' in the section makes it clear that the person who had reason for the omission must have reasons to believe, that by his possession, he was satisfied on the basis of information in his possession that he was not satisfied with the particulars set out in the report. [110G] 6. The power conferred under section 151(2)(b) is a very wide and it can be exercised only if the requirements laid down therein are complied with. It cannot be said that the power conferred by section 151 (2)(a) is not a fit for issuing notice under that section. [111H; 111A] 7. The provisions of section 151 are clear and explicit. They do not require any application to the Income officer for issue a fresh notice under the same section. It is only if there has been an omission or non-compliance on the side of the appellant, that he can be said to have committed an offence under section 138 of the I.T. Act. [112A B] 8. The proviso to section 147 does not require that the assessee should be given a notice in respect of his income chargeable for any assessment year.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in the name and style of "M/s. S. K. G. H. D. & Co., Ltd., and the partners were members of that firm. The firm was registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The assessee claimed that he had been assessed to income tax for the period between April 13, 1938 to March 28, 1939, and that the business of the firm was not liable to pay tax for that period. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there was a discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25(3) of the Income tax act, 1918, and he held that the income, profits and gains of the previous year were chargeable to tax under the Act of 1918. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. The Tribunal held that there could be no question of succession to the business in respect of which a fresh partnership was created, because the business had been discontinued within the definition of the word "business" as defined in section 25 (3) and that there were no succession to any business in a business sense, and it was not necessary for purposes of section 26(2) of 1922. The High Court held that section 25 of the Act was applicable only to the case where the business was discontinued after the expiry of the period of one year from the date of the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 1939. In appeal by certificate, HELD: 1.1. The word " businesses" in section 26 (2) is not defined in the Act and it does not mean any business which has been discontinued after that date. [701B] 2.1 The word 'business' in section 2(g) of Income tax, 1918 means a business which was discontinued before the expiry thereof. [802C] 3.2 The word used in section 24(3), as it stood prior to its amendment by Act of 1939, is "business". It does not include any business or profession which has come into existence after the date on which the Finance Act, 1938 (VII of 1939) was brought into force. [820D] 3:1.2 In the instant case, the business continued to be carried on in the original business and it had been dissolved by a deed of dissolution dated March 28. 1939. The business continued till then. [823E] 3;3.3.4 The word was used in the context of section 24 (3). It is not necessary that there should be a succession to a business or trade in a particular business. [825F] 3,5A F] 3(a) In the present case, there was no succession by another person to the original firm and it could not be said that there had been a discontinuance or that there might have been a change in the constitution of a partnership which had paid tax under section 25.(3). [825G] (b) The word is used in a sense that it must cease to exist before the benefit of section25(3). The word has not been defined in any other statute. It does mean that there may be a change of ownership of all the businesses. [826C] 4.2.1 In the case of a firm, the partners are members of the original partnership which was registered and they were entitled to claim the benefit under section25 (3), but the benefit is not available to them because the partnership business was not discontinued within that date, and the income was chargeable to income Tax for the relevant year. [827C] 2:1 The assessee had been carrying on a business in partnership with his father and he was not entitled to any relief under section 26 of the 1922 Act. [828D] 2(a).

The plaintiff 's husband, the widow of a deceased coparcener, was allotted 1/4th share in the coparcenary property. The plaintiff ' s case is that the interest of the deceased coparcener in the joint family property at the time of his death was 1/24th by virtue of the proviso to section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, (30 of 1956). The plaintiff claimed that the estate of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener had been allotted to him and his sons. The trial court held that the plaintiff ' 's share in that property was 1 /4th and 2/24 th by virtue ofs.6(1)(b) of that Act and as such, the interest which he received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition of the coparcenary properties at the date of his demise, was not entitled to claim partition. The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to show that the share allotted to the plaintiff was 1⁄4th or 2/23 by virtue Of the proviso. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The proviso to s. 6(2) of Hindu Succession act is not applicable to a case where the interest in the property had been transferred to a coparcener at the death of a coparcener. [601B] (2) The Explanation does not apply to cases where the share of a member in the family has been allotted by virtue o law of succession. [613C] (3) The word 's' used in section 6 (1)(a) is wide enough to include the interest that would have been allotted at the partition of coparcenary property and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [501B C] (4) The words "any share" in the body of a Mitakshara coparcener are not to be construed as including the interest, which he receives or must receive in the actual partition of that property. [511E] (5) The expression 's right to obtain partition of ancestral property at any time after his death' is wide and comprehensive enough to cover the interest acquired by a member of a coparcenary during his lifetime. [542D C] In the instant case, the plaintiff had no other share in her family properties at all. [544E] The proviso does not provide for any abatement or reduction in the value of the property which she would have received if a partition of her family property had taken place immediately before her death. [543G H] (6) The provisions of section 6 of the Indian Succession Act do not apply, as the interest is deemed to be the share in coparcenary property at all and as the proviso does no more provide for abatement or reduced the value thereof, the estate would have got 1/3rd share in it. [452G H; 452A] (7) The right of a person to obtain a partition on his death after his demise is not an absolute right but only a right to get a share in his family property. It is only when the heirs are entitled to get 1/2th share, that the right would have accrued to them at the earliest point of time when the death took place immediately prior to their death. The proviso cannot be construed to mean that the heirs will get 1 /3rd shares in the ancestral property and the interest will be deemed as the share which they received or she received in his notional partition. [454B C, G] (8) In the present case, there is no evidence to show whether the right of the plaintiff to obtain any partition on her death had takenplace immediately before his death. There was no material on record that the property was allotted to her by virtue s.6 (1). The proviso merely provides for a fictional fictional and not a fictionally expedient to the simple effect that the interests of a family shall be deemed in addition to the share acquired by the deceased at the relevant time.

The appellant was appointed as a Class III employee in the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was promoted to Class II and Class III posts by the Corporation with effect from 1st October, 1956 and he completed 58 years of age subject to the usual clause (b) of section 49(2) of the Act. The appellant was promoted as a class III employee on or before 1st January, 1976. On completion of his age of 60 years he was retired on completion of 58 years. He filed an application for review of the order of retirement and the review petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had been appointed as Class III employees in the service of the Corporation after 1 st September, 1955 and he was entitled to continue in service till he attained the age of 58. The High Court rejected the application on the ground that the age o f superannuation of the employees belonging to Class I or Class II was not applicable to them because they were appointed after 1St September,1956 and they had been promoted to a Class II post by the appellant after 1 St December, 1956, and they were entitled to continued in service upto the age 58 years on completion o f the age as 58. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in striking down regulation 19(2). [601B] (2) The power of the State Government under section 49 (2), is not an absolute one and it is only a discretionary power which can be exercised by the State Govern ment. It is not a case where the age has been fixed as 58 years or at any time thereafter on 1st November, 1956 after 1ST September, 1959. [602C] (3) The appellant had retired from service on 31st December, 1958 and he had completed 58 year of age on 1 st January, 1956 when he attained 60 years. Therefore, the age fixed by the Government for retirement was not a relevant factor to determine the age at any point of time after 1t September, 1957. [063D] (4) The order of superannuation passed by the respondent is in accordance with the provisions of section 48(2)(b) and (c). [065E] (5) The respondent was not entitled to retain his services till he completed 60 years of service on 1St December, 1955. He had been given three months notice or salary in lieu thereof. Therefore the order passed by respondent is illegal and void. [2006G] (6) The State Government has power under section 48 (2)(a) to extend the age for one year at a time upto 60 years but it was not open to the appellant to continue his services beyond the age prescribed by the regulations.

The appellant was appointed as a Member of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri, Haryana. On the basis of an application made by him to the President of India with copies to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the respondent No. 1 as a member of the District Bar Association. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no contempt of court. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the letter dated 20th February 1975 did not constitute any contempt and that the High court had no jurisdiction to take any action against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: (1) The letter dated 19th February 1974 does not constitute a contempt of Court. It merely states that the Chief Minister of Haryana had expressed his opinion on the question whether any Judge did speak on the matters complained of by the writer or otherwise. [782C] (2) The High court was right in holding that the letters were not part of the letter and that they were not signed by the deponent himself. [882D] (3) The letters were written by the appellant to the respondent no. 1, the Chief Secretary of Haryana and the Chief Justices of Punjab, Haryana and Haryana. They did not contain any reference to the letter of the deponents nor did they state that the contents thereof were incorrect or false. [982E] (4) The appellant had not made out a case for contempt of the court. It was only on the basis that the allegations in the letters are supported by the affidavit filed by the respondent nos. 1 to 3, the High Cou rt held that there is no contempt. [1083G] (5) The order of the High Cour t dated 20 th February 1975 does not amount to contempt of this Court. [1182A] (6) The fact that the appellant had made a representation to the Governor of Haryana, Haryana on 20th March 1975 and the same was received by the Chief justice of Punjab on 15th March, 1975 clearly shows that the respondent had no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge or to weaken in any manner to weakly in any way to weakens in any form. [1282E H] (7) The contempt proceedings are not maintainable against the appellant because of the fact that he was a member and was not aware of the contents of the letters. He had no knowledge of the facts which were stated by him in his letter dated 15th February, 1975.

The appellant, Suraj Mall Mohta & Co. (Porus A. Mehta and Porus A., B. Sen, a member of the Commission, was appointed as an officer authorised by the Government to investigate into certain matters relating to income tax on income. The appellant was appointed by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Income Tax Act as an Officer authorised by it in this behalf. On the basis of the report submitted by the Commission the Central Govt. issued a notification dated January 9, 1956, under section 4(4) of that Act, declaring that the income chargeable to tax on the income of the appellant was exempt from payment of income tax and directed the Central government to refer the case of persons whose cases are referred to it for investigation into certain points or points in a case or points which were not referred to the Commission. The Central Govt., by its order dated January 10, 1956 declared that the Income tax Officer had jurisdiction to investigate any case or point or points mentioned in section 5 and hears and decides the case. On appeal, the High Court of Bombay held that sub section (4) was a piece of discriminatory legislation and that the provisions of section 5 were not applicable to persons who were included in section 4 of the Act. The High Court further held that the impugned Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution because it was not a law made by Parliament under clause (3) of Article 20 of the constitution, and that sub sections (4), (7) and (8) of section 6(5) were not ultra vires the provisions. The appellants are aggrieved by the decision of the High court on the question whether sub section 4 is a piece or an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to carry on trade or business guaranteed under article 19(1)(g).
