Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned Act is violative of Article 14 of Constitution and is void ab initio. [601B] 2. The power conferred by sub section 3 of section 4 to make an enquiry into certain specified matters relating thereto is a part of the legislative power conferred on the Commission under sub section(4). It is not a matter of procedure or that it is a matter which is outside the scope of the power conferred upon the Commission and the Commission has to be exercised by any member thereof authorised by them in this regard. [701C] 3. The powers conferred by subsection (4)(a) are not limited to any period and this does not affect the substantive rights of the persons concerned. [802D] 4. The provisions of sub section 2(1), (2) and sub section 5 of section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, are not applicable in respect of income chargeable under section 3 or section 5. [820E] 5. The Commission has power to investigate the case and to form an opinion that it may make a report to the Central Govts. 6. The word 'may' used in sub section 1(4)(b) is wide enough to include within its scope any period of time, but it does not include within it any period. [823E] 7. The expression 'shall 'shall' in sub clause (1) means the Central Govern ment or the State Government. It does not mean that the Commission can make a reference to the Commissioner for investigation. The words 'may ' are wide enough, and they cannot be read as comprehending within it all the time. [825E] 8. The scheme of section 3(4), which is in pari materia with sub section 6 (5) of Section 5, makes it clear that the power to make a complaint under sub clause(1). is not limited only to any particular period and it does include within itself any period but it includes within it every period of eight years. [826E] 9.

The appellant, a Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (hereinafter referred to as "the Association ') is an industry within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The appellant is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. It carries on its business in various parts of India including the country at Calcutta. In the year 1965, the appellant was registered under the provisions of the Indian Trade Unions Act, 1926 (hereinafter called 'the Act'). On or about the first day of January, 1966, the Association filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Memorandum of Association and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Memorandum did not disclose any material facts which would justify the application of the provisions to the Federation. In appeal by certificate, this Court held that the memorandum of association was not a "industry" within the definition of the expression ' industry ' in section 2 (5) and that it was not an industrial establishment within the ambit of the definition given in section2(5). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Memorandum of Understanding is a commercial establishment within [the meaning of the word 'industry ' as defined in section II(j) of Act. It does not refer to any activity carried on by it in a premises in which the registered office of the Federation is located. The expression "industrial establishment" has been defined in s. 2 (9) of that Act and includes an association of any individual trader, industrialists or businessmen. [601B] 2. The word 'trade' in section 3(5)(a) of this Act does not include the activity carried out by a person for his own benefit. It is only when the activity of a trade or business is incidental to trade or commerce that it can be said that the activity is an industrial activity. [701C] 3. The words "any work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to trade" do not necessarily mean that the activities carried on in a factory are not "industry". It does cover activities which are connected with trade or industry. [802D] 4. The definition of 'industry' in s 2(9) is wide enough to include any activity of an industrial nature, including trade or profession. [820E] 5. The activity carried by the Federation consists of various kinds of activities which may be incidental or incidental to the trade or commercial establishment. It cannot be said to be a "industrial undertaking" within its ambit. [823A D] 6. The activities of the Association are not in the nature of business or trade. The same are not connected with any activity which is carried on for profit. [825E] 7. The mere fact that the association carries on business does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that it is an "industry", and that the said activity is not an "industrial" undertaking. [826A D; 882F] 8. The question whether a particular activity of the association is an 'industry or not has to be decided in each case. [828B C] 9. In order to appreciate the contention raised by the appellant, it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of this Chapter which are as under: "The expression "industry " means any business carried on with a view to carrying on any trade or Commerce or profession." The word "industry ' has been used in section 10(1) of The Act. [829B C D] 9 (a) The word "'industry" is not defined in the Act and it does not mean any activity by which a business is carried out for profit, but includes any activity incidental or consequential to trade. [827C] (b) The expression 'industry " has been interpreted in the light of the above definition of "industry ".

The appellant was assessed on the income of the trust for the purpose of payment of pension. He claimed that he had been paying the amount in instalments of the value of the land and rent collections to him as his remuneration. The Income tax Officer held that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act, and, therefore, the appellant was not liable to pay income tax under the Act. He further held that he was entitled to receive a sum of Rs. 36,396/ towards the income from land and the amount payable as remuneration for management of the Trust. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence on record to show that the payment of the amount was in fact made by the appellant as his salary or rent collections. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the Income tax officer and held that it was not a case of income from property within the definition of agricultural income under section 2 (1)(b) of Act. The High Court also held that if the amount is not paid by the assessee as his income, the receipt would be an asset in the hands of the appellant and, consequently, the income could not be said to be derived from land within the ambit of the definition in section 2.(1)(c) of Income tax Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the amount paid by way of remuneration for the management of a trust is not an asset within the purview of the expression "land revenue" and, as such, the assessee is not entitled to any deduction under section 4(3)(viii) of 'the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "any income" in the definition are used in a wide sense and it cannot be said that the income derived from lands used for agricultural purposes is not agricultural income. [601B] 2.2 The word "income" in section 4 (3)(vii) of "the Act" means income derived by an assessee from land which is used for agriculture or as a source of his income. It does not include any income derived therefrom. [702C] 3.3 The expression "any sum paid by him as remuneration" in clause (viii) includes any amount collected as remuneration by way o compensation for the acquisition of the character of the income. The word 'income' is used in the context of the provisions contained in section 3(1) of that Act and, in the absence of any material to show what was the source of the said amount, it cannot come within the mischief of the explanation to section 4.(3)(vi). [703D] 2: The word "'income" is used only in a broad sense and not in a narrow sense. It is not defined in the Act nor does it include any sum collected as salary or remuneration for any purpose. [802E] 3:1.2 In the context in which the word " income" occurs, the words "an allowance" are used to indicate that the said allowance is not a source or source of income. Therefore, the amount so paid by an individual cannot be regarded as his own income. If it is held that such allowance is a source and source of salary or is a receipt for the benefit of the individual, it would be a source which could be regarded in law as the source. [902F] 3;2.3 In the present case, the payment was made by way Of remuneration to the appellant. The amount so received was not merely a measure but a measure and the nature of the allowance was also such that it could not have been regarded as the income earned by him. [1001G] 3(i) The word ''income" has no relation to the income which is derived from the land used for any agricultural purposes. It cannot be held that any amount was received by the Appellant as his personal remuneration.

The petitioners were appointed as Chargeman 's in the various departments of the State Government. They were promoted to the post of Chargeman and they were granted promotion as Chargemen 's w ith effect from 1st April, 1983. The petitioners were promoted as Charge Man 's on completion of two years' service as Charge man 's. In the year 1981, the petitioners were placed in the gradation list of Chargemen' Grade A. They had been promoted to that post with effect from 2nd February, 1981 and they continued to work as Chargei s' on completion o f two years'. The petitioners filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said promotion order dated 4th April, 1982. The High Court by its judgment dated 4 th April,1983 allowed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners are entitled to be treated as Charge I 's and they are entitled for all the benefits of seniority and promotion from the date their juniors were promoted. In appeal, the Division Bench of the High court held that the circular dated 6th November, 1962 was not applicable to the petitioners and the same was also quashed by its order dated 2nd March, 1981. The appellants filed a special leave petition before this Court against the said judgment of the Division bench. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1 The circular dated 20 th January, 1966 is not applicable in the case of the petitioners because they were appointed on completionof two years ' service as Supervisor 's by the Madhya Prade s' Grade I and they had been granted promotion to the said post with retrospective effect from a date when their juniors i t were promoted and they have been given the benefit of seniority. [901F] 1.2 The circular was not in force at all because the petitioners had been appointed as Supervisor by the High C ourt on 2nd April, 1984. They could not be promoted to any higher post with prospective effect from the dates when their cases were considered for promotion. [1001G] 1.(a) The circular issued by the Government of India dated 20th January, 1967 was in force w.e.f. 6 th November,1962 and it was not a case where the petitioners could be promoted as Supervisor. [1101F G] (b) The circulars dated 6 th October, 1962 and 20th February, 1966 were applicable to all those who had been recruited in 1963 and they could not have been promoted as Supervisors 'A 's from the said date when they were promoted on completion thereof. [110G] 2.(a)(i) The petitioners are not entitled to any relief for seniority or promotion as Supervisor since they were given the benefits as per the circular of 6th October,1962. They cannot be treated at par with Chargeman II because they had already been appointed in 1963. [111H; 111A B] (ii) The High Cour t has rightly held that there was no discrimination between Chargemen and Chargeman I who were promoted from the post to which they were entitled to. [112B D] 3.(a). In view of the fact that the circulars dated 20 nd January,1966 and 20 th February, 1967 were applicable in respect of Charge Man ol who were appointed in the other departments of State Government, the High cour t was not justified in holding that there had been no discrimination against Chargeman. [113B D; 111E] (iii) The impugned judgment dated 2 nd March, 1979 is clearly unsustainable and it is set aside. The appeal is allowed. No costs.

The appellant, a State Transport Undertaking, filed an application for permit to ply in the inter State route of Karnataka. The Regional Transport Authority granted permits to the appellant and the State Tourism Development Corporation, the State Transport Authority, under section 68F(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, on the basis that it was satisfied that the State transport undertaking would be able to operate in any inter State routes without detriment to its responsibility for providing adequate road transport services in any notified area or notified route. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the permit granted to the State Government Transport Undertaking was valid for the purpose of promoting tourism in any other notified area, and that the appellant was not entitled to get preference to be given under section 47(1). In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the permits were granted to all the private operators of tourist cars and travel agents, and therefore, the appellant could not have been denied preference to the private operator. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Transport undertaking is entitled to preference in the matter of grant of permits to its employees, but it cannot be denied that the Government Undertaking would be unable to operate within a notified area. [801B] 2. The permit granted by the State Road Transport Authority under section 69F(2) of Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1988, is valid for all purposes including the purpose for promoting tourism. It does not say that the private parties are entitled to have preference in respect of any notified route or notified area unless they are otherwise eligible. [901C] 3. The grant of permit by the Government under section 70F(3) of Act 1939, is a matter of policy and it cannot therefore be denied. [1001D] 4. The Government has to consider the claims of all eligible applicants in all other cases and if they are not otherwise eligible, then the State Public Transport Undertaking would have preference for applying the rules of preference and giving preference to them. [092E] 5. The right to get a permit under section 71F(4) is an infringement of article 14 of the Constitution. [103G] 6. The power conferred on the State to grant permits to private operators is not confined to matters of policy but extends only to matters relating to tourism. [104H; 104A] 7. In the instant case, the permit was granted to private operator for a period of five years and it was valid upto 31st March, 1986. The permits were issued in respect thereof on the same date. It is not disputed that the operators of the tourist cars had applied for permits from the State Tourist Undertaking for operating in any one inter State area without detriment or detriment to their responsibility for provide adequate road Transport services in a notified Area or notified routes. [105A B] 8. The proviso to section 63(7) does not give preference to applications for permits to be granted to them, but only applies in relation to such permits as are available in respect thereto. [106C] 9. In view of the provisions contained in sections 49 and 50 of the Act, the Regional Transport Authorities have no right to grant permit to any person other than the State Undertaking. The applications for permit were not made by the private persons. [107D] 10. The High Court was wrong in holding that section 47 (1) H.L.C. vs Union of India, ; , followed.

The respondent was a dealer in the business of selling and purchasing goods. The appellant, who is the purchaser of the business, filed a suit against the State Government for recovery of arrears of sales tax due from him on the basis that he had purchased the goods from the seller. The respondent contended that the liability to pay the arrears of taxes was not discharged by him as he had no undertaking on the part of the transferor and that he did not have any undertaking on his behalf. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was liable to pay tax under section 19(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the State Legislature had power under section 20(2)(c) of Act to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the said Act and that the provisions of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 were ultra vires of the rule making power of the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The liability to tax on the respondent is not a statutory liability created by the statute but a legal fiction created by section 19 (1) and it is a statutory obligation created by law. [601B] 2. The State Legislature has power under Section 20(4)(c). It is a well settled principle of interpretation that the words "any undertaking on behalf of the dealer" in section 19 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956 are not to be construed as including the right to recover arrears of tax due by him from the purchaser. [701C] 3. The word 'assessment' used in section 20 (2)(b) of Central Sales tax Act, 1956 is not defined in the Act and it does not include the power of recovery of tax on account of arrears payable by a dealer. [76G] 4. The expression "any person" in the context of section 19 has to be understood in its ordinary sense as including an undertaking on whose behalf the business was carried on by the purchaser himself. [77H; 77A B] 5. The words 'any person' in the section are not defined either in the Central Act or in the State Sales Tax Acts, 1939. It is only when a person who purchases a business has to pay arrears of sale tax due on his goods purchased by him and the liability is discharged by the dealer, he cannot be said to have any liability created inter se between the State and the purchaser and the State legislature. [78A B C] 6. The language used in the rule makes it clear that the person liable to tax under the Act must be a person liable for payment of the arrears on the date of service of the notice of assessment, not being less than fifteen days from the date on which he purchased the business. [79C D] 7. The position is well settled by this Court in the case of State of Madras vs V. V.R.S. Sathyanarayana Chettiar, ; , followed. 8. In the present case, the respondent had not obtained any undertaking from the appellant on the strength of which he acquired the business and the respondent did not carry on his business. The undertaking was only a part of his business and it was not a part thereof. [80D] 9. The fact that the undertaking was a part and parcel of the trade is not in dispute. It was not disputed before us that the appellant had undertaken to pay all the arrears due from the respondent on the dates of the sale of the goods. [81E F] 10. In view of the provisions contained in section 18(1)(c), the liability of the respondent to pay sales tax is not discharged but only the right of recovery which he obtained under section 18 (2) of The liability of payment of sales Tax is not disputed by the appellant. [82G] 11. The question whether the liability created on the appellant is a liability created in respect of the turnover or not, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellant was appointed as a Government servant on probation for the period of one year and he was confirmed in his post. He was promoted to the post of Head Constable on January 1, 1956. On February 2, 1955, he was posted at the Central Reserve Police Force. The State of Gujarat, by an order dated March 22, 1955 appointed him as a Head Constable. On April 5, 1955 he was transferred from the Central Government Service to the State of Bombay. He filed a suit in the Court of Civil Judge, Senior Division, Baroda for recovery of his salary for the time during which he had served as a Sub Inspector on January 2, 1956 and for arrears of pay on March 22. 1955. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any arrears of salary for three years prior to the date of his appointment as Head Constable and that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. On appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by certificate, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that there had been a breach of contract within section 60(2)(a) of the Act because the order was not passed in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding, that the suit was not barred by time. [701B] 2. The appellant was entitled to a decree for arrears on the basis of his pay during the period when he had been appointed as Head constable. [802C] 3. The order of termination of service is not an award within section 61(2) (a). It does not say that the respondent was entitled, under section 60, to recover his salary from January 1 1956. [601D] 4. The question whether the appellant could be said to have been in Government service or not has to be determined by the appropriate authority. [820E] 5. The word 'in this context' is wide enough to include within it any liability of the State Government, which may accrue or may accrue under any contract. It does mean that the State must be a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contracts. [823A D] 6. The words 'in such circumstances as are not inconsistent with a power to determine a contract ' in the exercise of executive power for any purposes of the Government, cannot be construed to mean that it is only a liability arising out of a contract. [825E] 7.

The appellant was a lessee of the coal mines in the year 1941. The lease deed executed by him in favour of the respondents, which was in the years 1941 and 1943, was not in the nature of a lease. He had no right to remove the coal from the encroached area. The respondents were entitled to remove all the coal left by them in the encroached areas. The appellant filed an application under section 47 of the Indian Contract Act for a declaration that he was liable to pay royalty and damages for use of the land. The trial court held that the lease deed did not confer any right on the appellant to remove or remove the goods from the said area, but it was only a part of the leased property. The High Court held that under the Rules 76 of the Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, the appellant could remove the materials from the land and, therefore, he was entitled to exemption from the operation of rule 76 of Indian Coal Mines Regulations, 1946. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were not liable to be evicted under section 48 of the Act because they had no intention to remove coal from their land. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent 's right to removal or remove coal is completely lost to them for ever. [701B] 2. The right to removed coal from a encroached area is not by any means accessible to the plaintiffs and being so lost to themselves for ever, it cannot be said that the appellant had no knowledge of the removal of coal by him. [802C] 3. The appellants were entitled only to remove and remove the material from the area. [820D] 4. The mere fact that the respondent ' s right to lift or remove goods from a reserved forest land was lost to the appellants, does not make any difference in this case because the respondents had no reasonable cause for their removal of the goods. [823E] 5. The position is well settled by decisions of this Court in the cases of [State of Bombay vs Shri S.R. Tendolkar & Ors.] , and State of Maharashtra vs Shri N.C. Mardikar, A.I.R., referred to.

The appellant was employed as a crosscutter in the year 1958. He was suspended by the management of the company on June 25, 1958 and he was removed from service on July 8, 1958. The appellant challenged his removal under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders which were challenged before the tribunal. The tribunal held that the appellant had not proved that there was in fact a breach of the standing orders or that the action taken under r.. 18(b) was mala fide and was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. It further held that since the appellant was suspended on June 21, 1958, he could not be said to have been prejudiced if he was retained in service. The Tribunal also held that there were no allegations against the appellant that he had committed any misconduct under r 18(c) and therefore the action was invalid. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant: (1) that the order terminating his services was mala fides; (2) that since he was suspended, the termination of service was bad in law; (3) that as the appellant did not challenge his removal, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to intervene and set aside the order of dismissal. HELD : (1)(a) The power under r., 18(A) is a colourable exercise of the power conferred on the employer by r. 19(a). [18D] (b) The powers given under r.(18(a), (c) are not merely administrative or quasi judicial functions but they are intended to be exercised in public interest and therefore it cannot be said that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction, either to intervene or to set aside such termination. [18E] (2)(a). In the instant case, the appellant's services were terminated under r, 18(e) of Standing Orders and he had not challenged his termination under rs. 18 (a) and (c). [19F] (3)(b) It is true that the power under s. 10 of the Act is a discretionary power conferred by the Standing orders but it cannot also be said in any way that the employer has no power to take action under r,. 18(d), (e) or (f) of standing orders. [19G] (4)(a)(b). The power given under s.(18)(a),(c), (d) and(g) is not merely an administrative or quasijudicial function but it can be exercised by the industrial court in this case, if it is satisfied that the decision taken under R. 18 was a colourable exercising of the powers conferred on it under r; 18(h). [20G] The power conferred under r.'18(b), (g) and.(i) are merely administrative functions and they cannot be exercised as a result or as a consequence of victimisation, unfair labour practices or otherwise. [20H] (5)(a)] (b)(c) It was not open to the industrial courts to interfere with the decision of the tribunal in this regard. [21G] In the present case, it is not disputed that the management had no power under R 18(g). The Tribunal has held that r.18(h) and r.19(a)(c), are merely procedural or quasi administrative functions. [22A F] (6) The Tribunal was in error in holding that r..18(d) is an enabling provision which is a mandatory provision and that the tribunal had no powers under r 19(e). [23B] (7) The order of termination of services of the appellant is not mala fide or is a result to be passed by the Industrial Tribunal.

The appellant, a tenant in the theatre, filed an application under section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act for eviction of the respondents from the premises in dispute. The City Civil Court, Ahmedabad, by its order dated December 1, 1960, dismissed the said application and directed that the suit be tried as a whole. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the consent decree passed by the trial court was not a judgment within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure; that the agreement dated December 27, 1954, was a lease and that the tenancy was governed by the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and that it was not an agreement between the parties to let out the premises for a period of six months. The High Court held that the said agreement was a transfer of property and that there was no concluded contract between the appellant and Filmistan. On further appeal by Special Leave to this court it was submitted on behalf Of the appellant, that the compromise decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 was not binding on the parties and that since the consent order was not challenged before the High Court, the said compromise decree could not operate as res judicata between the respondents. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The consent decree is a judgment by consent and it cannot be regarded as a decision of the Court in the suit. [901 D] 2. The agreement dated November 27,1954, was an agreement to let into the theatre under which the rights were granted in the year 1954. The said agreement did not create any tenancy or other character. It was only a lease. The question whether the consent was a judgment of the trial Court or not was a matter to be decided at the trial and the consent terms were binding on parties in the earlier suit No 149 of 1961. [0901 E] 3. The compromise decree did not operate, as resjudicata between the defendants and the plaintiff. It is not necessary that the question whether any right or obligation of the parties in controversy was in the nature of a lease or other capacity has to be determined at the time when the consent judgment was pronounced. [1001 A] 4. The terms of the compromise agreement dated October 27, 1955, were not challenged by the defendants before the trial Judge and the High court had no occasion to go into that question. [1102 B E] 5. The plaintiff in the present case did not dispute the agreement between them and Filmsan. It only raised a contention that the terms of compromise decree dated October 25, 1954 were not binding upon the parties. The trial Judge held that there could be no concluded contracts between the plaintiff and Filmansan. [110 A B] 6. The appellant had not disputed the agreement to sell dated November 28, 1954. It did not raise any dispute as to the terms on which the consent award was made. The respondents were not entitled to raise any objection in regard to the question that the appellant had no subsisting right or liability of Filmsansan under section 92 of the Evidence Act. [111 A B C] 7. In view of the fact that the parties had agreed to let off the premises, the trial judge was justified in holding that the respondents were entitled to a decree in the absence of any concluded contract. [112 D E] 8. The facts are not disputed. It may be true that the respondent had filed an affidavit in reply to the application for leave to appeal but it is admitted that the same was not filed by the appellant. The respondent did not deny the fact of the agreement being a lease, and he also denied the fact as to whether the agreement was executed by him or not. [113 A B D] 9.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer on contract basis in the Indian Air Force on 30.8.1985 and he was appointed on probation for a period of one year on 24.3.1988. He was confirmed in service by the order dated 10.7.1986. On his appointment, he was promoted to the post of Pilot officer on 25.3,1988. The respondent was not entitled to any salary till 30th August, 1985 when he completed the age of 58 years. The High Court had directed that the respondent be paid salary upto 30th of August,1985 and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service on the basis of his term of office. The appellant challenged the order of termination by filing a Writ Petition before the Allahabad High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.2. In view of the provisions contained in Rule 3(b) of the U.P. Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, it is open to the Government to terminate the services of a person on the ground that he has not been given an opportunity of being heard before terminating his service. [701B] 1.3 The order of appointment issued in favour of the respondent was valid till 30.08.1985 when he was selected and appointed on 25th March, 1988. He had not been paid salary for a long period of time after his first appointment. He could not have been given any opportunity to be heard before termination of his service or the fresh appointment. [801C] 1.(a) The order dated 24.03.1988 was valid only till 30 th August, 1984 when he had been appointed on contract. It is open for the Government not to appoint a person in Government Service beyond 30th September, 1985 unless there is an order of extension of service. The order does not affect in any way what the High Court has stated in the penultimate paragraph of the Judgment dated 24th March 1988 that the appointment was in the nature of contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30st August,85 were liable to be ignored. [901D] 1(b). The order is not an order which can be passed by the Governor after expiry of the period of probation. It does not give any indication that the Government had extended the period beyond 30 th September,1985 when the respondent had been selected and engaged on 25 th March,1988 and he would continue in service till 30 st August, 85. [1001E] 1 (c). The High court was right in holding that the order terminating the services is not a valid order of confirmation and no further order could be passed without giving an opportunity to the respondent to be considered for appointment on the post in question. [1101F] 2.(a)(i) In view thereof, the High court had rightly set aside the order passed by it on 24th April, 1988 and directed that he would be entitled to continue in his service till 31st August 1985 when the order was issued in his case. [110G] 3.(ii) The High Cour t has committed a manifest error of law in setting aside the impugned order dated 26.7,1988 passed by this Court. [111H; 111A] 4.(a). In view whereof, the respondent is entitled to be reinstated in service on his original post with all consequential benefits including seniority and back wages. [112B] 5.(b) The respondent had not challenged the judgment of the High Curt dated 24 th March 1988 passed by a learned Single Judge of the Allahabad Court in Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1986.

The appellant was married to one P.W. 1 and the deceased Subhadramma was the wife of P. W. 2. The prosecution case is that on 19th December, 1972 at about 10 p.m., P.Ws. 1 to 3 went to the house of P,W. 2 and the appellant told him that he had gone to the village of P and that he would give a beating to the deceased. On hearing the cries of the deceased, P. Ws. 1, 2 and 3 came out and saw the appellant giving a beating. The deceased Subharamma went to his house and saw P.w. 1 who was sitting by the side of the house. The evidence of P W. 1 is corroborated by the evidence of the other witnesses who were present at the time when the occurrence took place. The High Court has not accepted the evidence that P. w. 2 had seen the deceased in his house. It is true that the appellant was not examined by the prosecution as a witness to the recovery of the knife from his possession but he did not state that he was told by P. 1 that he could give a blow to him on the cot made by the appellant. The fact that the deceased had been stabbed in the abdomen of P does not affect the evidence given by P W, 2. In view of the above discussion, we are of the opinion that the High Court was right in holding that the prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the murder took place at about 5 p. m.m. on 19 th December,1972 and that the death had taken place at 10 p., when P. S. 3 went ahead with the further investigation which was taken over by the Inspector of Police. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Madras on May 30, 1949. He was posted at the Madras High Court. On June 5, 1950, he was transferred to the Madras State Administrative Tribunal and was posted in the same district. The appellant filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for his removal from office under Section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Tribunal by its order dated July 9, 1951, dismissed the application holding that the appellant had failed to prove that he had committed any misconduct or misbehaviour in respect of which a reasonable doubt was sought to be raised by him. On appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Tribunal and held that the removal from service was not a punishment but only a dismissal. The High Court held that there was no evidence on record to prove the charges against the appellant and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of removal passed by the President of India under Article 124(4) of Constitution was not in accordance with law and, therefore, the High court had no jurisdiction to try the offence alleged against the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the President under Article 125(3) is a judicial function and it cannot be exercised by any other authority except the High Courts. [701B] 2. The President of the State Legislature has no legislative competence to enact any law for the trial or punishment of corruption against a superior Judge. It is not competent to the Parliament to enact such law for trial or penalty of corruption in respect thereof, even if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the legislature had no power to enact a law for investigation and proof of misbehaviour or incapacity. [801C] 3. The word 'may 'shall 'may' in clause (c) means that the Parliament has not made any law in respect whereof the President has no power of superintendence. It does not include an order passed by a superior court, but only an order which is passed by another competent authority. [901D] 4. The expression 'may" in clause(c) must be construed as comprehending within its scope all the powers conferred on the President and it must be interpreted strictly. [1001E] 5. The words 'shall' in clauses (a) and (b) of Article 124 read with article 124(5) are not to be construed in a manner which would bring into play the provisions of Articles 124(1) and 125(4). It is only when the President makes an order under clause (a), that he can be removed from office by the Governor. [1101F] 6. The language used in Article 124 does not make any difference to the position in law as it was never intended to confer on the Governor a power of control over the High courts and the Chief Justice of India. It only means that if the President is satisfied that there is an emergency, he can remove him from office. [110H] 7. The fact that the President may be satisfied that the situation in which the High judiciary is functioning has not been so grave as to justify his removal under Article 217(4), does not mean that the Chief Judge of a High Court or the Chief justice of a Division cannot be removed therefrom without any such consultation with the Governor, because he can only remove him if he is satisfied on the basis of evidence adduced by the prosecution that there are circumstances which indicate that the accused has committed the offence. [111H; 111A] 8. The question whether the President can remove a Judge or not does not arise in view of the provisions contained in Article 125 (4) and Article 124 (5). It cannot be said that the power conferred on him under Article 127(1), is an enabling provision which cannot apply to the Chief Judges of a division.

The appellant was a Sunri by caste and he was a member of the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant to the seat of the Saha group of Sunris. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that the appellant belonged to a smaller group called Sahas. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that he was not a member belonging to a larger group called the Sahas and, therefore, he could not be excluded from the Scheduled Castes specified in the Schedule Caste specified under item 40 of the Schedule. The learned Judge held that the respondent had failed to establish that the Saha's community was a smaller one and that the members of the same group were members of that group. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the said Sahas belonged to the larger group of Sahas, and that, therefore the appellant could not claim any benefit under item 41 of the schedule to the Act. The Election Tribunal dismissed the election petition holding that there had been a separate category of members of a smaller caste called Saha. The Tribunal held that since the respondent was a Scheduled Caste, he did not belong to the same class as Sahas in the case of the respondent. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal erred in holding that a larger number of Saha's group constituted a smaller category of Saha and that there were no other members of such group. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any other member" in item 41 is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the sense of "a member belonging" in the same category. [701B] 2. The word "any" in Item 40 means a person belonging to another group called "the Scheduled Caste". It does not mean that the word "other member" must be understood as including a member who is a smaller by caste or a different group. [802C] 3. The words "any Other member" are not defined either in the Constitution or in any other statute. [820E] 4. The term "any person belonging" has been defined in article 40 of Schedule Caste to the Constitution and it means a member thereof who is an independent class by caste. [823C] 5. The definition of "Scheduled Castes" in article 41 of Schedule Castes is not exhaustive and it does not include any other category of persons. [825D] 6. The language used in item 42 of the list of Scheduled Caste is not very clear and it only refers to a person who has been included in the Scheduled caste. It does refer to a member whose name is included in that list. [822E] 7. The fact that the words "other members" are used in article 39 of Schedule Tribes indicates that they must be persons belonging to the Scheduled Tribe. [826C] 8. In the instant case, the respondent belonged to an independent caste and was a larger one. He was not included in any such list. It is true that the name given in the schedule is not a larger than that of a member in the scheduled tribe but it does refer only to a Scheduled Tribe which has been specified in Schedule Caste. [828E] 9. The object of the Act is to provide for social welfare and reform of the weaker sections of the society. It provides for social justice and reform. [829G] 10. In view of the fact that there is no evidence on record to show as to what was the caste or the tribe which has come into existence in a larger category, the Tribunal was right in holding the respondent 's case to be a member within the Sunri caste. The finding of the Tribunal that the appellants belonged to different group called ' Sahas' and not a smaller class is correct. [827G] 11. In this view of things, the appeal must fail. [824E] 12.

The appellant, who was the tenant of the flat, entered into negotiations with the complainant for putting him in vacant possession of the same. The appellant, however, agreed to pay the sum of Rs. 29,500 as consideration for the furniture and the balance due in respect of the furniture. He also paid him a guarantee against disposal of Rs 1,000 by the appellant. The complainant was given an opportunity to put his case on trial but he did not appear before the learned Magistrate. The learned Magistrate held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had entered into negotiation with the landlord and that the possession of flat was delivered to him by the complainant. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the complainant had paid any sum or consideration for his tenancy. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in holding that the offence under section 19(2) of the Act was not attracted because the appellant was not a tenant of his tenancy and as such he was not entitled to be convicted under section 20(1)(b) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 18(1) of Act are applicable only in respect to cases where the offence is committed by a tenant or any person acting on behalf o f the landlord. [701B] 2. The words "relinquish ment" used in section 18 (1) are not applicable to cases in which the offence was committed by the tenant or a person acting for and on behalf af the landlord, who receives any rent, premium, or other like sum or deposit or any sum of money or deposit, or any amount as a security for the release of the premises. [801C] 3. The word "relivish ment " used in the section clearly indicates that the legislature intended by the legislature to include only such sums or deposits as are mentioned in the sub clause (i) of section 19 of the said Act. [820D] 4. The expression "relation" is not defined in the Act. It does not mean any amount or consideration received by a person for his benefit. [823E] 5. In the instant case, the appellant did not enter into negotiations between him and the complainant nor he had given any guarantee against the disposal of the property of the complainant to the complainant but he was only entitled to receive the sum or the consideration as a condition of the relin quarant tion by the landlord to the appellant, namely, the complainant, who is the tenant. [825E] 6. The High Court was right in holding, that the words "relating to" in section 19 (2) were not applicable because the word "relating" used therein meant only such amounts or deposits which are mentioned therein. [822F] 7. In view of the fact that the word 'relivate' is not used in any strict sense and it was intended by Parliament to include all sums or payments received by way of rent, compensation or other sum or deposits, or otherwise, the intention of the legislature was clear that the amount or deposit would be less than the sum which is given by the owner of the accommodation. [826E] 8. The language used in clause (b) is not applicable where the word has been used in a sense and the word is used in an inclusive sense. It is only such amount or deposits that have been mentioned therein, namely the rent, royalty, or consideration paid by the person for the premises, which is equivalent to the rent payable by him. [828E] 9.

The appellant, who was employed as a Draughtsman in the category of Draughtsmen and other categories of Draftsmen, was drawing Rs. 150/ per month as his basic pay. The Tribunal held that the increase in the basic pay of each employee was intended to be a flat increase of Rs. 100/ in the case of Draftsman and other employees. The appellant challenged the award by filing an appeal before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal holding that the fixation of the wage scales by the Tribunal was not correct, but it was only a revision of the pay scale of all categories of Draughtsman and Draftsmen and directed the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay with effect from the date of the award. In appeal before this Court, HELD: 1. The increase in basic pay is intended to give an additional benefit to all employees who were entitled to get the same at par with those who were already in service on the date when the award was pronounced and the revised wage scales were also awarded to them. [701C] 2. The award of the Tribunal dated December 20, 1978 was not a correct one. It was merely a revision for the pay scales of all employees in the categories of Draftsman and Draftsman. [802D] 3. The High Court had clearly erred in holding that there was no justification for the increase of basic pay to all those who had already been working on the post of Draughts man and were entitled only to get additional pay at par. [820G] 4. The Award of the Industrial Tribunal dated 12th December, 1978 is not correct one because it has clearly stated in its award that the increased basic pay was intended for giving an additional advantage to all the employees who had been working as Draftsmen on the basis of the recommendations of the Pay Commission. [823A D] 5. The fact that the appellant was a Senior Draftsman and he was also getting Rs. 200/ per day as his salary in the scale of Rs 150/ does not mean that the Tribunal had only fixed the pay of all those employees who are already in the same category of Drafts man and they were entitled for the additional benefit of Rs, 150/. [825E] 6. The view taken by the Industrial Court was clearly erroneous. It is true that the award of industrial Tribunal dated 20th December 1978 was based on a finding that the revised scales of Pay were not correct but it has been held that there had been no justification in the increase to Rs.150/ and Rs.100/. In the present case, the increase was intended only for giving additional benefit. [822A D; 882E] 7. The Industrial Court had also given a finding on the question whether the increase would be more appropriate than the one incorporated in the revised pay scales. It could not have been said that the change was intended merely to give additional benefits. [821B C] 8. In view of the fact that there were no corresponding increases in each category of posts, the Tribunal did not have any jurisdiction to make a fresh award. [824E] 9. The question whether a particular increase would amount to a flat enhancement or not was essentially a matter for the Industrial court to decide. [828B C; 883G] 10. In this case, there is no dispute that the existing wage scales of the workmen were revised and they had been given a flat rate increase in each type of posts. The appellants have not challenged the finding of the industrial Court that the enhancement was intended solely for giving a flat rates increase in every category of employees.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the provisions of the Act, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The appellant was employed by the respondent as a contractor for the manufacture and sale of sugar. It had entered into an agreement with the respondent on January 1, 1958, to supply certain quantity of sugar to its employees. The terms of the contract were: (i) that the wages payable to the workmen would be Rs. 2,000/- per month; (ii) that in respect of the period for which it remained binding on the parties, the appellant would be paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/per month as wages and (iii) that if the wages prescribed by an award were not paid to the employees within one year from the date of the agreement, the respondent would be entitled to receive the same. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the authority under section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act (3) contending that the provisions contained in sections 23 and 29 were not applicable to the case because they were not expressly mentioned in the agreement between the parties. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to get wages at the rate prescribed by the award, in view of the provisions relating to payment of wages prescribed under section 2(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and so, it had no jurisdiction to decide the question as a preliminary issue. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'wages' used in section 2 (vi) is not defined in the Act. It does not include wages prescribed for the purposes of the industrial adjudication. [801B] 2. The word 'wages" has been defined in section 3(vi), and it includes all remuneration payable to an employee under any award made by an Industrial Tribunal. [902C] 3. The words 'wages ' have been used in sections 2(vii) and 29 respectively of the said Act, and they are not defined either in the definition or in the Payment Of Wages Act. [1001F] 4. The term 'wages " has been used for the purpose of the present case, and it does not refer to wages prescribed in section 15. It is not necessary that the terms of employment should be expressed in terms of money, which would, if the terms prescribed by a notification issued under section 23 or section 24A of the Bombay Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Act, 1948, be applicable to workmen employed in any industrial establishment. [1101F G] 5. The definition of wages is not exhaustive and it only refers to wages payable for the period of operation of the award. It refers to the wages which would be payable to employees employed in an industrial establishment, and the terms thereof are not exhaustive. [110G] 6. The question whether the wages fixed by an industrial tribunal under section 25(1) of that Act are applicable to cases where the wages are prescribed by notification issued by an employer under section 16 of the Minimum Wages Act or under section 30 of the Factories Act, is a matter which can be decided only after recording evidence and it cannot be said that the wage structure prescribed by such notification is not applicable. [111H; 111A] 7. The Tribunal has held that since the wages were fixed by the employer in accordance with the terms and conditions prescribed by it, the same would be governed by the provisions as contained in section 25 of the aforesaid Act. The said view was affirmed by this Court in [110B D] 8. In the present appeal, the only question which arises for consideration is whether the wage structures prescribed by section 15 are applicable or not to the cases where they are framed under section 26 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was appointed as an Assistant Executive Engineer in the PWD Department of the State of Punjab on June 30, 1953. On July 1, 1954, he was transferred to the Public Health Department of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appellant was posted as an Executive Engineer at the Public works Department, Patiala. On August 9, 1955, he received a letter from the Superintendent of Police, Patiala, informing him that his services were being terminated by the order dated July 1. 1954, and that he had been asked to show cause why he should not be prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The Superintendent of police, Patiala sent a reply on August 9. 1955, to the appellant stating that the appellant was not guilty of criminal misappropriation or forgery as he had not been able to establish his guilt before the trial Magistrate and that the order of discharge was necessary in all cases where the act complained of is directly concerned with his official character. The Chief Engineer, Patiala forwarded a reply to the Superintendent on August 10, 1955. On September 9, 1956, the appellant filed an application under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for sanction under section 270 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and prayed that the sanction should be granted in respect of the offence of criminal breach of trust or forgery. The High Court rejected the contention of the appellant holding that the prosecution was not launched without sanction under sections 197(I) of Criminal procedure Code. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the charge against the appellant had been framed by the trial magistrate and the order passed by him was a valid order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sanction required under section 199(1)(a) of Cr. P.C. is necessary for prosecution under section 465 or 409 of Indian Penal code. [801 C] 2. The prosecution has been launched without any sanction under Section 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure and the appellant cannot be prosecuted in respect thereof under section 466 or 409, as he was not actually engaged in the performance of his official duties. [902 D] 3. The mere fact that the accused was not duly authorised to act in the discharge of his duty does not justify a reversal of the verdict by the appellate Court. [093 E] 4. The provisions of section 197 (1) are similar in terms to section 409, and the absence of such sanction is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution under sections 465 or409 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [1001 C D] 5. The fact that a sanction under s. 197(2) of C.P.C., was necessary for prosecuting a public servant under section 19(1), does not make it necessary for the prosecution to establish an offence either under section 471 or under section 420, as the case may be. [1101 D] 6. The question whether sanction is necessary in respect to a prosecution under Section 409 of IPC depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [110E] 7. In the instant case, the prosecution has not been launched by the appellant himself. It was only after the charge was framed that he could be prosecuted for his alleged criminal breach. The offence of cheating is committed by a public officer who is not authorised to do so under section 198(1). [110G H] 8. In view of the fact that there was no sanction under the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act, the conviction of the accused cannot be sustained. [111A D] 9. The charge against him is not a valid one and he can be prosecuted only for his criminal breach in respect thereto. [112E] 10. In this case, it is clear that the offence under section 120B of the Penal Code was committed by the public officer while acting in the official capacity.

The appellant was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed that he had not received any income from business in British India and that he was entitled to have the amount of loss set off against profits or gains accruing or arising within British India. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the loss arose outside British India but held that the losses were not taxable under section 12B of the Indian Act. He also held that in view of the provisions of section 10(2) of the Travancore Act, the loss could not be set off except against profits and gains accruing to the assessee within British Indian States. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the amount set off under section 10 (2) was not a part of the total income of the assessee and that the profits or gain could not have been included in the computation of the rate of tax. Held, that the words " income accruing or arise within British territories" in section 10 of the Act were wide enough to include the loss arising outside British Indian territory and that it was not an Indian State but a part thereof. The word "income" in the proviso to section 24(1) of Travancore Act did not mean income accruing, or arising outside India. It was only if the profits and gain arose outside India that the assessee could be included in computation of his total income under section 11 of the 1922 Act. In the present case the loss incurred by the appellant was not part of British India nor was it a business in India. [419C] The word 'income" is used in the main section and not in any other section. It does not mean that the income accruing to an assessee outside British territory could be excluded from computation of its total income if the loss had accrued or arisen within British territory. [520F] In the case of a resident who has been assessed to tax under section 20(1)(c) of Income Tax Act, 1961, the profits earned by him in the previous year cannot be included for computing his total world income. The expression "income accruing or arose within British country" in Section 10(3) of 1922 Act does not include income accruing outside India but only income accruing from business or profession.

The respondent Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1959 and it had entered into an agreement with the appellant Company for the retirement age of 55 years. In the year 1960, the age of retirement was fixed at 60. The age of superannuation was fixed as 58 years. On the basis of this agreement, the respondent company made a request to fix the age at 60 years. The Company agreed that the age should be fixed at 55 years and it would be appropriate if the age was fixed in 60 years for all workmen in all industries. In pursuance of the agreement, it was decided by the appellant company to fix its retirement age at 58 years and the age so fixed was fixed on the basis that the retirement of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 was fixed below 60 years and that the date of retirement should be determined at 60 or 60 years as the case may be. The Tribunal held that the respondent Company had not proved that the superannuation age of the workmen was fixed by it at 60 and, therefore, the retirement was justified. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The age fixed for retirement at 60 is a relevant consideration for fixing the age in the Bombay region. It is true that the Tribunal has not given any finding on the question whether the age fixed at 58 is correct or not. But it has been held by this Court that the retire age of 58 years should be taken into account at 60, and that it would have to be determined in light of other material and relevant circumstances. [849 D] (2) The Tribunal had not given a finding on any other material that the retiring age was 55 or 58. [950 E] (3) The respondent Company has failed to show that the service conditions of the employees were comparable with those of the Bombay Region. [1052 A] (4) The award made by the Tribunal is, therefore bad in law and it must be set aside. [1153 C] (5) The Award made by it is not based on any evidence which could justify a revision of the age to the age. [1254 D] In the present case, the Tribunal had found that the appellant workmen were represented at the time of retirement and they were represented by their representatives in the capacity of employees. They were represented only at the age 55 or 60. [1355 E] The age was not fixed at the date when the age came to be fixed. [1454 C] In view of the fact that the award made in all cases had been confirmed by this court, it would not be proper for the Tribunal to say that the birth of retirement age should have been fixed at 50 years and if the retirement is fixed at a 60 or 55 years as case may justify a revised age of retire at 60 because the age is fixed on a day when the last date of superannuation is fixed, the same would be reasonable. [1554 D E] In this connection it was observed by this High Court that in all the awards made in the present cases the age has been fixed as 55 or 55 and in some cases it has not been shown that the employees represented at that time were represented on the date fixed. The fact that in many cases the retirement would be 60 or 58 years as if the retirees were represented before the age could have been determined at 55 or 57 years as a case may require, is of no consequence because the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the parents and relatives of the deceased employees were represented when the retirement came to an end.

The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company had been functioning as a managing agent of the company and its members. It had been carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Barium Chemicals Ltd., which is a registered office at Bombay. The Company Law Board by its order dated February 6, 1964 directed that the affairs of the appellant company be conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members and other persons and others and also that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs thereof were being conducted with intention to defraud their creditors, member and other person and others. The first respondent challenged the said order by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Board had no power under section 237(b) to appoint an investigation and report thereon in such manner as it could and did not form the opinion to be formed under section 235(b). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 is a judicial function. It cannot be delegated to any other body or authority subordinate to it. [801 E] (2) The Board has no power to delegate its functions to another body or authorities subordinate to them. The power of appointment of an investigation officer and the powers of the Board are not administrative in nature but are merely administrative in character. [902 F] (3) The powers conferred on a Board under section 236(b), cannot be exercised by any other authority subordinate thereto. [1001 G] (4) The word 'authority' used in section 237 has to be construed as an administrative power and not a judicial power. [1101 A B] (5) The expression 'authority" is not defined in the Companies act, 1956 but it has been used in a wide sense. It does not include any body or Authority subordinate to the Board. [110 C] (6) The words 'authority ' have to be interpreted in their widest amplitude and they must be construed in their ordinary sense. [111 D] (7) The function of the Company Law board is to carry out its functions under section 239(b)(i). It cannot delegate its function to another person or persons subordinate to him.

The appellant was convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was also convicted under sections 395 and 412 of the I.P.C. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had erred in drawing a presumption against him under section 114 of the Evidence Act because he had not been able to establish his complicity in the crime. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The presumption is only drawn when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons with the crime and it is impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of. [723 B] 2. The prosecution has not established any other circumstance which would lead to the inference that the appellant was dacoits at night. [824 C] 3. The fact that the dacoity had taken place in the house of the appellants and the witnesses were found with the looted goods, clearly shows that the presumption under section 113 of the Criminal Procedure Code is only rebuttable. [925 D] 4. The evidence on record does not show that the dacoits were either the dacoits or the dacoits at the time when they were found. It is true that the appellants were not the dacoits but it was a case where the dacoity took place in their houses and the looted articles were found in their house. [1025 E] 5. The conviction of the accused under section 396 of the Penal Code cannot be sustained on the sole evidence of the witnesses who are alleged to have been present at the scene of occurrence. [1126 F] 6. The circumstances clearly show that there was no other evidence on which the presumption could be drawn against the appellants. [1227 G] 7. In view of the fact that there is no other reliable evidence to establish the complicity in this crime, it cannot be said that the conviction of these appellants under section 397 of the Code is not sustainable. [1328 C] 8. The facts are clearly established and therefore the conviction recorded by the courts is correct in law. [1427 G H] 9. In the circumstances, the conviction under section 394 of the IPC is set aside and the appellants are acquitted of all the charges framed against them.

The petitioner 's company was manufacturing a drug in the name of "Goa" which is a medicinal preparation containing alcohol. The petitioner purchased a drug from the market and obtained a licence for the manufacture of "Propyl" which was granted to him by the Drugs Controller, Delhi. On the strength of an agreement between the petitioner and the Drugs Inspector, the petitioner purchased the said drug from a registered dealer. The Drugs Inspector issued a notice under Section 7(1) of the Act calling upon the petitioner to show cause why the licence should not be cancelled. The respondent filed a reply denying the allegations made in the petition. The State Government rejected the petition on the ground that the petitioner did not come within the definition of 'thinner ' as contained in Rule 2(x)(2) of Rules, 1926 and that the said rule was ultra vires the Act. The High Court held that the provisions of the Drugs (Propes) Rules, 1924 were ultra vires and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned order was not a speaking order as the same was passed without giving an opportunity to the petitioner before passing the order. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The provisions of Rule 2 (x)(1) are mandatory in character and do not confer any right on the petitioner for sale or purchase of the specified poison. [601B] 2. The impugned order is a speaking one and does not give an opportunity of hearing to the respondent before passing it. [702C] 3. The procedure prescribed under Rule 13(1)(2), which is mandatory in nature, has been substantially complied with by the petitioner. The Rules have been framed in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government under Section 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the rules made thereunder. [76G] 4. The power to regulate the possession of the substance as a poison is not a matter of right to carry on the same. It is only when it is found that the substance is not poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning, it can be said that the same substance should be declared as poison for purposes of the law and that no other substance is liable to be included in the list of substances contained in the Rules. [77G] 5. The object of the enactment is to regulate possession of a substance which is not an ingredient of trade in poison. It does not confer right on any person to have an absolute right to have a share or interest in the quantity maintained by him. [78A B] 6. The word 'thine' used in Rule 13 (1) is wide enough to include all substances specified in the Schedule and it cannot be said to be exhaustive of all substances which are included in a list of substance contained in a rule. It only means that the article must be capable of being used for human consumption or use as a medicine. [79C] 7. The expression 'thines' is not defined in the Act but it has been defined in Section 2(xi) of that Act. [80D] 8. The definition of "thine" in Rule 3 of Rules is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all substances included in any list of Substances specified in a Rule. It cannot be held that all substances enumerated in a Schedule are not covered by the Schedule. [81E] 9. In view of the provisions contained in Section 5 of the , the Act does not apply to the substance specified in Rule 12(1). The definition is wide, comprehensive and exhaustive. The said expression has been used in the context of the Rules and it must be construed strictly. [82F] 10. It would be a matter for the legislature to decide whether the substance contained therein is a poison or not. If the substance contains any other substance which can be used for causing death, it cannot fall within the ambit of the definition.

The assessee firm was carrying on business of money lending business in the name and style of "B.C.I.T. (India) Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The assessee firm had advanced loans to the Bombay firm for the purpose of its business. The Bombay firm was registered as a dealer under section 10(2)(xi) of the Income tax Act, 1922. During the assessment year 1955, the assessee firm made an application to the tribunal under section 66(1) of that Act for the issue of a statement of case on the ground that the debt in question was not one incurred in the course of its money lending trade and that it was doubtful debts. The tribunal by its order dated July 29, 1969 held that the amount in question had been written off by the assessee in his books of account as irrecoverable debt representing loss sustained in the other business of the assessee and disallowed the claim of the department on the following grounds: (i) that the amounts were not drawn in the ordinary course of the money lending Business of the appellant firm at the time when it became a debtor in Samvat year 2007, and (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the monies sent by the Bombay Firm as loans were not in the normal course of business of its income. The Tribunal held that since the debt was not a bad debt, the amount could not be said to have been written down in the books of accounts as irrecoverable debts. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court had erred in holding that the debts were not one of the business of a money lending firm at that time when they became a creditor in Sampat year 2007 and that the liability incurred by the appellant in the said business of loan was not an "s debt" within the meaning of section 10 (2)(xii) of Income tax act, 1922, and that since there was a debt in the assessee 's business of his own money lending, it could not have been claimed as one of its assets. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "any other business" in section 10 of the Act means any business which is carried on by or through the assessee himself and includes any business relating to such business. [701B] 2.2 The expression 'any other Business' in section 8(4) of Act 1922, does not include a business relating only to money lending transactions. It does not mean that the money lent business must be carried on in the regular course of his business. In the instant case, the debt which was due at the end of each year at the relevant time was not in existence at the date when it become a debtor. [801C] 2:1 The liability incurred in connection with such business cannot be said as one incurred by a money lender in the business. It is only if the amount is written off or written off, that the same can be claimed as an "any Other Business" in the hands of the person who has been carrying on any other business. If the debt is not one which was in existence and the liability is not known to the assessee at all, it cannot be held that there is a debt incurred by him in the previous year. [901D] 2(a) The expression used in section 7 of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, does refer only to "any business relating" in respect of which the liability was incurred by an assessee in the earlier year. It cannot be construed that the said expression is not confined to money lent transactions and it does not cover any other activity carried on with a view to enable the assessee to claim as one "s debts". [902F] 2.(b) The word 'any Other business" has been used in the sense of "business relating to moneylending business", and it is not necessary that the entire amount should be written off.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands in the State of Karnataka. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the acquisition proceedings on various grounds, including that the acquisition was not made within two years from the date of the stay orders and that the respondents had failed to disclose the same in their counter affidavit. The High Court dismissed the said writ petitions holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 136 of the Constitution. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, HELD: 1.1. The impugned judgment of the High court is set aside and the matter is remitted back to the High Judge for deciding the question raised in the writ petitions afresh after giving an opportunity to the petitioners to file their counter affidavits. [824B] 2.2. In view of the fact that the stay order was passed by this Court on April 29, 1987, the respondents were not able to disclose all the facts and circumstances which led them to make out a case for grant of interim relief. The respondents had filed their counteraffidavit in response to the notice issued by this court. They also produced certain documents showing the acquisition of the lands in question. [924B C] 3.3.1 The High court has committed an error in holding that there was no material on record to show that the land in question was acquired for a public purpose and that it was not a private land. [1025E] 4.2 In view thereof, the High Courts have committed an illegality in rejecting the writ petition filed by the respondents. The Special Leave Petition is liable to be dismissed. [1124F G] 3:1.3 The High Courts were right in holding, that the award was not passed within two year from the commencement of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 and that there is no reference in the determination of the question of acquisition of lands in terms of Section 11 A of the Act. [1224F] 3;2.3 In view whereof, the writ petitioners were entitled to an interim relief under Section 11A of the said Act. The appellants are not entitled for any interim relief as prayed for by them. [1325E C] 4:1 The respondents have failed to show any material on the basis of which they could be granted interim relief in their favour. [1424F H] 3,2.4 In view Of the fact, the appellants were not given an opportunity of being heard before passing the final order of acquisition. [1525E G] 4;3.5 The HighCourt has committed a manifest error in rejecting all the writ applications filed by them and holding that they are not maintainable. [1824F C] 5:1 In view, however, of the facts of the present case, it is clear that the appellants have failed in showing any material before this Court to show their bonafides. The interim relief granted by this High Court cannot be said to be a mere formality or an exercise of discretion. [1924F; 1825A] 3 :1.6 In the instant case, the acquisition has been made within the stipulated time and the appellants are entitled for interim relief only from the stage of passing the award. [2026E] 2:1 It is well settled that the interim relief cannot be granted by way of an interim order. The Court must be satisfied that the facts disclosed in the application for grant or the reasons stated therein are such which would justify the grant of a final relief. [182B C; 1824A B] 3 (a) In the present cases, the award has been passed on March 29, 1988 and the same was published on September 20, 1984. The stay orders were passed by the HighCourt on April 30, 1987 and the respondents have not disclosed any material to show the bonafides of the appellants.

The appellant was appointed as a permanent employee in the bank of Baroda on January 1, 1959. He was promoted to the post of a permanent servant by order dated March 31, 1962. On February 1, 1963 he was confirmed in the service of the bank and his salary was fixed at Rs. (b) and (c). The appellant challenged the award before the Central Government under s. 10(2)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Central Government dismissed the appeal on March 31/1963.
