On appeal by the bank the Central Govt. confirmed the order of the Desai Tribunal. In the meanwhile the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award and prayed for a declaration that he was entitled to be paid his salary from January 1 1963 as on January 2, 1959 and also for the years 1960 and 1961 and for the year 1960 and 1962 respectively. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the award was not in accordance with cl. (d) and cl. 12 of the Sastry Award and that the appellant was entitled only to increments under sub cl. 182 of the standing award. On further appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The award is not a final award. It does not say that the workmen were entitled to any increments under cl. 18 of the Standing Award. [815 C] 2. The Tribunal has rightly held that the Sastry award was in accordancewith cl. 16 of the Ordinance and the Desai award was correctly made. [916 D] 3. The appellant was not entitled to the increments under s, 18 of this Ordinance as on February 1. 1959. [1017 E] 4. The question whether the award is a final or a final one has to be decided in the light of cl. 15 of the Award and the reasons given by the Tribunal for its decision are not correct. [1116 D C] 5. The language used in cl. 14 of the award shows that it was intended to give relief to workmen who were drawing basic pay at a stage when they entered service of bank before January 1 1959, but this was done with the object of giving relief to them under cl.(d) which was not so far as the present case is concerned. [1216 E] 6. The words "regular" in cl.(c) of cl.(b) of s. 18 are clear and unambiguous. It must be given effect to, and it cannot be implied that the words "average basic pay" were intended to convey a meaning which would give relief only to workmen drawing basic salary at a time when they enter service of Bank before January 1959. The word "regular " in cl(c) is not used in the sense of giving benefit to workmen drawn from an existing scale or the actual basic pay as on 1st January 1959, and therefore it cannot mean that the terms "regularity" were meant to convey any meaning which could give relief even to workmen draw basic salary. [13 F] 7. The expression "regularisation" in the Sastry awards means that the basic pay fixed by the Sastry Tribunal was Rs. 2,000/- and not Rs. 1,000/-. It is true that the Desai Award was given in 1962 but it does not mean that it should be given retrospective effect to the Sastry Awards. [14 F] 8. The Sastry Award was clearly a final Award. It did not say anything about the basic salary fixed by cl.(a) of el. (c) and the two increments provided by sub cl.(aa) of Cl. (a), (b), (c), (d). The Sastry award is clear and consistent with the provisions of cl(d)and cl.12 of the agreement. [15 F] 9.

The Government of West Bengal, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') issued a notification under section 4(1)(a) of that Act on June 29, 1981. The Government of India published a notification on June 30, 1981 and published a notice in the official gazette on July 28, 1981 calling upon the Taj Group of Hotels to sell the land to the Government of Calcutta for the construction of a Five Star Hotel at Calcutta. The Taj Group 's representation was made by the Government to the Chief Minister that the land should be allotted to the Taj group of Hotels and that the Government should not allot any land to them. On July 29,1981 the Government issued a notice under section 5(1), (a) stating that the Tajgroup of Hotels would be set up within the State for the purpose of setting up of hotels in Calcutta. In response to this notice, the Government filed an application before the High Court of Calcutta praying for a direction to the effect that the lands should be given to the hotel group of Hotel for the purposes of settingup of industries within the state and for the benefit of the TajGroup of Hotels. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State was not in a position to make available the land allotted to it for the public interest. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government is duty bound to allot any lands to the Hotel group of hotels within the country and if the Government is satisfied that the hotel is set up in a Five star hotel, it can refuse to give such land to any person who has been allotted any land for the said purpose. [701B] 1.2 The Government cannot be allowed to take over the land from the Zoo or other hotels without the necessary permission of the Government. [802C] 2.1 In view of the fact that the Hotel was set up by the Taj groups of Hotels, the State Government could not have allotted any lands for the hotel to the exclusion of the hotel. [820D] 1.(a) The Government has no power under section 3 (1) to allot land to a hotel group or to permit allotment of any land in favour of the Govt. of West Bengary. [823C] 1(b) The State Government cannot make any allotment of land to Taj Group for the aforesaid purpose. It is not open to the State to take away any land from Zoo without the requisite permission of Government. The State has no right to allot such land in accordance with the provisions of section 3. [825D] 2.(a)(i) The question whether a hotel can be setup within the territory of West Pakistan or outside India is not relevant for deciding the present case. [822E] (b) In view thereof, it cannot be said that the Municipality was in any way concerned with the construction and development of the Five Star hotel in Calcutta and that it had no authority to grant lease of Begumbari land to an Taj Group. [821F] 3.(a). The Government could have granted a lease of the land only if it wanted to start a Fivestar Hotel in Calcutta, but not for any other purpose. The Municipality was bound to give permission to the Raja of West Punjab for setting up a Fivel Star hotel within the territories of West India. [824E] 4.(a), (b)(i), (c) and (ii) of section 2(1). The State is under an obligation to provide facilities for construction of Five Star Hotels in Calcutta as a policy decision to the hotels. [828A D] 5.(a)... (b). The Municipality has no authority, either to grant or refuse permission to start any Five Star hotels in West Bengal.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, purchased a property from the firm of his son and paid Rs.50,000 to his wife. The assessee was not in possession of any money lending business. He had no overdraft facility. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee at Rs. 50,000 and the Tribunal held that the amount of Rs.67,560/12 was not available with the firm. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court reversed the decision of the Tribunal and held that there was no valid gift in favour of the deceased. The High Court also held that section 10 did not apply to the gifts of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.25,000 made by the assessee. In this case, the assessee had made a valid gift of Rs 50, 000 and Rs 25,000 on 1.1. 1957. The Tribunal held in favour on the ground that the assessee was entitled to the amount mentioned in the books of account of his father. On further appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High court had erred in holding that the gift was not valid and that the same was not made by debiting the amounts to the accounts of the firm and that there were no receipts from the assessee's account. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The amount of money advanced by the deceased to his son was not a valid one. [701B] 2. The fact that the money was transferred in the personal account of the minores does not make any difference because the amount was not received from the deceased and the same had been credited in the account of L. K. The amounts were credited in his account in the firm's personal account. [802C] 3. The mere fact that there is a valid transfer in the name of the father, does not mean that the said amount was transferred to his account. It is only when the money is received from his wife that it can be included in the property passing on the death of the donor. [901D] 4. The expression "in the personal accounts" has been used in section 10(1) of the Act and not in the context of the entries made in the book of account. The word "in any other account" is not defined in the Act. It does not include a deposit or a receipt for money advanced to his father by a banking company or a company which was not an Indian company. [1001E] 5. The words "in such other account", occurring in section 9(1)(b) of that Act, refer to the account maintained by the firm as well as the account. In the present case, there is no evidence on record to show that the amounts were debited in the accounts. There was no evidence to show how the amount received from L.K. and K. were credited into the account in his personal account in their account. There is nothing to show whether the amount had been transferred to the assessee or not. [1101F] 6. The entries in the general diary of the Hindu undivided families are not relevant for the purpose of this case. It was only when money was received from a banking Company or a firm or a Company which was a company that it could be included. [110G H] 7. In view of the fact that money had been transmitted to the firm, the amount paid by L. Kumar and K were credited to his personal accounts in the individual account of her father, there was nothing to indicate that the moneys were credited as they were received from her. [111H; 111A B] 8. The position is clear that the payment of Rs 2 lakhs made by L,K and K to his daughter was not genuine. There could be no doubt that the payments were made by him in the ordinary course of business.

The appellant, Shri B.K. Misra was appointed as the law secretary to the government of Orissa, the government in the secretariat and he was posted as the Law Secretary to the Government of Orissa. On October 10, 1966, he was transferred from the secretarial department to the district courts. He was posted at the district court. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his transfer order dated October 10/10, 1966. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no authority to hold the posts in the Secretariat and that he was not the law Secretary to Government of India. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has jurisdiction under article 235 of the Constitution to direct transfer of district courts from one cadre to another cadre. [601B] 2.2 The High Courts have jurisdiction to issue directions for transfer of judicial officers from one district court to another district courts and to transfer them from one department to another. [702C] 3.1 In view of the above, the High court had no jurisdiction to direct the transfer of the judicial officers posted at district courts to any other district court or district court in the State of Orissa and that the transfer was not made by the High Courts within their powers under article 233. [801D] 2:1 The power of the High courts to direct transfers of judicial officer from one division to another is vested in the High judiciary under article 234 of the constitution. [820E] 3:2.3 In view thereof, the impugned orders of transfer are quashed and set aside. [823G] 3;2.4 The High courts have jurisdiction under Article 235 of Constitution to issue appropriate directions for transferring the judicial officer posted at one district courts or district courts in the district judiciary from one place to another within their jurisdiction. [825E] 2 5:1.3 The High judiciary has no power to direct that any district court subordinate to it shall be transferred to another division or district judiciary. [826A D] 3,2.5 In view Of the above two decisions of this Court, the appellant was not entitled to any relief in these appeals. [822B] 3(a) The High judicial officers working in the office of District Judges were posted at different places and they were transferred from one Division to another by transfer from one District Judge to another and that they were posted in the administrative department of district judges. [828C] 2 (b) The appellant was appointed on a temporary basis as an Assistant Law Secretary, Deputy Legal Adviser and Legal Remembrancer, Deputy Director General of Police, Orissa, who is the appointing authority for the district judges and the High Judicial officers working there. He had been transferred to the Secretariat cadre in the month of October 10. 1966. He continued to work in the said office till December 10, 1967 when he was appointed to the post of Law Secretary. The transfer order was issued on November 10, 1968. The respondent No. 1 was posted in a district court at Cuttack and he joined his duty as Law Secretary on January 11, 1969. On February 12, 1970, he filed an application before the Chief Justice for transferring him from one High Court to another State. He also made an application for transfer to another High Court. The Chief Justice by his order dated March 6, 1971 directed that the respondent No 1 be transferred from his present place of posting at Cuttack to another District court and that if he was so posted in any other District court, he would be entitled to all the benefits of seniority and promotion. On April 4, 1972, the Chief justice made an order transferring him to another Division of district court and directed that he should be transferred back to his present station. The State Government by its order dated May 7, 1971 transferred him to one High court. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Civil Procedure Code for quashing the transfer order.

The appellant, who was the co- sharer in the suit land, purchased a share of 5.5 acres of land from one Smt. Ram Sarup and sold it to the vendor 's son 's brother 's sons 's brothers 's father 's sister 's husband 's daughter 's mother 's sisters 's wife 's children 's daughters 's elder brother ' sister 's family. The appellant purchased a part of the land from Smt. Chand Rani and sold the same to the co sharers. The sale was made in favour of the appellant, but the vendor did not execute any sale deed in respect of the remaining portion of the property. On the other hand, the appellant purchased another part of his share in the land and sold a part thereof to Smt. Chander Rani who was also a co-sharer. The suit was filed on behalf of the vendors 's co-sharers claiming pre entption under clause (b) of section 15(1)(c) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913. The trial court held that the appellant had not proved that he purchased any part of land or property from Smt Chander Rani and that he did not have any right to pre emption under section 15 (1)(b) as a co sharer. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The expression 's share in a co­sharer' in the first three clauses of section15(1) (a) is a reasonable restriction on the right of pre entrants to the share of the vendor or vendors in the property sold. [901F] 2. The word 's' in clause (c) means that the right to preemption under clause(b) includes only those co-owners who do not have a share in any property sold and that the sale is by a female co­sharers. [1001G] 3. The right of preemption conferred on co-holders in the case of pre ferption is a restriction on their right of re entrants. [091F] 4. The words 's right of ad emption' in section 15 of the Act are not to be read as wide enough to include only those persons who do or have a right to acquire, or dispose of property conferred by Article 14 or 15(2)(b). [902B] 5. The legal position is well settled that the word 'S' in clauses (c), (d) and (e) of Section 15(l)(a) are not words which can be read into it but they must be read in the context. [991F G] 6. In the instant case, the right conferred on the appellant by clause (a)(b), (c). is a right vested in co­holders in respect thereof. The definition of 's 'co-sharers' in Section 15 (l)(b)(c), is not exhaustive and it does not include any person who has a share or interest in any land sold or a part held by him. [981F H] 7. In view of the fact that the suit property belonged to more than one co­ sharers, the rights of pre emplated on them cannot be denied. [19982A F] 8. The High Court was right in holding that the definition of "co-sharer" in section15 (1)(b)(a), (b)(b)] and (c)(d) is not applicable to the facts of this case. [19993F H; 901 A B] 9.

The appellant and his two sons, who were the alienees of the properties in question, had executed a compromise deed dated 21.8.1987 between the father and the alieneeees of different properties in favour of the alienors. The second respondent herein, who was the alienor, had filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property in question against the appellant and the second respondent. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the compromise deed executed by the alieners did not bind them and that the sale deeds were valid and binding on them. The High Court held that the said compromise was void and non est and that it was not open to the alienes to file a suit against the alienators for partition of the same property. In appeal, this Court reversed the judgment of the High Court holding that there was no reason to interfere with the findings recorded by the Trial Court and dismissed the suit. Dismissing the special leave petition, HELD: 1.1 The compromise deed is valid and does not bind the alienates. It is a document which has been accepted by all parties. [901B] 2.2 The compromise is valid. There was no need for the alienator to file any suit against him for partition. [093C] 3.3 The compromise was not binding on the aliener and he had no interest in the property prior to the compromise. [1026D] 4.1 In view of the fact that there were improvements made by the parties, it is clear that the second Respondent had no right in the properties prior to 21.08.1987. [1127E] 3:1 The High court was not justified in holding that a compromise decree was valid and legal. [110G] 2:2.3 In view thereof, the compromise decree cannot be said to be invalid or illegal. [109H; 110A] 3 :2.4 The compromise decree is valid, legal and binding. [111B] 3] 4:1.5 The compromise has been arrived at after a full and complete settlement of all the disputes between the parties. It was not necessary for the parties to have signed the compromise petition which had been accepted and all the parties had accepted the document of compromise. There is no reason why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis thereof, it cannot be held that there has been an attempt to hold out any interest in favour or part with the property. [112A B] 3;2.6 The compromise does not create any interest or claim any right in favour nor does it create any right or claim interest in respect of the entire property. It only provides for a settlement of the disputes by way of compromise and no other mode of settlement is permissible.

The appellant company, a registered medical practitioner, was granted sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958. The workmen of the Alembic Glass Industries Ltd., Baroda, applied for sick leave under section 49 of the Act before the Tribunal. The Tribunal by its award dated August 29, 1958 allowed the application of the workmen holding that the sickness benefit would be lost for the first two days of sickness. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the ground that it was not competent to grant sick leave and that the workmen did not deserve any special treatment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the sickness benefits were granted by the Tribunal, the benefit of the sick leave could not be categorised as privilege. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1. The question whether the appellant company is entitled to the benefit under section 48 of the Industrial Disputes Act or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [701B] 2.2. In order to appreciate the contentions raised on behalf of the appellant, it would be necessary to set out the relevant provisions of the industrial Disputes Act. The relevant provisions are: (i) Section 49(1)(a) of the said Act provides that where a workman is entitled for sick Leave under section 47 of the , he shall not be entitled to any benefit under this Act; (ii) The proviso to section 49(2) of that Act provides, inter alia, that if the workman has availed himself of the benefits of sick leave granted by him, he would not be eligible for such benefit. [801C] 2.(a) In view of the provisions of section 48(1), the appellant is entitled only to the benefits under section 50 of the . The Tribunal was therefore justified in allowing the claim of the respondent company. [820D] 3.2 The Tribunal has committed an error in holding that as the sickness relief was granted by it, the appellant was not entitled to such benefit and that it did not require any special medical treatment. [823E] 3.(b) In the present case, the workmen had claimed that they were entitled to receive the benefits from the appellant under section 51 of the '[820F G] 4.3 The Tribunal had also held that the claim for grant of sick Leave was barred by limitation. [822G] 4.(a)(i) The question as to whether the sickness treatment benefit would cease to be available to the workmen or not, is a matter which has to be decided on the facts of each individual case. In the instant case, it is not disputed that the appellant had availed of the benefit for the period from January 1, 1975 to January 1 1975 and that they did not have any special health facility. [821F] 4(a)(ii) It is true that the question whether a sickness benefit can be claimed by the workmen under section 45 of the I.D. Act or whether the same would cease on the expiry of the period of one year from January1, 1975 has to depend upon the circumstances of the case and not on the question as regards the adequacy of the sickness. [825G] 5.(a). The appellant is not entitled for any special benefit under the provisions contained in section 48 (1) of '[821F G H] 6.2 In view thereof, the appeal fails and it is dismissed.

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as 'the PASA Act') by an order dated August 7, 1955. The grounds were vague and not specific. The detaining authority rejected the representation on the ground that it was not made in a case where particulars were furnished. The appellant challenged the validity of the detention order on the following grounds: (1) that the grounds furnished are vague and non-specific; (2) that there is no material to show that the activities alleged to have been taken place by the appellant were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order; (3) that in any case, the detaining authority has not applied its mind to the facts of the case and had not given a proper opportunity of representation to the detenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of detention is vitiated on account of non-application of mind by the detaining authorities. [601B] 2. The power under section 10 of the PASA is not an absolute one but is an extraordinary power conferred on the State Government and it is a duty cast upon the detaining Authority to disclose facts which are in public interest. If the grounds are vague or non-existent, the order cannot be sustained. [701C] 3. The affidavit filed by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay discloses that the appellant was not furnished with the particulars as required under section 5(1) of the Act and that he had not made any representation against his detention. He has also not given any particulars in respect of the activities which were prejudicial or which were likely to be prejudicial to maintenance of the public order. [801D] 4. The mere fact that the detaining Authorities have applied their mind to these facts, does not mean that they have applied its own mind to those facts. [820E] 5. In the instant case, there is nothing to show as to what was stated in the affidavit filed on behalf of the Under Secretaries to the Govt. of Bombay that the particulars were not furnished. There is no evidence to suggest that the contents of the grounds were false or that they were vague or that the copies of the documents were not supplied to the appellant. [823E] 6. The fact that there was a serious dispute as to whether the grounds contained in the grounds had been explained by the petitioner does not make any difference because the affidavit is silent about the contents thereof. It is true that the affidavit does not disclose the facts which were stated in public interests but it is also clear from the affidavit that the petitioner has made a representation against the order of his detention and that the same was considered by the Government before rejecting his representation. [825E] 7. The petition must be dismissed.

The respondent was serving as a warrant officer in the Army. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed misconduct under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The respondent challenged his dismissal before the Central Government by way of an application under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service. The Central Government rejected the application and the respondent filed a petition under article 227 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition on the view that the order was not in conformity with r.14 of the Rules, 1955, and the Central Gove rnment had no power to remove him from service, and that the Central Govt. could not make any order under r 14 of Army Rules 1954. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of dismissal is bad in law as it was passed by a court martial without being tried by a Court Martial. [901 A] 2. The power to dismiss or remove from service is not absolute and is subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. It is only when the officer is found guilty of misconduct under s. 19 of the General Clauses Act, that he can be removed from service by a competent court martial. [1001 B] 3. The powers conferred on the Central government under r., 14 of Rules 1954 are not absolute. The same cannot be exercised in derogation of the provisions contained in r. 15 of the rules, 1955. [093 C] 4. The language used in r, 14 is clear and unambiguous. It does not say that the power to suspend or dismiss a person subject to this Act is not an absolute one. The words "subject to the other provisions of this Act" occurring in r.,14 are wide enough to include within its scope all the powers which may be exercised by a civil court martial, including the power of dismissal or removal from the service. [1101 D] 5. The word 'discharge' is not defined in the Act. It only means that the officer who is dismissed or removed from the services must be placed under suspension pending enquiry into his conduct. [110E] 6. The expression "Dismissal" has been used in s. 2(a) of the Indian Army Rules. The term 'dispensing' is defined in r 14 as meaning a person who is found to have committed misconduct, and not an officer who was found guilty by court martial or tried by the court martial for misconduct under the Act, and such other provisions are also included within its ambit. [111E] 7. In view of the clear language used by the legislature in r,. 14, it must be held that the respondent was a person subjected to the Army Rule 14 of 1954. [112F G] 8. The appellant had been dismissed from the Army on the charge of misconduct and he was not found guilty. [113G] 9. In the circumstances, the order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal is not sustainable in law.

The appellant Company imported tea from outside the octroi limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale therein. The appellant Company claimed that it was entitled to levy octroi on the tea imported into the octroi limit of the Municipality and that the Government had no power to impose octroi duty from January 14, 1964, in accordance with the resolutions dated February 25, 1963 and March 17, 1963. The High Court held that the appellant Company was not liable to pay octroi duty under r. 3(b) of the rules framed by the Panchayat. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the High Court had no jurisdiction to deal with the question whether the Company imported the tea for consumption or sale within the octroi area, and that since the appellant had not produced any evidence in support of its contention that the tea was manufactured, processed or otherwise dealt with, the High court should have remanded the case to the Panchayat Samiti. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order is set aside. The matter is remitted to the High 'Court for disposal according to law. [701B] 2. The question whether a Company imported from outside octroi limits or not was within the municipal limits of a Panchayat would be decided by the High' Court only after the decision of the Standing Committee on January 14 and March 18, 1963, and if it is found that the Company had imported tea for use or consumption, used or sold therein. [801C] 3. The fact that the company was not importing tea within the limits of Panchayat would not make any difference to its case. [820D] 4. The word "sale" in r.3(b), as it stood at the relevant time, must be interpreted in the sense that the sale must be understood as a matter of law and that it is only when the sale is effected by a Panchayat or otherwise dealing with it that the thing is done and that there is an element of sale in the form of octroi. [823E] 5. The expression "sale " in rs. 3 (b) must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules made thereunder. [825F] 6. The words "sale ' in r..3(a), " in s. 3, " are not to be interpreted as requiring the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy of octroi from January 15, 1964 but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean that the tax so selected by the Standing committee would be determined by it. [822F] 7. The object of the Act is to provide for the imposition of octroi duty on tea imported in the octroi areas and to regulate the sale thereof in accordance therewith. [826B] 8. The Legislature has not intended to confer any power on the Panchayat or to impose a tax on tea which is sold within the municipality limits. It does not say that the levy of Octroi duty from time to time would be governed by the provisions of r.2(b). [823G] 9. In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to the octroi duty at the rate mentioned in r.(b) and the High Courts were right in holding that the Notification issued under r.(c) was invalid. [827A D] 10. The notification issued by the Government under r., 4(a) of r.(d), is valid.

The appellant No. 1 was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33 of the Act for an offence punishable under section 30(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and he was convicted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, under section 12(6) of that Act. The appellants were also convicted under section 32(1), (2) readwith section 31 of the said Act and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of six months or fine or with both. The appellant No 1 filed an appeal before the High Court against his conviction under section 33(1). The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the conciliation proceedings were not pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed by the Conciliation Officer and therefore the appellants could not be convicted under sections 31(2) and (3) of this Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the dispute between the parties had been referred to the Labour Court for adjudication and the High court had no jurisdiction to try the same. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The conciliation proceedings are deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the report of the Conciliation officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the Conciliation Officers do not make his report within 14 days but which is not a period specified in section 12 (6) and therefore there was no termination of the conciliation proceeding. [701B] 2. The expression " Pending proceedings" used in section 20(2), as it stood at the time when the conciliation officer has commenced, would mean that the Conciliation Office is bound to make its report within a fortnight but not thereafter. [802C] 3. The words " Pending proceeding" occurring in section 10 of the 1947 Act are wide enough to include all proceedings pending before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal or before a Board or of any proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board, as the case may be. [820D E] 4. The word ' Pending proceeding' used in Section 20(1)(b), is wider than what was contemplated by the Act and therefore it would not mean that proceedings pending on the date when the settlement is arrived at, when a report of conciliation officer is sent to the appropriate government or where the ConciliationOfficer has commenced and the proceedings are closed. [823E] 5. The language used in the section clearly shows that the intention of the legislature was to get a settlement made with expedition and if it is not possible to complete the proceedings within 14 months, then the conciliation Officer would have to make his award within 14 weeks but not later than 14 days. [825F] 6. In view of the language used by the Legislature in section 30 of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1950, the expression " pending proceeding" has been interpreted in a manner which is consistent with the object of the legislation and it cannot be said that the proceedings before a Conciliation Officer are not closed. The definition of ' Pending proceedings' in section 2(1A)(b)(i) of 1947 Act does not mean any proceeding pending on a Labour court or Tribunal, as they were before a reference under section 10(2). [823G] 7. In the instant case, the conciliation Proceedings had continued for a long time and therefore after 14 days the Conciliation Proceedings were taken on a complaint by Assistant Commissioner of Labour under section 3(1D) read along with section 31 (1A) of Act, the Conciliation proceedings were taken and the Conciliation Report was submitted to the Government. [822E] 8. The provisions of section 12 of the Indian Contract Labour Act, 1872, do not apply to a case where the conciliation process has been completed.

The petitioner was in jail for a period of about two years. He was arrested on 2nd January 1986 and he was released on bail on 22nd February, 1986. The detention order was passed on the basis of the statement made by the District Magistrate that the detenu had already surrendered but he was not in jail. On the basis thereof the petitioner was detained under the Act on 2 nd January 1986. He filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention and also challenged his detention on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of detention was illegal because the detaining authority had not applied its mind to all relevant aspects and had mechanically confirmed the order. In appeal, the Division Bench of the High Court held that the detention order could be justified only if the detenu was in custody and there was no imminent possibility of his being released on the bail. The Division Bench also held that since the detaining authorities were not satisfied with the necessity to detain the petitioner, they could not have been detained under section 3(2) of the Act. In the present case, the High court has held that there was a clear nexus between the detenu and the order passed by the Government on 2th January 1986 which was in force till the date of his release on bail. It is also held by the Division bench that the detaining Authority had not considered all relevant factors while passing the detention orders and had merely relied upon the statements made by him in the petition and the documents referred to and/or relied upon by the detaining officer. The order of the Government was, therefore, invalid and the detenu could not be detained under any of the provisions of the [Special Courts Act, 1985]. In the affidavit filed on behalf of the State it has been stated that the petitioner had surrendered in respect of criminal case which was pending against him and he had already been released on 22 nd February 1986. It has also been stated therein that the grounds for detention were not on proper consideration but on relevant considerations. The detenu was not served with all the documents relied upon and/ or relied upon. In these circumstances, it is clear that the impugned order of preventive detention was passed after the order was served on the petitioner. The detaining authority was fully justified in putting him back in jail and he could not validly be detained in jail even if the order had been passed by him on 2 1st January 1986 when it was passed. In view of the above, the petition is allowed.

The appellant, a dealer carrying on business in gold ornaments and articles of gold ornaments, was granted permission to carry on the business in the same premises in which he carried on his business as a money lender, banker or any other business in which the appellant was intending to carryon money lending business. The Administrator by virtue of the powers conferred upon him under sec. 28 of the Act, issued a license to a dealer for carrying on the trade in gold jewellery and articles in the premises in question. On the basis of the aforesaid provision, the appellant filed an application before the Administrator praying that he may be granted permission or renewed a license for carrying out his business in such premises. The application was rejected by the Administrator holding that the appellant had no right to carry out his trade in the gold jewellery. The appellant preferred an appeal against the order of the Administrator. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order passed by the Estate Officer. In the appeal, the Tribunal held that the Administrator had power under secs. 28(6) to grant or renew a license in respect of any article, ornament or both in the said premises. On appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned provision was violative of Art. 14 of the Constitution and the High Court should not have struck down the same on the ground that it was arbitrary and uncanalised power. Dismissing the appeal by this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the Administrator under sec.(6) is a very wide and vague power which can be exercised only in the matter of exercising his discretion in the matters of grant or renewal of a license. [954B] 2. The discretion conferred on the Administrator by sec.28(6), to grant permission or renew the same, is not decisive of the matter. It does not impose any blanket ban upon the exercise of power by the administrator. [1055C] 3. The expression 'region ' in the Act means a reasonable restriction which has been imposed by the statute and it cannot be arbitrary or uncanalised. [1154D] 4. The word 'regard ' in sec.29(6)(b) is wide enough to include within its ambit all kinds of restrictions which have been put on the exercise by the authority concerned. It is not a case where the discretion has been conferred upon an Administrator under section 28(2) of the , but the same has been done in the manner prescribed by sec.(5). [955E] 5. The words 'regards ' in any other matter or for purposes connected therewith or incidental thereto have to be interpreted in the light of the policy and purpose of the enactment and the scheme afforded sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the exercise thereof. [0954F G] 6. The phrase 'regarding 'regulate ' in respect only of the matters specified therein has to be read as comprehending within its scope all kinds or matters which have already been put upon the legislative policy and purposes of the statute. [995B] 7. In view of the above, it is not possible to hold that the word 'regulation ' in section 28 (2) has any wider meaning than what has been given by the Legislature. [985C] 8. The High Court was right in holding that sec. 29(6A) was invalid on the grounds that it conferred a very limited power upon the administrator to grant and renew a licence to a person for carryingon money lent business, in which case the Administrator could not exercise his discretion under section28(2). [997D] 9. The language of sec. 30(1) is clear and unambiguous. It provides that the Governor may by order direct that any license granted or renewed under this Act shall be subject to such conditions as he may specify in the order. [1005E] 10.

The appellant, who was the manager of a temple, filed a suit against respondents 1 to 3 for possession of the properties in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the alienor had been removed from office by other persons who were in management of the temple and that he had become de facto managers of the trust. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the courts below and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was wrong in holding that a transfer effected by the manager as not belonging to the temple could not be affected by the provisions of article 134B. HELD: (1) The transfer made by the Manager of a religious endowment is void under article 134 B(2). [601 C] (2) The mere fact that the transfer was for valuable consideration does not make it void under section 14(3) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1959. [602 D] (3) The High Court was wrong on its finding that the transfers were made by a previous manager and the alienors and that they had been transferred to the religious endowment. [062 E] (4) The fact that there was no transfer of the property in question from the temple to the appellant, does not show that the assignor had any interest in the properties which he had transferred to him. [63 F] (5) The facts established by the evidence on record clearly establish that the appellant was in management and control of the religious endowments. [64 G] (6) The question whether the transfer is void or not does not arise because the alienee has been removed by other person who had left the village. [65 F] In the present case, the transfer made was for a valuable consideration. It was not a transfer which could be affected under article 133 B(1). [64 H] (7) The evidence on the record clearly shows that the transferor and his family had been in management or control of its affairs.

The respondent firm Apsara Theatre was running a Cinema in the name of Apsar Theatre. The licence was granted to one Shri Krishan Kumar, who had been found to be the sole licensee and the cinema shows were conducted by some persons other than the licensee. On September 26, 1980, the District Magistrate issued a notice under Section 6 of the Act calling upon the firm Apara Theatre to show cause why the license should not be suspended. The District Magistrate passed an order on December 29, 1977 directing suspension of the cinema show in the Theatre and also for a direction that the licence be suspended pending disposal of the writ petition. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court set aside the order of the District Collector and directed the District magistrate to pass fresh orders after hearing the parties concerned. The State Government preferred an appeal against the said order before this Court. During the pendency of the appeal, the State of Jammu & Kashmir passed a judgment on December 26, 1979 in favour of the firm and against the licensee Apsa Theatre. On April 19, 1979, the Superintendent of Police, Jammu, issued a show cause notice under section 6 F of the , as well as to the District Magistrates asking them to show causes why the licence should not been suspended pending hearing and disposal of this appeal. The appellants challenged the said judgment by filing a writ petition in the High court which was dismissed on December 30, 1979. Apsari Theatre filed an application before the District Judge for quashing the order passed by the District Superintendent of police, Jammu. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the District Government had no power under the Act or the Rules to suspend a cinema show and that the license in question was not a licence within the meaning of Section 6 F(2) of the act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned order passed against the firm was violative of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as the District Officer had no jurisdiction under the provisions of the statute or the rules to make such an order. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The District Collector had no authority to suspend the cinema and therefore, the licence in question could not be said to have been suspended by the licensing authority. [701B] 2.2 The District Magistrates were competent to pass orders under Section 5 F(3) of Act. They had jurisdiction to suspend or cancel a license pending disposal thereof. [802C] 3.1 In view of the provisions contained in Sections 6 and 6 F (2), the District Magisrate had no competence to suspend any cinema show. The order passed under Section 4 F(4) was, therefore, not valid. [901F G] 2.(a) The District magistrate had no powers under the statute to suspend an exhibition in a Theatre without a licence in contravention of the provision contained in Section 6 and 7 F(1). [902A B] (b) The order of suspension passed by District Magistrate was not valid because the District Registrar had no such power under Section 9 F(5) of A.P. Excise Act, 1968 to suspend cinema show or to cancel a licence pending disposal. [1001F] 3.(a)(i) In view thereof, the impugned judgment of the High Courts cannot be sustained and is set aside. The writ petitions are allowed. No costs.

The respondent was a displaced person from Pakistan. He had been in possession of certain properties belonging to the evacuee, and he had been granted a lease by the Custodian for a period of five years on the terms of the agreement to sell the mills. The appellants were not entitled to any relief under section 12 of the Act as it stood at the relevant time. The respondent filed an application before the Custodian claiming that the property in question was his evacuee property and that he had no authority under section 10 of the said Act, and that the notice Exhibit C was illegal. The Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the lease granted by him was not a valid one and that it was not liable to be cancelled. The appeal filed by the appellants against the order of the Custodian was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The appellant then preferred an appeal before the High Court under article 133(1)(b) of the Constitution, which was allowed by the impugned judgment dated 13th April 1954. In this appeal, it is contended that the respondent had no power to cancel the lease in favour of the appellants and that since the Custodian had no jurisdiction to cancel a lease granted in his favour, the order passed by him could not be sustained. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to have the notice under section 13(1) of Act No. 982 and directed the Custodian to issue a fresh notice to the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned notice Exhibit A, which is a notice issued by the respondent under section 11 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, was invalid as it had not been issued in accordance with the provisions of section 12(1), and that therefore the notice was illegal and void. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notice dated 13 th April 1954 is bad because it was issued by an evacuee and not by the evacuee. [782 A] 2. The notice was invalid because it had been issued under section 8(1). The Custodian had power to issue the notice in accordance therewith. [882 B] 3. The order of cancellation was passed on 13th May 1954, and therefore the respondent could not have cancelled the lease by reason of the impugned order dated 13 4 1954. [982 C] 4. The question whether the respondent was entitled to cancel or vary the terms thereof is a matter which has to be determined by the appropriate authorities under section 981 of the Code. [1083 D] 5. The power conferred on the Custodian under section 3(1A) of Bombay Land revenue Code, was not an absolute and absolute power but only a conditional power. It could not therefore be exercised by the Collector in exercise of his powers under section 4(2). [984 E] 6. The right to cancel is a statutory right and it can be exercised only if there is a valid order or a valid notice issued under that section.

The appellant was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and he had three sons. He was born in the year 1964. The Board of Revenue by its order dated 5th May, 1976 held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant herein) was born on 14 th March, 1962 and was only 13 years old at the time when the ceiling proceedings were finalized by the Sub Divisional Officer. The appellant filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority against the said order of the Board of revenue. The Revenue Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that Surendra Pal Singh (Appellant herein) had not filed any appeal under section 230 of the Act of 1955 and, therefore, the Board was right in holding that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh could be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956. The High Court held that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside the order of Sub Divisional officer dated 5 th May,1976 and the Board 's order setting aside the orders of the Revenue appellate authority was correct. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Board in revision was not correct and the High Court should have set aside that part of the order. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred by Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the board over revenue courts subordinate to the Board. [701B] 2. The powers conferred by Sections 9 and 10 are not subject to the other provisions of the Constitution of India. It is only in respect of matters relating to the administration of the land that the State Government can exercise its power under Section 9. [802C] 3. The State Government has no jurisdiction over revenue court subordinate to it. [820D] 4. The word "judicial authority" used in section 9(2) of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Code, 1959 is not a word which is capable of any precise interpretation. It does not mean that the powers conferred on the Board by Section 230 of Act of 1958 are subject to other provisions. [823E] 5. The expression 'judicial authority' has been defined in section 2(h) of Act No. 9 of 1955 as meaning "a judicial officer". The word 'judicial officer" is a term which is not capable of precise interpretation and it does not include the executive or appellate authority. It only means that the executive, appellate authority, appellate or revisional authority, as the case may be, has no power to make use of its powers of superintendence and control over revenue Courts subordinate to them. [825E] 6. The words 'judicial officers' in section 24(2)(a) of Rajasthan Land Reforms Act, 1955 are not capable to any precise construction and it is only when the Board exercises its powers under Section 230 that the power conferred on a judicial officer by the said section can be exercised by the State or revisional authorities. [826E] 7. The term 'judicial Officer' in Section 24(1) of Land Revenue, Act of 1957 has been used in the sense of an appellate authority and it cannot be construed as giving to the High Courts any jurisdiction to make a decision or to make any order which would be contrary to law. [827A D] 8. The Legislature has not provided for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Government of India Act, 1935. It merely provides for separate units in Chapter IV B of that Act and it only means the executive and appellate authority as well as revisional authority. [828E] 9. In view of the fact that the members of the Boards have been given a different unit in the State of Rajasthan, the question whether the Board has jurisdiction to decide or not does not arise for consideration. [829F] 10. The Act of 1950 is a special statute and it provides for two separate units. It provides for one unit and another unit in each State. The other unit is a single unit.

The appellant, a newspaper establishment, filed an application under section 2(b) of the Act for registration of its newspaper establishments. The High Court by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983 allowed the said application and declared that the law reports published by the Ist respondent were not newspapers within the meaning of the expression 'newspaper '. The appellant, aggrieved by the order made by the High Court, filed a writ petition before this Court. The State Government contended that the newspaper establishments had been registered under section 3(b)(ii) of Act No. X of 1954 and that the said law reports were published in the official Gazette of India which was not a newspaper within the definition of the word 'new' as defined in the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'oldpaper ' is defined by section 2 (b) to mean any printed periodical work containing news or information which is published by a newspaper in which the members of the public ordinarily read in order to get reports of recent events, comments on them etc. It is not necessary for a newspaper to make a law report to make it a newspaper. [701B] 2. The word 'old' has been defined in section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 as meaning newspapers which are published by an official publication of all kinds of news orinformation. It does not include newspapers which have been published by any other newspaper in India but also by a publisher thereof. [801C] 3. The term 'newpaper ' has been used in section 3 (b)(i) of this Act to mean the publication of every kind of news and information which may be published by such newspaper or newspapers which may cease to be a newspaper, if it is not so required. [820D] 4. The words 'new paper ' have been used for improving the conditions of service of the employees employed by the appellant in their production or publication of the said Law Reports. It cannot be denied that the word "newpaper" has been deliberately used in the definition and that it is only a newspaper which may not occupy a substantial part of a newspaper but also a newspaper containing news andinformation. [823D] 5. The publication of any other law reports in the Press and Registration of Books of Books by the first respondent does not amount to newspapers within section 2A(b). It is, therefore, not necessary that the publication should be made a newspaper or a newspaper with which the employees are employed. [825E] 6. The question whether the word ''newpaper' in the context of the provisions of the Orissa Public Employment (Conditions Of Service) Act, 1954, was used in connection with the production or publishing of newspapers does not arise for consideration in this case because the expression "news paper ' has not been defined either in the statute or in the rules framed under it. [826E] 7. The definition of newspaper is wide enough to include newspapers and news items which are not published by them. It may be that the expression ''news papers ' has also been used as a word 'in the Act, but it does not mean any paper containing news. [828F] 8. The language employed in section 4(b), (i) and (ii) is wide and there is no scope for any interpretation of the words 'older' or 'new newspaper '. [827G] 9. In the present case, the appellant was not registered under the Act as defined by the Act but it was a newspaper incorporated in the year 1967. The notification issued by the State Government on 22nd May, 1982 was published in which it was clearly mentioned that the working Journalists were not to be registered under this Act. [829F] 9 A. The object of the legislation is to provide for better protection of the interests of the community and to protect the interest of the general public.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant and he had obtained an implied licence for the use and occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973. The respondent filed a suit in the Small Cause Court for eviction of the appellants from the premises in question on the ground that the respondent was not a licensee and that he was not entitled to possession under an agreement with a landlord. The Small Cause court dismissed the suit holding that the licence was not put an end to by the appellant licensor and, therefore, the respondent had no right to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution and should have allowed the revision on 17th of November, 1980. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court had no power to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the Small Causes Court. [701B] 2.1 The High court was not justified in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the trial Judge and the appellate court on the question of jurisdiction. [802C] 3.2 The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere in a matter which is not a pure question of law. [601D] 2:1.1 In the instant case, the appellant was a sub tenant of respondent and he was a licensee. He was also a sub lessee of the building on 1 st February, 1972. The licence was granted by the licensor to the respondent for a period of five years from 1st of September, 1965 till 31st March, 1966. The appellant had not been able to show that he had any subsisting agreement with the licensor for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a further period of 5 years from January, 1973 to 31st of August, 1970. [820E] 2(a) The respondent was in occupation of premises on the basis of an agreement entered into between the parties on 1.2.1973 and he continued to be in possession until a decree for eviction was made in his favor. [823B] 3(b) The High Curt had no authority to interfere under Article 226 of the constitution. [825E] 4.1.2 In view of the fact that the appellant had been in occupation on 1St February,1973 and the licence had come to an end by 31st May, 1966, it was not open for the respondent to contend that he could not be evicted from the building after 31st August, 1965. [822E] 3.(c) The question whether the respondent is a tenant or a licensee does not arise in view of Section 2(d)(ii) of the Bombay Rent Act. It is true that the rent payable by the respondent under the agreement was Rs. 1,000/- per month and the appellant did not pay any amount towards rent for the period of licence. But it is well settled that the tenant cannot be evicted on the grounds mentioned in Section 2 (d)(i) of that Act unless he has paid the rent for a particular period. [821F] 3:1 The respondent had been paying rent for more than one year and the respondent did not have any subsisting licence to use and occupy the premises for a continuous period of three years from the date of his application till 31 st March, 1967. [824E] 1.3.2 It is well established that the landlord can be evicted only on the plea of breach of any of the terms and conditions of the agreement entered between him and the licensor. The tenant cannot claim protection under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. [826A D] 3 (a) In view thereof, the High court had no option but to allow the revision application on 17 th November, 1979. [828B] 4(b)(i), (ii) & (iii) of Section 21(1)

The appellant was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant was incorporated in the United States of America and was registered as a Company under the provisions of the Companies Act. On April 1, 1950, the appellant filed an application for registration of its name as a company under section 5 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The application was rejected by the Assistant Registrar of Companies on May 2, 1951. The respondent applied to the High Court for a certificate under article 226 of the Constitution and obtained a certificate on June 3, 1951, which was granted by the High court. On July 4, 1952, the High Judge dismissed the appellant's application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the agreement in question was not a law within the meaning of article 295(2) of the constitution and that the appellant had no authority to confer any right on the company as against the new sovereign. HELD: The agreement was not an act of State but was a law which was in existence at the time when it came into force. [801 E] In the present case, there was no recognition by the new Ruler of the former Jodhpur State of Rajasthan and therefore the appellant could not be said to have any right to exemption from taxation under article 295 (2) as against its existing sovereign. The agreement in fact continued till it came to be recognised by the old sovereign. [901 A] In view of the provisions contained in article 295, the new Rulers of the erstwhile States were entitled to exemption under article 294(2), and they could not claim any immunity from taxation on their properties. [1001 B] The appellant had a right to exempt it from taxation. [1101 C] The agreement did not confer any rights on the appellant as against his existing sovereign, nor did it create any right in the appellant to exemption.

The appellant, a trader in the notified area for which he was granted a licence to sell and sell agricultural crops, purchased at Rs. 1,000 per acre, from the market committee on behalf of the appellant, under section 14(1) of the Act, by virtue of an order made by the Collector under section 3 of the Tamil Nadu Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1961, hereinafter referred to as 'the Act', for short, and for a licence for sale and purchase of agricultural crops. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras, against the Market Committee, for recovery of a sum of Rs. 2,000 from him on account of trade allowance. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the allowance was not a trade allowance but a trade allowances. On appeal by the appellant to the High Court, it held that the allowances were not a 's trade allowance and did not operate upon any other commodity or goods; that the Market committee had no licence to purchase, sell or sale of a notified commercial crop at Rs.. 3,000 and that the appellant was not prohibited from holding the market as property. The High Court dismissed the appeal by its judgment dated July 10, 1953. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf Of the appellant that the order made under section 2(1)(a) of Act was bad because the Market Committees had no licences to purchase or sell agricultural crop at a particular place within the notified market area; that in any case, the Market committees were not prohibited for holding the markets established subject to the regulations and also that the licence to sale and sell commercial crops was not an 's Trade allowance but an 'Mahimai '. Held, further, that the word 'mahim ' is a trade Allowance and does not operate on any other transaction in respect of commercial crop; that it is a restriction upon the right to do business outside the prescribed area and that no licence for the purchase or sale can be granted or renewed in respect thereof. The word 'Machimai' as used in section 14 of the Agricultural Produce Market Act, 1962, does not mean any trade allowance or does not have any relation with the use of the premises or services rendered by a trader outside the notified agricultural area for the purpose of the said Act; that under section 15(1), the word "mahim" is a term used in connection with the business of buying and selling of a specified commercial crop. The words 'Metimai', 'mahi ' and 'Magimai are not identical to those used in sections 14(2) and 14(3). The word "Machinai" as used therein is a word of wide import, and it does not include any trade allowances or do not have relation with use of any place for the purposes of business of purchasing and selling. The expression 'mahalimai" in section 15 (1) means any person who is having a licence or a licence under this Act to sell or purchase agricultural crops at a specified market area for such period as may from time to time be fixed by the State Government, but does not fall within the terms of the bye law framed thereunder.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge of the offence under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. He was also convicted for an offence under sections 148, 302/149 and 307/149 I. P. C. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the appellant had not given any specific instance of a particular blow on the body of the deceased and that he could not have been held guilty for an act which was done by him in furtherance of the common intention of all the accused persons. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of Rasika and Subhana is corroborated by the medical evidence and the medical opinion. [801B] 2. The prosecution case is that the deceased had been last seen together with the appellant and his family members on the morning of the date of the occurrence. He had not seen any one or more of them at the time of the incident. It was only after he had gone to the house of the accused, he found that there were some other persons present in the attack and they were also seen by him. [901C] 3. The medical evidence does not disclose any injury on the person of the appellant. There is no reason to depart from this practice in this case. [1001D] 4. The fact that the accused had been arrested at the house when he was last seen with the deceased, and his father, the appellant, who was also present in his house, does not indicate any injury which could have been caused by a stick or sticks. [092E] 5. The mere fact that there was no other evidence to show that the assault had been made on the deceased does not mean that he had been seen together at the relevant time and that it did not disclose anything about the occurrence when he went to the police station. [1101F] 6. In the present case, the prosecution has failed to establish that the injuries which could be caused by the stick or stick were not on the part of the body or the person who had come to the place of occurrence and therefore the appellant was guilty for murder. [110G] 7. The facts disclosed in the charge sheet clearly show that there had been a sudden quarrel between the two accused persons and they had also received injuries which resulted in their death. There was no reason for the Sessions judge to disbelieve the evidence of the eye witnesses because of the fact that they were not present at the place where the occurrence had taken place. [109G] 8. The circumstances disclosed by the prosecution clearly show the existence of a sudden fight between two accused and the deceased. It is true that there is no direct evidence to indicate that the appellants had any intention to cause death or that they had caused such bodily injury as was likely to cause the death. But, in the present cases, the medical report does not say anything about any external injuries which might have been inflicted by a weapon like stick or a sticks. The doctor who examined the deceased has clearly stated that there could be no external injuries on the dead body and therefore he did not give any names of the assailants. [111G] 9. In view of the above discussion, the appeal is allowed and the conviction and sentences passed against the appellants are set aside. They are acquitted of all charges.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I or Class II service on a substantive post and he had completed the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on completion of his normal superannuation, he would be entitled to receive from the Government servant concerned pension at the rate applicable to him under Fundamental Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner was promoted as officiating Engineer in class I or class II service and was posted in Class III service on ad hoc basis. He was promoted to officiate as officiating Assistant Engineer in the same post on 25.5.1972. On completion of the normal superannuation he would continue to hold the said post till the date of his superannuation. The Government servant, however, did not exercise his option under Rule 56 (j) and, thus, he could be reverted to the post of officiating Executive Engin eer in Class II or Class III services on regular basis. On appeal by the petitioner, the Appellate Authority set aside the order of compulsory retirement and directed that the period from 10.02.1972 to 5.11.1976 would be treated as duty for all purposes including pay and allowances. The appellant challenged the validity of the order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the order was not illegal and void ab initio. He held that the appellant had no right to the posts on substantive basis and, consequently, he was entitled to be paid salary and other service allowances at the rates applicable to his post from which he has been promoted on an officiating basis. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal holding that Rule 56 of Fundamental Rules 56(i) applied to Government servants in Class 1 or ClassII service or posts as a member of Class I service or post and, accordingly, the appellant was entitled for salary and allowances at rates applicable for his post on substantive appointment. The present appeal by special leave is against the judgment of the Division Bench. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The order of the Government dated 10.12.1976 was not in accordance with law. [601B] (2) The appellant had been appointed as an officiating Executive Engineers on a temporary basis and he was promoted on ad mituary basis. It is true that the post held by him was a Class I post but he was reverted to his substantive post from where he entered service on an ad mity in Class 11 or Class 11 service or Post. [701C] (3) The power of the appropriate authority under Rule 57(j)(i) of Fundamental Rule56(j), is not confined to a person who has been appointed de novo on an substantive post, but he had entered service before attaining the age o f 50 years after attaining the said age. [801D] (4) The exercise of power under Rule 55(j). of Fundamental FR 56(k) was not permissible in view of the fact that the petitioner had not attained the ageof 50 years by the date on which he entered into service before his superannuation and, as such, he cannot be said to have been appointed on a regular basis or on an adhoc basis. [823E] The order dated 10th December, 1976 was passed under Rule 54(j); that the said rule was applicable to the facts of this case as well as to the fact whether the petitioner has been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The appellant Corporation had issued a cheque for Rs.7,000/- in favour of the respondents on 11th January, 1961 and the same was encashed by the respondents. The respondents were informed that the proposal was not accepted by the Corporation but it was adjusted towards the premium amount required for the proposal. The Corporation thereupon filed a suit against the deceased and his children for recovery of the amount covered under the insurance policy. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract of insurance between the deceased on 11 th January, 1962 and the Corporation and therefore the respondents were not entitled to any amount as claimed by them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the High Court was in error in holding that the insurance contract of Insurance was a concluded contract and therefore there was a completed contract of policy between the appellant and the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The insurance contract is an agreement between the parties to settle the claim of the insured and the corporation. It does not create any contract of life insurance which ever happened in this case. [701B] 2. The proposal was for Rs..7,500/- and the amount required was not fixed. The premium amount was not calculated. [802C] 3. The deceased had died on 11 January,1961 and therefore he was entitled to get the amount of the insurance amount covered by the insurance. [901D] 4. The High Court has committed a manifest error in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the Trial Court that there is no concluded contracts between the respondents and the appellant. [1001E] 5. The contract of the Insurance was not a concluded one and therefore it could not be said that the respondents had waived their right to accept the proposal as a matter of fact. [1102F] 6. The facts in this particular case are different from the facts of the present case. There is no doubt that there were two contracts between both the deceased, the appellant corporation and the respondents but the High court has committed an error in coming to the conclusion that there had been a concluded contracts of insurance which never happened in the present matter. [110G] 7. The fact that the Insurance Company did not dispute the acceptance of the proposal by the deceased was admitted by the appellant in its written statement and also admitted by it in its evidence that the amount was accepted by it as a result of the acceptance by the Insurance company. [111A D] 8. The question whether the insurance contracts were concluded or not is a mixed question of law and fact which has to be determined on the basis of the evidence adduced before the Trial Judge. [112E] 9. In the instant case, there was an agreement of insurance with the deceased that the sum assured would be paid by him in his accounts and the said amount would be appropriated towards the premiums payable by him. The Insurance Company had not disputed the acceptance to the proposal but it admitted the fact that there could be a concluded insurance contract between the insured or the Corporation. [113A D E] 9: The High court was of the opinion that there must be an agreement to settle a claim for Rs 55,000/ and the premium payable by the respondent was not determined as a dispute between the Insurance and the insured. [114E] 10: In the present appeal, the insurance company had contended that the deceased had committed breach of contract of indemnity and therefore, the High Curt should have set aside the decree passed by the trial court.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Druva Coal Company Ltd., a registered firm. The appellant was carrying out business in coal mines at the relevant time. On or about October 9, 1968, the appellant filed an application for winding up of a company as a result of the order passed by the High Court in a petition for windingup of a Company as to the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matters in dispute in the suit or proceeding. The application was dismissed on the ground that the appellant had not vested in the assignee, and the order was confirmed in appeal by this Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of the High court was final and could not be treated as a judgment or an interlocutory order within the meaning of article 133 (1) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed under section 205 read with section 114 I.P. Code is final and cannot be called an interlocutory orders. [859F] 2. The expression "final order" in section 109(a) of Civil Procedure Code means an order which is finally decided by the trial court in a suit or proceedings, but does not finally dispose of a suit, or proceeding, and it does not decide any question or disputes in relation thereto in relation there to. [959F G] 3. The word "final" in article 133(1) means an interlocutory judgment or final order which the parties have for determination in the case before them. It is not necessary that the decision on the rights of the party in dispute should be final and conclusive. [1060A B] 4. The words "final orders" in Article 133 (2) are not intended to convey a meaning different from that given by the Constitution Bench of this Court in Druvardas case(1). It is only when an order is finally disposed of, it can be said that an order passed on the merits of the dispute in a proceeding cannot be deemed to be final. [1160A C] 5. The High Court was right in holding that the application for setting aside the order dated October 9/10, 1968 was not maintainable since the appellant did not vest in the assignor, and therefore, the order could not attach to the suit as a final order within section 109 (a) or section 114 of the Government of India Act, 1935. [110B C] 6. The question whether an order can be deemed under article 133 of the constitution is a question which has been finally decided in the appeal by the Supreme Court. [111E] 7. In the present case, the question whether the order can attach to a suit as to its final order was not determined by the appellate court and it was open to the appellant to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief, if it did not finally decide any issue or dispute in relation thereof. [112E] 8. The power under article 136(1)(c) is not an interlocutory one. It does not dispose of any question which had been finally determined by a competent court and has become final. The jurisdiction of the appellate Court to grant interim injunction is not a matter that can be considered in appeal. [113G H] 9. In view of the provisions contained in article 136 (1)(a) and (b), it is open to an order under article 132(1), to be made final, subject to the result of such appeal. The appellate court has no power to grant a certificate under article 134(1); but it can only dispose of the suit if it does so finally decide a matter in accordance with law. [114E] 9 A. In this case, there is no question of any finality between the parties and the rights or obligations of parties in regard to the matter in dispute are not determined.

The respondent company was manufacturing cotton fabrics and the respondent company had been selling the processed fabrics to its processor 's factory. The respondent company sold the processed fabric to its workers who were selling the same on job work basis. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the validity of Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 (hereinafter referred to as the "Rules") and prayed for quashing of the said rule. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to the relief claimed by it. Hence this appeal by special leave.
