Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court has held that Rule 174(2) of the Rules is a complete code in itself and the rules made thereunder are not applicable to the case. [601B] 2.2 The respondent was selling the grey cloth manufactured by it on job worked basis. It had been manufacturing cotton fabric at the factory gate for the processing of the fabrics. The process of manufacture was carried out by the processor ' sessable value and expenses were incurred in respect of the processed goods. The processor 'Sessable Value and expenses incurred in the processing were not includible in the assessable value of the grey fabric or fabric plus the cost of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and expenses. [701C] 2.(a) The respondent had been purchasing the processed cotton fabrics at the factories gate for processing on job works basis. In order to show that the processor was selling his processed fabrics at their factory gate, it was contended that the process of processing was carried on by the respondent and not by the manufacturer. [801D] (b) The High Curt held that the processes undertaken by the appellant were not manufacture 's manufacturing activity but were only incidental to the processing. [901E] 3.(a)(i) The expression "manufacture" in Rule 174 was interpreted by this Court in the case of [Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. vs Collector of Central Excise, Madras], ; , followed. (ii) The process undertaken by a processor ' Sessablevalue and expenses was not includible as the manufacturing activity. [1001F] 4.(a). In view of the above decision of this Court, it is clear that the processing done by the Respondent was only incidental or ancillary to the manufacturing activities. [1101G] (c) The processes undertaken were incidental or incidental to processing. The processes carried out were not incidental or subsidiary to the process. [110H; 1101A B] 5.(a), (b)(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) of Rule 173B(2). The process was incidental or auxiliary to the manufacture of processed fabrics. It was, therefore, necessary that the processed cloth should be sold by the manufacturers at the time of processing. In view thereof, it could not be said that the Respondent had been using the processed yarn for processing. (iii)(a) [110G] 6.(b)The process undertaken was incidental to manufacture and the manufacturing process was carried in the factory premises. The processing was done by a manufacturer who was selling processed fabrics on jobwork basis. [111H; 111A B C] 7.(c)The processor ' 's finished fabric' was not used for processing of fabrics. He had been making the processed material only after the processing was made. [112E] 829D] 9(a). The processes were incidental to manufacturing process and the process was not incidental to such processing. It could not therefore be said to be incidental or supplemental to the activity. The expression 'manufacture' in Rule 173G(2)(i)(ii) of Rules, is a word of wide import. [113E] 9 (a).The process carried out was incidental and ancillary to manufacturing operations. The processed fabrics were not manufactured by the processing agency.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 13, 1973. He was promoted to the post of Head Clerk in January 1974 and he was absorbed in Government service on June 1, 1975. The Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which is respondent 3 in this appeal, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the order of his absorption as a clerk in the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant contended that the appointment of the appellant as Head Clerk was not by way of promotion but by way otherwise than on an ad hoc basis and that he was entitled to be absorbed in the Government service as a Clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled only to be considered for promotion to the said post of a Head clerk after June 13. 1973, when the Panchayat Samitis had lost its power to make appointments to the posts of Head Clerks. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The appointment of a person as a head Clerk is not by the State Government and the appellant cannot be denied his right to be appointed on a regular basis. [701B] 2.2. The post in which the appellant is working was a Head Clerks and the post in the Lohasu Panchayat Samiti was a permanent one. It was, therefore, not open to the appellant to claim that he should be absorbed as a permanent Head Clerk. [802C] 3.1 The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 14(4) of the Amending Act of 1973. [820D] 2:1.2 The appellant had been appointed as an Assistant Head Clerk by the Panchayat and his appointment was in accordance with the terms and conditions of his service. He, therefore could not have been absorbed in a Government service. [823E] 3:1 The High court was right in holding that there was no question of absorption of the respondent in the State Service. [825F] 2.(a) The appellant having been appointed on an adhoc basis and in accordance therewith, he was not bound to absorb him in the post which he was lawfully employed by the Government on June 14, 1973, as a result of the amendment of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, the appellant could not be denied the right to continue in service until he was appointed in April 1, 1973 on an Ad hoc basis. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the impugned order of the High court is set aside. [822E] 2(b) In view of the fact that the post held by the appellant in the Department of Panchayat Samiti had been abolished, the Government could not make any appointment to the Post of Head clerk on June 12, 1973 as a regular Head Clerk and that the respondent was entitled for all benefits under section 32 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis Act, 1961. [821F] 3.(a)(i) The post held in the Gram Panchayat Samiti is a permanent post and it cannot be abolished unless there is an order of appointment by the competent authority. [826A] (b) The Government had no power to appoint a person on ad hoc or temporary basis as Head clerk. It could not, therefore have been compelled to absorb the appellant on a lower post in view of section 14 (4) read with section 32(3). [823F] 4.(a). In the instant case, the appointment was made by the Gram Sabha and the Panchayat had lost their power to absorb them in the service. The Government could, therefore. not have absorbed the appellant from the post on which he had been absorbed. [827G] 5.(b) It is true that the Government has no power under section 35(3) to appoint any person as Head Clerks on ad interim basis or in April 1975 when the Government had lost power to employ him in a Panchayat Samiti until he is absorbed in it, until he has been absorbed into it.

The appellant, Shivshankar Yati was the Mahant of the Math and he died in 1917. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties of the deceased Mahant Shivshanker Yacat, which included the personal property of the Mahant Shiv Shankar Yagat. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Amauli properties were not the personal properties of Uma Shankar Yati but were the personal assets of the deity and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. The High Court held that the properties in question constituted the personal estate of the respondent and therefore the respondent could not be said to be the personal owner of the trust property. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was not maintainable as the Amaul properties were acquired by the Mahant and the Mahant had no right to claim exemption from payment of the tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Commissioner of Income Tax has rightly held that there is a presumption in favour of the appellant that the property in question was the personal asset of the temple or the deity. [701B] 2. The position in regard to the properties acquired by Mahant Shivdas Yagit, is not disputed before us. The fact that the respondent had purchased the Amaoti properties from the Math is not in dispute. The evidence on record shows that the appellant was the owner of these properties and he had purchased it for the purpose of his personal benefit. [801C] 3. The income tax authorities have rightly held the property to be a personal asset. The appeal must, therefore, fail. [901D] 4. The question whether the respondent is entitled to exemption under section 10(2) (iii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [1001E] 5. The decision of the High Court is correct and it is accordingly set aside. The suit filed by the appellant is dismissed with costs.

The appellant was allotted a plot of land in village Raikot in the State of Punjab. The allotment was made in favour of one Shri Ram Singh, who had been allotted a piece of land by the Custodian General under section 12(1) of the 1954 Act. On March 24, 1955, the Central Government issued an order under section 10 of the Act directing that the evacuee property would cease to be evacuee property and that the Custodian shall dispose of such property in accordance with the provisions of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 19(1)(a) of 1954 Act as he had been deprived of his right in the property allotted to him by reason of the impugned notification. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Deputy Custodian General was illegal and void because the Custodian had not taken away the possession of the evacuee properties from the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the Deputy Commissioner cancelling the allotment in favour the appellant is clearly unsustainable. [857 C] 2. The impugned order of cancellation of allotment made in his favour by the Central government is set aside and he is directed to be restored to the position as if he had not been allotted any property in his possession. [58 D] 3. The appeal is allowed, but in the circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

The selection of the two candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) was challenged by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the select list on the ground that the selection of two candidates was vitiated by violation of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had committed an error in quashing the entire recruitment process and directing that the fresh interview be completed within four years from the date of the advertisement and that the State Public Service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have suffered public time. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The selection of candidates for a fresh interview is vitiated by non-compliance of the provisions of the rules. [801B] 2. The procedure adopted by the Commission was not fair and reasonable. It was not open to the State Government to cancel the entire process of selection without giving any reasons therefor. [901C] 3. The process of re­examination was vitiated because of non-supply of the relevant information. The State Public Services Commission had failed to comply with the provisions contained in Rule 4(1) of the Rules and had not given any reason for cancelling the entire selection. [1001D] 4. The Selection Committee had acted arbitrarily in cancelling the whole process of the recruitment and had ignored the fact that the candidates who were selected on the basis of the written examination and the freshly selected candidates on the same date were not called for interview. [092E F] 5. The Commission was justified in cancelling all the selections without giving reasons therefor, as it did not give any reason therefor. It had been done arbitrarily and without giving an opportunity to the candidates to be heard before cancelling the selection. The order of the Public Service Com mission was vitiated on account of non­compliance of Rule 4 (1) and the principles contained in the Rules. [1101F] 6. The appellant, who was selected on a fresh basis, had not been called for interviews nor had he secured lesser marks in the written test. He was also not called upon to appear for interview but only got selected. [110G] 7. The Public Service Commissions were justified in holding that the process adopted by them was vitiated as they did not call for any reason whatsoever. [109H; 110A] 8. The fact that there was no justification for cancelling all of the selections was also denied. It is well settled that if a candidate has been selected on an open basis, he cannot be allowed to challenge the selection without any valid reasons therefor and his candidature can be cancelled only on the grounds mentioned in Rule 9(1). [110B] 9. The power of cancellation of the entire examination is not confined to the grounds for cancelling a candidate who had better performance in the public service. It does not mean that the Public Services Commissions were bound by the principles laid down in the rules and they could have been allowed to cancel all the selection on the sole ground that it was vitiated. [111A] 10. The principle of natural Justice is well established that a candidate cannot be permitted to challenge an administrative decision unless he has been given a show cause notice as to why his candidature should not be cancelled.

The appellant was appointed as mahant of the Dera by the respondent on a temporary basis. He was appointed in the year 1970 and continued to be the mahant till his death. On the death of Som Dass, the appellant became entitled to manage the properties appertaining to it by virtue of his election as mahants of the dera. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree of the trial court on the ground that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of Order 22, rule 10 and that the appeal was barred by time. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal under section 100 C.P.C. against the judgment of the first appellate court. The High Court could not have entertained an application for setting aside the abatement or for setting it aside on the basis of the ground of limitation prescribed by Order 22. [834 F] In the instant case, the suit had been filed in the representative capacity and the appellant was entitled to be impleaded as a party under Order 22 Rule 10. The suit was instituted on the footing that the appellant had no right to continue against the mahantship of the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed. In appeal, the High court held that the trial Court had jurisdiction to try the suit and that it was open to the appellant to file a second suit on the same grounds as he had filed in his capacity as maitars of the institution. The appeal was allowed by the High Judge holding that there was no ground for setting up the appellant as mais of the Institution. In the result, the appeal filed by the appellant against the order of the High Curt was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The suit is not maintainable on the grounds mentioned in Order 22 rule 10. [934 F H] 2.2 The suit has been instituted on a wrong ground that there had been no devolution of interest during the pendency of the suit. [1034 A B] 3.3 The suit filed by Som Dass was for possession and management of the properties attached to it. [1134 C] 4.1 In view of section 100, CPC, the trial Judge could not entertain a suit on that ground. [1234 D] 2:1.2 It is true that the provisions contained in Order 23, Rule 10 are applicable to suits filed by persons who have been appointed as trustees and who had filed the suit but the suit has not been instituted within the period of limitation for impleading them as parties under Order 23. The proviso to section 100 CPC provides that where a person who was appointed or elected as trustee or successor in interest of a deceased person is a minor, he shall be deemed to have been duly appointed or nominated as trustees or successor and the suit shall not be continued against such minor unless he has been given an opportunity of being heard. [1334 E] 2.(a) The proviso provides that if a person is appointed or appointed as trustee, then he shall become the owner of the property attached to the institution and his interest in the subject matter of the litigation shall devolve upon him. [1434 C D] 3.(b) In view thereof, the provisions relating to limitation for an application to set aside the decree are applicable only to suits instituted by or against a person in his individual capacity and not to any other person who is appointed as a trustee or a successor in management of such institution. [1534 E F] 4.(a)(i) The suit must be filed within three years from the date of the death or retirement of the deceased member of the family. [1835 A B C] (b) The provisions relating thereto are applicable even to suits which have been instituted after the death and before the death. [1634 E H] 5.(a).

The petitioners were appointed as Junior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Service on October 29, 1979. They were promoted to the post of Junior Assistant on November 30, 1979 and they were confirmed in that post by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said order of reduction of age of retirement from 58 to 55 years. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the proviso was not arbitrary or unreasonable and that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The proviso is a measure of social justice and does not violate any of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the constitution. [701B] 2.2 The proviso confers a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, which cannot be amended retrospectively so as to take away rights which had already accrued to them by protecting them from the prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be altered retrospectively so that to take place away rights conferred on Government servants under Article 311(2) of the. [801C] 3.1 The proviso does not confer a benefit on Government servant by protecting his conditions of Service, which is a protection against him from the hardship and prejudice caused to them. [820G] 2:1.3 The proviso merely confers a right upon Government servant to alter or amend the conditions of his service. It does not give any right to the Government servant who has been reduced in rank to a lower post. [823E] 3:2.4 The proviso makes it clear that the Government servants can only change their conditions and they cannot claim any protection against them from being changed retrospectively so long as they are found fit for promotion. [825G] 3; 2.5 The proviso has no retrospective effect. It merely gives a right to alter the conditions to take effect retrospectively so far as it is not arbitrary, unreasonable or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. [822E] 4.1 In the instant case, the Government had accepted the recommendation of the Commission and that the age of superannuation was raised from 55 to 58 years. It was not open to the State Government to alter those conditions retrospectively so much as to bring them into line with the recommendations of the Second Central Pay Commission.

The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of goods specified in Schedule B, from various sources in the State and exported out of India within the meaning of sub section (1) of section 5 of the C.S.T. Act, 1956. The appellants were assessed to tax under the provisions of the Act on the basis that they had purchased raw materials for manufacture of the goods specified therein and sold them by way of sale in the course of export outside the territory of India. The Sales Tax Officer, Karnal, assessed the appellants 's turnover at Rs. 1,000 per metric tonne. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who confirmed the order of assessment. The Tribunal held that the purchases were not liable to tax u/s 9(1) (b) and section 5(3) of the Central Sales Tax Act, but were made by way o sale in course of inter State trade or commerce within the territory f rom the State. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner and held that since the purchases had been made outside the State, the sales tax was not leviable under section 9(2) of C.T Act, 1961. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the transactions in question were not taxable u/ss 9(3), 9(4) and 9(5). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The purchases are not liable for tax under section 5 (1)(b) of Act 20 of 197. [601B] 2.2. The goods purchased by a dealer from outside the country are not taxable under section 4(3). The goods manufactured in the territory are not sold within the State but are found to be used in the manufacturing process. Therefore, the purchases made by the assessees are not exigible to tax. [701C] 3.2 The goods imported by the appellants were not covered by the definition of 'turnover ' as defined under section 2(d) of Central Sales tax Act, 1957. The transactions in the present case were not sales within the ambit of sub Section (1), but were purchased outside the purview of sub clause (b). [702D] 3.(a) The goods were sold by a registered dealer to a dealer who purchases them from outside India and sells them by a person other than the registered dealer. Therefore the transactions are not covered under section 7(3)(b). The sales tax authorities, therefore, have rightly assessed the appellant 's goods liable to be taxed under section 8(1)(a) of that Act. [802E] 3(b) The High court has committed a serious error in holding that since there was no sale within the purview o f section 9 (1). [803F] 4.(c) The sales were not exempt from tax u nder section 24(3); and the goods purchased outside India were not sold by any dealer to another person. [820G] 5.(a)(b), (c) & (d)

The appellant, a registered dealer, purchased the goods from the purchasers in Bombay and sold them to the purchasers outside the State of Bombay. The goods were brought on board the ship and they were not intended for despatch outside the state of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of export. The appellant was therefore entitled to the benefit of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The Sales Tax Officer, who heard the appeal, held that the goods were not despatched by the appellant to the buyer at the time of export and that the appellant had no intention of the parties to comply with the requirements of cl. (b) and that he was therefore not liable for having made a false declaration as regards the intention of sale. The High Court in appeal confirmed the order of the Sales Tax officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The sales were exempted from tax under article 286 (1)(a) of Part XIII of the constitution and that they were exempt from tax on the ground that the property was not intended to pass and did not pass. [601B] 2.2. The words " a registered person" in section 10(b) are wide enough to include a registered firm as defined in article 286 of the Indian Constitution. [613D] 3.3. The word " a dealer" in article 285(1) (a) is not used in any sense and it must be construed in its popular sense. It does not mean that the person who has purchased the property for being sent outside the country should be called a registered owner of the goods. [501E] 3: The word ' a dealer' in article 289(1), as interpreted by this Court in the case of [P.C.I.R.] State of Madras vs M/s. K.S.K.D.C., ; , referred to. 4.1 The words ' a registered manufacturer " have been used in section 8 and 10(a) in order that the purchaser should be registered as a dealer under article 285 (1) of Constitution. It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to refer to the provisions of article 285 which are similar to those contained in article 366(1). [602F] 4.2 The words used in article 19(1A)(b), are wide and they must be read as comprehending a person who is not a registereddealer, but who is a registered dealers for despatch of the said goods outside the territory of India within a reasonable time after the date on which they sell them to a person other than a registered consumer. [643D] 4:1.2 In view of the provisions contained in section 3(a), the purchaser must be registered under the Act and he must be deemed to have purchased the said property for the purposes of being sent out of the State to a place outside the territories of India. [64E] 2:1 The word used in the article is wide enough not to include any person who was not a dealer but a registered user of the property at the point of time when they sell it to a registered customer. [65F] 3;2.3 In view, therefore, of the language used in articles 286(I)(b)(b). The word must be understood in its common sense and in its ordinary meaning. [63G] 2.(a) The words must be interpreted in their popular sense and they should be construed as including any person to whom the goods have been sent out from the State. [62F] 2(b), 3(c) and 3(d)(i). (ii) The word is wide and it has to be understood according to its ordinary dictionary meaning. It must be given its ordinary popular sense, but it must mean that it should be interpreted as including a person to which the goods are sent out. [61G] 4.(a), 3 (c)

The respondent, who was married to the appellant on January 28, 1962, had filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the Magistrate. The Magistrate passed an order under section 127(3) (b) of the Criminal Procedure Code directing that the respondent should pay Rs. 400/ towards maintenance allowance to her and her child. The appellant challenged the said order by filing a revision application before the Sessions Judge, who allowed the same on January 11, 1976. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any allowance under section 126(3)(b) read with section 127 of the code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Magistrate was illegal and void as it had been made without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 125(1) (a) are not attracted in the present case because the respondent had failed to prove that she had been divorced by her husband or had obtained a divorce from her husband. [701B] 2. The burden of proof is on the appellant to establish that she was divorced by the husband and that she has received, whether before or after the date of the order, any amount which was due to her husband under section125(3). [702C E] 3. The onus of proving that the wife had not remarried was upon the respondent who failed to discharge that burden. [601D] 4. The respondent had not proved that she did not remarry and that there was a settlement by consent decree in 1962, which could not have been in the contemplation of parties in the obtaining of a divorce. [76G] 5. The fact that the husband has obtained a decree in 1963 does not mean that he has received a divorce on account of the payment made before such order. [77A B] 6. In view of the provisions of sections 125(3), (b), (c) and (d) read together, it is clear that the liability to pay maintenance allowance under the Code was not disputed by the respondent. The question whether the appellant had proved that he had been a divorced by him or had received any amount from her was also a matter of fact which could be decided on evidence adduced by the parties. [78A B E] 7. In the instant case, the appellant has failed to establish his claim under section 12(3B) (c). The respondent has not proved the payment of maintenance allowance for the period prior to January 28 1962. He had also failed to show that he was a divorced wife and had obtained divorce from him. [79A B D] 8. In any event, the respondent cannot be said to have established his claim on account thereof. [80C E; 80D] 9. The case of the respondent is not that she is a divorced woman but that she does not remarries. [81F] 10. The payment of Rs.400/ for her maintenance allowance was not proved by the appellant. [82A B C] 8A] 9A. In this view of matter, the High Court was right in holding that the application filed by the wife under section 128(3A) (d), was not maintainable.

The appellant was a dealer in respect of the business of the respondent and he had deposited dak amount with the State Government. The Collector, Samastipur by his order dated 25th March, 1988 cancelled the bid of the appellant for the future contracts under the orders passed by the Collector, Patna. The appellant filed an appeal before the Collector which was dismissed on 27th March 1988. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the cancellation of the bid and also the order directing that the appellant be placed in black list. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the cancellation was illegal and void. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has committed a serious error in quashing the cancellation order on the ground that it is an administrative order which affects the business or interest of the person concerned. [868 B] 2.2 The cancellation order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector and not on account of any subsequent action taken by the State. [968 C] 3.3 The cancellation of bid was illegal because the appellant had deposited the dak money with the Government. [1069 D] 4.1 In view of the fact that the High court had quashed the cancellation, the order passed by it is not sustainable in law. [1170 E] 2:1.2. The cancellation is illegal and invalid as the appellant was not given any notice before black listing the appellant. [11072 C] 2.:3.1. In view thereof, the cancellation is bad in law and is set aside. [108 D] 3:2.2 It is true that the Collector had cancelled the bids of the appellants on 27 th March 1988 but he was given a notice before the black listing of the petitioner in respect thereof on 27 March 1988 which was also challenged by filing a writ application in the Patna High Court. The Division Bench of the HighCourt quashed the order cancelling the bid on the sole ground that the same was illegal as it had been passed without following the rules and procedure prescribed under the Rules. [107 D] 2.(a) In view whereof, the High Courts have committed an error in setting aside the cancellation. [109 E] 3.(b) The cancellation was not in accordance with law. It is a well settled principle of law that a person who has been blacklisted by the authorities under the Act cannot be heard to say that he had no notice before blacklisting the appellant nor can be heard. [106 C] 4.(a). In the instant case, the Collector cancelled the auction and the order was also passed on 25th April 1988. [105 D] (b) In the present case, there is no requirement in the rule of natural justice that a notice should have been given before black listed the appellant in respect whereof the cancellation has been quashed. [104 E] 5.(a)(i) The High Courts committed an illegality by quashing the order dated 27th April, 1988 cancelling the auction. [117 A] (ii) The Collector had not given a prior notice before cancelling the bids and the cancellation thereof was illegal. [118 D] 6.2 In the facts of this case, it is clear that the action taken against the appellant is in accordance to law. The order passed on 27.3.1988 is also bad in the eyes of law. (iii) The order dated 24th March 1989 cancelling the bidding process is not a valid order and the same cannot be sustained in law as it has been passed after following the due procedure prescribed by the Rules and the High courts committed an irregularity in quashing such cancellation. The appeal is allowed, but without costs.

The appellant, a tenant in the premises covered by exhibit P 1, filed an application under section 4 of the Act for fixation of fair rent in respect of the building on the site in item 17(2) of the schedule to the lease. The Rent Controller passed an order on the basis that the appellant was entitled to recover the rent from the tenants and directed the LIC to pay the same. The appeal filed by the appellant against the said order was dismissed by the Appellate Authority. On appeal, the High Court held that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit for fixation the fair rent of item 1 at Rs.994 p.m. and that the question as to whether the appellant is a tenant or not did not arise in view of section 4(1) (a) of Act. The High Court, however, held that since the Rent Control Act had no application to the facts of this case, the Rent controller was right in holding that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties and that, therefore, the question whether the rent fixed by the Rent Sta te Officer in an order under section 64 C could be ignored as an order in the earlier proceedings would be completely ignored as a final decision on the issue as to the fair rents of the premises. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Rent Act are not conclusive and cannot be ignored by the courts below as to what is the proper rent of the property. [901B] 2. The rent control proceedings have been decided in favour of the appellant by the High court on a proper construction of the provisions of section 64C of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. [091F] 3. The question whether a landlord or a tenant is entitled to get fixation of the fair Rent fixed by an order passed under section 11(4) of that Act is not open to the appellant because the rent control proceeding has become final as to which the court can give its decision on any other issue in accordance with the provisions contained in section 64D of the said Act. [1001F] 4. The expression 'landlord ' in section 2(1)(a) means a person who is entitled for possession under the provisions relating to protection against eviction and includes a person claiming as a tenant. [1101G] 5. In view of the definition of landlord ' in Section 2(2), the Rent control proceedings are not open for the appellant to challenge the validity of the order passed by the court of Small Causes in respect thereof. [110H; 1101A B] 6. The word 'landlord' is a term used in section 4 (1) and it has been defined in section 3(2)(a). It does not include a person whose property is sought to be acquired under any law for the time being in force. The definition of 'landlord" in section 5(3) of Tamil Nadu Act 21 of 1961 clearly indicates that the landlord is entitled only to recover rent from his tenant and not from the tenant. The words 'landlord " are not decisive on the point whether the landlord has a relationship with the tenant or whether he has a right to recover it from the appellant. [109H; 110A B D] 7. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the rent was payable by the LIC in respect whereof the appellant had already paid the amount of Rs. 994 p., and the appellant has not challenged the order of the court on any ground other than the one which was available to him under section 5 (3) or section 4. [111A B C] 8. The landlord is a person entitled only for possession in respect to the building standing on the land covered by Exhibit P 1. He cannot be said to have any right to get the rent determined by the Controller unless he has been given an opportunity of hearing and cross examined by the tenant himself.

The petitioner was appointed as a Forest Officer on a provisional basis in the Mysore State Forest Service, and he was confirmed in that post. He was promoted to the rank of Deputy Conservator of Forests by order dated January 5, 1968. On his confirmation in that cadre, he was given an opportunity to be heard against the final list. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisional seniority list and also the consequential seniority list. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High court had erred in holding that the petitioner 's case was not covered by the decision of this Court in Shankariah 's Case (supra) and, therefore, he could not be heard by the High C ourt. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no material before it to come to a conclusion that the final seniority list was prepared without due regard to the particular important points which had to be considered before finalisation of the list. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The appellant 's contention that he was not heard before finalisation is wholly untenable and must fail. [701B] 2.2. The final seniority lists were prepared without any regard to any particular important point which had been considered before preparing the provisional list. Therefore, it cannot be said that the appellant ' s case was covered by either of the two decisions of this court or of the High Courts. [802C D] 3.1 The High Curt has erred in not considering the question whether the final gradation list prepared under Section 115 of the Act was a provisional one and, if so, whether it could be said to be a provisional or an opportunity. [901F G] 2.(a) In view of the decisions of the Mysore High Court and this Court, the appellant was not entitled to any relief against the provisional gradation list. [1002B] (b) The High court has erred by holding that since the final Seniority List had been prepared without giving due regard t o the relevant points which were considered before the final order was passed, it could not have been said that there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts of a case or in the application of those rules. [0901F] (c) The appellant was entitled to relief against provisional seniority lists prepared under section 115 of,the Act. [103G] 3.(a)(i) In the present case, the High c ourt has committed an error by holding otherwise that the provisional Seniority List was prepared in accordance with the provisions of the .The final senioritylist was prepared on an integrated basis without any further reference to the relevant rules governing seniority. [104H; 104A] (ii) The final list was not prepared under s. 115 of ,the Act and, as such, it was open to the appellant to challenge the provisional inter se seniority list in accordance therewith. [105B] 4.(a). In view thereof, the writ petitions are allowed. The impugned judgment of the Karnataka High Court is set aside. The writ petitions filed by the petitioner are dismissed. No costs.

The petitioners were granted Additional licences under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 and 1979 79 respectively for import of canalised items under the said licence. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said licences on the ground that they had been granted Additional Licences under the Foreign Trade Policy which had expired during the pendency of these petitions. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the period of validity of Additional licences was not applicable to the petitioners and, therefore, the period for which the Additional licences were issued could not be extended by six months from the date of such extension. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Additional Licences granted under the Export Policy 1988 91 had expired in the pendency thereof and, as such, they could not avail the same so long as the period expired during which the said licenses were valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Additional Licences issued to the appellants under the Customs Policy 1988 90 are valid for 12 months and they can avail the said additional licences only if they have been granted an Additional licence under the Imports & Exports Policy 197879. [901B] 2.2 The period of limitation prescribed in the Import Policy 1988 89 is applicable to cases where import has expired during pendency of the matters pending before this court and the period has not expired during that period. [093C] 3.1 In view of the above, the appeals are allowed. The impugned orders are set aside. However, there shall be no order as to costs.

The appellant, a manufacturer of excisable goods, filed an application under section 35L(b) of the Central Excise Act for inclusion of cost of packing in the assessable value of the excisable goods. The Assistant Collector rejected the said application on the ground that the cost of such packing was not includible in the value of such pack ing and therefore, the cost incurred by the manufacturer could not be included in the price. On appeal to this Court, it was contended that the costs incurred by a manufacturer could be included only if the packing is of durable nature and returnable by the buyer to the assessee. The Appellate Collector rejected this contention on the view that the packing was of durability and returnable within the factory gate. In appeal to the Supreme Court, HELD: (1) The cost of the packing in question cannot be included within the assessable price of the goods for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods unless the packing consists of a durable character and returnable in nature and is returnable by such packing. [601B] (2) The packing was made by the appellant and not by the buyers. The cost incurred on the packing could not therefore be included as the cost thereof. [702C] (3) The mere fact that the goods were delivered at the time of removal from the factory does not in any manner alter the assessable values of the various excisable goods for the purpose of determining the value. [801D] (4) The normal price for which the packing has to be returnable by a buyer to his customer is not includible under section 4(4)(d)(i). The cost thereof cannot be added to the price except where the packing itself is of adurable nature. [820E] (5) The costs incurred on packing are not includible within the value for determining 'value' in relation thereto. [823A D] (6) The fact that some packing was delivered at a time of delivery does not alter the normal price of such Packing. It is only where the container is of the durable quality and returnable to the manufacturer, that it can be included even if the container has been packed in a durable nature and being returnable by him to his customers.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted by the Special Judge under section 5 (1)(d) read with section 5 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo R.I. for one year and a fine of Rs. 500/- and in default of payment of fine he was directed to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed his appeal holding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.1 Section 161 I, I. P.C., provides for presumption against the accused person in certain cases. The presumption is rebuttable and it is only when the prosecution has proved that the accused had received the amount of money or return of a loan or return thereof as a motive of reward for doing so. [801B] 1.2.1 In order to prove the guilt of the accused, the prosecution must establish that the person received the sum of Rs, 10,000/- and the receipt of the same was not in his personal custody. The burden resting on the accused is upon him to show that he had received such amount as a reward for rendering service to him. [901C] 1.(a) In order that the presumption may be rebutted, it must be shown that the explanation offered by the accused was reasonable and probable. [1001D] (b) The prosecution has not been able to prove beyond doubt that the money received by the appellant was a bribe or return for rendering services to him, as alleged by the prosecution. [1101E] 1(c) In the instant case, the evidence of PW 1 is insufficient and probable to establish that he received the said amount of Rs 10, 000/- and that he did not receive any such reward. The fact that PW 1 had returned the money for rendering his services to PW 1 does not make him a reliable witness. [1201E C] 2.(a)(i) In view of the evidence on record, it is clear that the demand was made by the Appellant in his own personal custody and that the same had been received by him as an advance of Rs 20,000/-. [1102F] 3.(ii) The presumption arising under section 4(1)(b) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act is not rebutted. [110G] 4.(a). In view thereof, the appellant could not be said to have committed any offence punishable under section 6(2), I. PC. [111A] (iii) The conviction of the appellant under section 7(1) readwith section 5 and section 161 of the Code is therefore unsustainable in law. [112B C] 4.1 It was not disputed that the amount received by PW 1 from PW 1 was not a legal fee but it was a reward to PW 2 for rendering the services to the appellant as a security for the running of the canteen. The prosecution had also failed to establish beyond doubt the explanation tendered by the appel lant that he paid Rs 10 lakhs and that PW 2 had returned a sum which was due to the Appellant as a legally payable amount. [113C] 4(a) The High court has not properly appreciated the evidence in this case. [114B C; 114A] 4 (b). In the present case, there is no evidence on the record to show the demand made by PW 2 and 6. There was no evidence that the Appellant had paid any amount to PW1. [115E] 5.(a); (i) The fact of the seizure of the currency notes from the appellant does not in any manner affect his case.

The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of various products. The Company had been carrying on its business under the name and style of M/s. Hindustan Lever Ltd., a company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company had been doing business of manufacture and sale of various goods. It was engaged as an employee of the company in the year 1962. On or about the date of the termination of the employment, the company was not entitled to any compensation for wrongful withholding of the property of the Company. The company was also carrying on the business under a name and styled M/S. Hindustan Steel Ltd., which was wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of a company. The offence under section 630(l)(b) of the Act was committed in the course of the business carried on by the appellant company. In the course thereof, the appellant Company had taken possession of the properties of the said company and sold them to various persons including past officers and employees of the appellant. The prosecution case is that the assets of the companies were wrongfully obtained from the officers or employees of a public company and that the company had not been able to obtain possession of any property of a person who was wrongfully withheld by an Officer or employee, but had obtained possession of such property during the course Of his employment. The High Court held that the offence under sections 630(1) (b) and 630(2) of section 630 was not made out against the officers and employee of company and, therefore, the provisions contained in sections 630 and 630 were not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.1 Section 630 of the Income Tax Act is an offence under Chapter VI of the Indian Penal Code. It does not extend to the person who is wrongfully obtains possession of property of any company or employee or employee. The words 'any such property of company or employees ' in the articles of association of the assessee must be interpreted in a manner which would lead to the conclusion that the provisions are attracted only to the assets and properties of a Company which was illegally obtained by the officer or employees. [601B] 1.2.1 The words "any such properties of company" used in cl. (b), of sub section (1) of Section 630, would be wider than those specified in clauses (a) and (b). It is not necessary that the word 'employee' should be interpreted to mean only a person or employee who was legally entitled to receive wrongfully withhold possession of properties of any Company which were illegally obtained from officers or employee but had been wrongfully withheld from them. [701C] 1:1.2 The words used in sub section(1), of section 631, would not be applicable to the present case because the appellant is an officer and employees ' of a private company which was lawfully entitled to take possession of certain properties of Company which had been illegally obtained. [802D] 1.:1.3 In the instant case, the offence of wrongful withholding the property by the officers/employees of the Appellant company was committed when they were wrongfully withheld in their possession. The offences under section 631 are not made punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding one year but which may extend to three years and fine. [820E] 1.(a) In the present cases, the acts of delinquency specified in sub sections (1), (2) and(3) of sections 630, were not committed when the appellant was wrongfully withholds possession of some property of Company. [821F] 1(b) The offence of theft is an act which is an offshoot of the commission of a criminal breach of trust by the person or employees who are in charge of the management of the affairs of the undertaking and who is responsible for the conduct of such business.

The appellant was appointed as a Pujari of the Sansthan by the respondent on October 16, 1959. He was appointed in the year 1860 and continued to be a Pujar of the temple till he died in 1960. The respondent filed an application for appointment of a Pujor of the Temple under section 4(1) of the Act before the Assistant Commissioner of Endowments, Bombay. The Assistant Commissioner rejected his application on the ground that the appellant was not a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of Act. On appeal by the appellant, the Assistant Collector set aside the order of the Assistant commissioner and directed the respondent to appoint him as Pujor. The appellant filed an appeal before the Deputy Commissioner who allowed the appeal holding that the temple was a private property and not a private one. He held that the respondent was entitled to be appointed as Pujari under section 2 (13) read with section 4 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950. The High Court set aside this order of appointment and directed that the appointment of the Pujor be made in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 4(2) of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1951 provides for appointment as Pujar by the Assistant Commissioners of Endowments. It is not a case where the temple is a private or public trust but a private endowment. [701B] 2.2 The respondent was appointed under section 3 of the Trust Act and continued in possession as Pujars till he expired. He had been maintaining a temple for the benefit of the Hindu public. [802C] 2:1 Section 2(14) of that Act provides for the appointment as aujor of a private trust. The word 'divor' is not defined in section 2 of the Public Trusts (Amendment) Act, 1960. It does not include a person who has been appointed as an Pujari by the trustee or manager of a public temple. [820D] 2(15) In view of the provisions contained in sections 4 and 5 of the Indian Trust Act read with sections 3 and 4 of that act, it is clear that the trust was a public religious endowment and not private one and therefore, the respondent could only be appointed by the trustees or manager as a public trustee. [823E] 2.(16) The temple was intended to maintain a temple and for that purpose the respondent had been authorised to take charge of the property. It was not an endowment but a public charitable trust within section 2[13] of the trust Act. [825F] 3.2 In view thereof, the appellant could only establish that he was a Pujan or a public Trust within the definition of Section 2[14] of that trust Act and therefore the temple had been dedicated for the purpose of maintaining it as a private religious endowment. The question whether the respondent is a public or a private temple depends on the facts and tradition and practice which are present in the mind of the founder and the founder. [901F G] 3.(16A) In the instant case, the temple has been dedicated to the deity for the welfare of the public. It cannot be said that it was not private or a religious endowment but an endowment. Therefore, the question whether it is a Public Trust within section 4[14)] of the Trusts Act does not arise at all. [826C] 3(17) The respondent had no right to worship at the temple and therefore he could only have been appointed by him as a trustee. He could not be appointed in accordance to the provisions under section 5[14]. [826D] 4.(18) In order that the property may not be private or personal, it must be shown that the public is a religious denomination within the scope of section 3(13). The respondent cannot be appointed either as Pujan nor as a servant.

The appellant was a defaulter in payment of the tax due under a decree passed by the Bombay City Land Revenue Tribunal, and he was prosecuted for recovery of the amount due from him as if it were an arrear of land revenue. The appellant filed a suit against the State Government for recovery on the ground that the certificate issued by the Collector was void under article 13(1) of the Constitution and that the same had been obtained by fraud. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 46(2) of Bombay City Revenue Act, 1876. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of section 47(2), which were in force at the time when the certificate was issued, were void under Article 13(3). The High Court also held that since the certificate had been issued by a competent authority and the same was not challenged before the Supreme Court, it could not be said to be invalid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is well settled that the State Legislature has no power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [801B] 2.2 The words "any tax" and "taxes on a property" are used in article 13 (1) and they are not limited to the recovery of taxes due under any law for the time being in force. [902C] 3.3 The word "tax" is defined in section 2(d) of that Act as including tax on income, which is payable by a person who has been convicted of an offence under any other law for such period. It does not include a tax on property or a tax which is due to be paid in respect of any property. [1002D] 3:1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had been arrested and was detained in execution of a warrant of arrest issued by his arrest under section 13(2). The appellant was arrested and is being detained in custody for a period which may be extended by him till he was released on bail.

The appellant, a worker employed in an establishment for more than nine hours on any day of work in a year, was entitled to wages at the rate of Rs. 2 per day for every hour or part thereof in a week. The appellant claimed that he had worked for more 10 hours in a day and that he should be paid for every day or part of a day on any working day. He also claimed that the workmen were not entitled to any wages at all since they were not employed in any other establishment. The Labour Court held that the appellant was entitled only to wages for overtime work and not for any day on which any day he could be compelled to break up the hours of work. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the award of the Labour Court. In this appeal, it is contended that the High court erred in holding that the provisions of section 13(2) were not applicable to the appellant because the appellant had worked only for a period of nine hours and not more than 9 hours on a day. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression ' weekly holiday ' has been used in section 13 (2) of the Act and the words ' weekly holidays ' have been used therein. [701B] 2. The word ' weekly' has been defined in section 2(g) of Chapter IV of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 which reads as under: "2. " weekly holiday" means a period specified in the Schedule to this Act or any other law for the time being in force and includes any day or hours on which work is performed by an adult worker in a factory. 3. The words 's weekly holiday' have been defined under section 2 (g) as follows: " weekly holidays" means such days as may be specified in respect of any day, as may, from time to time, be fixed by the Chief Inspector and includes such intervals for rest, if owing to the nature of the work there is difficulty in giving the intervals for remaining. 4. The definition of ' weekly off holiday' has not been defined either in section 3 or in section 4 of the Factories Act, 1948. [601C] 5. The term ' weekly day ' has not necessarily mean a working day and it includes any other day or hour which may be fixed as such night. It is clear that the word 's daily holiday' means a working days and it does not include any day. [613D] 6. The High Court was in error in holding, on the facts of this case, that the hours were not specified in section 12(2)(a) of Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [501E] 7. It cannot be said that the words " weekly off" have been deliberately used in sections 13 (1) and 14(2). The word "s weekly off", as defined in clause (b) of section 2 of the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1964, means a day or days on which the hours are not specified. [511E] 8. It was not necessary for the workmen to have their case examined by the management before the Labour Officer. The workmen were entitled to be paid wages at any rate in excess of what they were entitled under section 13 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. [504G] 9. In view of the provisions contained in section 25(1) of that Act, it was not open to the Labour officer to have his case examined before the labour Officer for determining whether the hours should be spread over more than 12 hours on an hour or less than 9. The question whether the workmen are entitled to get wages at a rate higher than what they had been paid in excess would depend upon the nature and extent of work performed by them. [506B] 10.

The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and therefore the protection under the Act will not apply. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant tenant was entitled to protection under Section 20(1) of the Act and the suit was dismissed. The High Court held that the provisions contained in sub section (2) of Section 39 were applicable to the premises in question during the pendency of the proceedings and therefore, the protection will not be available to the appellant if within 10 years have elapsed since the filing of the suit. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the protection granted under Section 40 of the Punjab Act is applicable only to a case pending on the date of commencement of the trial and therefore it cannot be applied for 10 years as provided for in sub Section (2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions contained therein will not come into operation during the pending proceedings. [901B] 2.1 In view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of this Act, the provisions of Sections39 and 40 are applicable to all cases pending on date of the commencement of this act and therefore they will not have to apply for 10 year as provided in sub sections (2), (3) and 40. [095B] 3.1 Section 39 of the East Punjab Act provides that nothing contained in this section shall apply to any case pending before a court or other authority on the commencement date of this enactment. The provisions of Section 40 are not applicable to cases pending before any court or any other authority. [1005C] 4.2 In view thereof, the provision of Sections 38 and 39 of this statute will not govern the rights of the parties to have the protection of the new Rent Act which became applicable to them on the day when the suit is filed. [1105D] 3:1 The protection under section 40 of Punjab Act cannot be extended to a tenant who has died during the proceedings before the commencement or pendency of this proceeding. [110E] 4:2 Section 39 does not apply to cases which are pending on that date and therefore section 39 will not affect the rights available to such tenants under the Rent Act. [111F] 3(3) The provisions relating to protection of Rent Act have been made applicable to a tenancy which is pending on 1st April, 1974 and therefore this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit filed by the appellant. [112G H] 4.(4) In view whereof the High Court was right in holding that section 39 of Punjab Rent Act will apply to a lease which is filed after 10 years and therefore Section 40 will not operate as a bar for the protection to such tenant under the provisions relating thereto. [113A D] 5.2 The provisions regarding protection of rent are applicable only if the tenancy is terminated by the landlord on the expiry of 10 years from the date on which the suit has been instituted. [114E] 6.3 In view, therefore, it cannot now be said that the provision relating to the protection given under section 39 is not applicable in the present case. [115F] 4(5) The High court was right when it held that section 40 was applicable only in respect of a tenancy and not in respect where the tenancy has been terminated by a landlord on expiry of ten years from 1st May, 1974. [116G H; 116A D C] 5.(6) In the instant case, the appellant had not filed any suit for ejectment against the respondent on the basis of section 39(1)(a). The respondent was entitled only to protection in respect thereof under section 20(2) and (3).

The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act of 1949 as amended by the Ordinance, 1952 and that the Controller had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent No 1 was not entitled to the benefit of the Ordinance of 1952. On appeal, the appellate Court confirmed the decree of eviction on the finding that the appellant was a tenant within section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1949 and that he had no right to eject the thika tenants after the Act had come into force. The High Court held that the provisions contained in sections 4 and 5 of the West Bengal Thika Land Reforms Act, 1949 were applicable to all suits pending on 21st October, 1952. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) Section 4 of the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1950 is prospective only. It does not apply to suits pending before the Controller or before any court or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the , but it applies to all appeals and proceedings pending on the date of commencement of the ordinance. [701B] (2) The expression "any suit" in section 3 means a suit pending on that day before the commencement of this Ordinance, and includes any proceeding which might be instituted after the commencement thereof. [802C] (3) Section 5 of Ordinance, 1953 is prospective in operation and does not affect the right of the landlord to eject a thki tenant after the Ordinance had come in force. [601D] (4) The word "any" in the Act means any proceeding pending on or before the date when the Act came into force and includes proceedings which might have been instituted after that day but before the expiry of three months from the commencement Of the Ordinance. [76G] (5) Section 3 of Ordinance No. 4 of 1952 is prospective and does apply to all cases pending on and after the date on which the Act comes into force, and if any such proceeding had been in operation on the said date, the Controller shall deal with all pre suits pending at that day and if so, he did not have to consider whether any of the grounds in section 4 were available to him. [77H] (6) Section 2 of Ordinance 1 of 1952 does not provide for a notice under section 4 of Ordinance I of 1952 as amended. The Controller has no jurisdiction or power to deal therewith in accordance With the provisions relating to notice under sections 4 & 5 of Act of 1953. [78A B] (7) Section 9 of Ordinance II of 1952 cannot apply to proceedings pending before a court or to any court when it had been filed after that date.

The appellant was appointed as a Bench Secretaries Grade I in the pay scale of Rs.500 1,000 on January 1, 1986. He was promoted to the post of Senior Section Officer with effect from October 1, 1975. On February 9, 1976, he was given the pay scales of Rs..291600 and Rs.4007. The appellant was also given the same pay scale as that of Bench Secretaries. In the year 1979, he filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the validity of the said order of July 2, 1976. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the classification made by the Pay Commission was not on the basis of any rational or scientific basis and that it was arbitrary and violative of the right to have equal pay for equal work. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The classification made under the Rules is clearly arbitrary and based on no rational or rational or legal basis. [701B] 2.2. The post of Bench Secretary Grade I is a higher scale than that of Section Officers. It is not possible for the High Court to say that there can be two scales of pay in the same cadre, one between the grade of Bench secretary and other posts. [802C] 3.1 The classification of Bench Assistants Grade I and Bench Secretaries in Group I was made on the recommendation of the Pay commission. It was not a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale. [820D] 2:1.2 The High court has completely ignored the fact that the post is a lower scale than Section Officers and that there cannot be two grades with different designations. [823E] 3:1 The High Courts have committed manifest error in holding that there was no rational, or legal foundation for classification of posts under the rules. [825G] 2.(a) In view of the fact, that the pay structure of Bench Members Grade I was not in accordance with the Rules and that the same was a matter of policy, the High court should have directed that all Benches Secretaries should be given the scale of pay which is being given to Bench Secretaries with effect on the principle of equal work and that too without any rational basis. (b) The High courts committed manifest illegality in holding otherwise. [822E] 2(a) The classification was made under rule 3(a)(i) of the Rules. It cannot be said that there could be two posts with different designation. [821F] 3.(a)(ii) The post is not a higher post but it is a post carrying higher pay scales. [824E] 4.1 In view thereof, the appellant was entitled to the same scale as was given to Benches Secretaries Grade II and Grade I. [828A D] 2 (b). The High Power Committee had recommended that Rs. 40000 be given to Judges Grade I for equal pay in terms of the recommendations made by it. [826B] 3(c) In the present case, the post was a higher grade than Section Officer Grade I, and therefore, the same cannot be equated with Section Officers or Private Secretaries GradeI. [829E] (d) The appellant is entitled to get the scale admissible to Section Officers Grade I from the date of his appointment as Bench Secretary in Group II. [827A D E] 4.(a). In view Of the fact whether the post can be said to be a higher pay or not, the principle that the posts cannot be termed as "equal for work" is applicable to the case. [82E] 5.(b) It is well settled that the principle is that the persons who are charged with fixing the scales of salary and other conditions of service must be given equal pay. The said principle has been reiterated in a number of cases. In [82F E] (c) The principle of "equal pay for work ' has to be applied in every case.

The appellant company was a declared industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. The State Government issued a notification on April 1, 1976 under section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 to acquire the land for the purpose of establishing a sugar undertaking in the area specified therein. The appellant company filed an application before the State Government for acquisition of the land. The Collector rejected that application and the State Legislature passed an order on March 31, 1976 declaring the industry as a declared industrial undertaking under section 2 of the Industries(Development and regulation) Act. The High Court held that the declaration made by the Parliament was in accordance with law and not void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the State legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List II. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The power conferred by the State legislation upon the Central Government under Entry 24, List I read with Entry 24 is subject to the provisions of Entry 23, List III and not to any other provision of the Constitution. [601B] 2.2 The power of the State to impose property tax on lands and buildings owned by or vesting in the Union Government under the Act is a legislative power which has been conferred upon Parliament alone. It is a power which is exercised by the Central Legislature and not by the States. [702C] 3.3 In the instant case, the State of Madhya Pradesh had no power to impose any property tax either on lands or buildings owned or vested in it under the State Act. [803D] 4.1 Section 127A of the M.P. Municipalities Act, 1961 provides for the constitution of a special area Development Authority and that the ownership rights could be validly acquired by the Government under that Act. It was held by this Court that the power to levy property tax is not in conflict with the power conferred on Parliament alone and that it was not open to the State Legislatures to pass a law on the subject. [777E] 4,2A] 3:1 The State Legislature has no competence or jurisdiction to pass an Act of 1957 by reason only of Entry 24 of List II read with entry 23, list I read as Entry 24. [783F] 2:2.3 The power to tax on land and buildings vested in the State is a legislation on the Union Parliament which had no legislative competence or authority to pass it. [780E] 3;2.4 In the present case, there was no question of any delegation of legislative powers by the Union Legislature. [78F] 4:1.5 The power under Entry 23 of List I to impose tax on buildings and lands owned by the appellant Company is a constitutional power which can be exercised by Parliament alone in relation to the matters specified in Entry 24 and not in relation thereto. [781A] 2, 3 & 4:2 In the case of a declared undertaking, the Central or State Legislature had no jurisdiction to impose such property tax. The power was conferred on the State under Entry 54, List 1 read with Section 127 A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act. Therefore, the declaration by Parliament in respect of a notified industry under Section 2 of that Act is subject only to the provision of Entry 54 and not otherwise. [77F] 3 &4:2 The notification issued by the President of India on April 25, 1976 was valid for a period of five years from April 1 1976 to March 31 1976. Therefore the declaration dated May 25, 1977 was valid in respect thereof. [76G] 4;3A] 5.1 In the light of the above discussion, it is clear that the impugned legislation is not violative of Article 14 of the constitution and is liable to be struck down as being violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution.

The appellant 's lease was for a period exceeding one year, and the Government had granted the lease to him on or after July 1, 1945. The appellant ' s lease was renewed from time to time by the Government in exercise of its powers under section 20(1) of the Estates Land Act, 1908. On August 14, 1947, the appellant ' made an application for renewal of his lease and the State Government granted a fresh lease on or before July 1. 1945, for a further period of one year. The State Government refused to renew the lease on the ground that the appellant had not been able to establish his right in the land leased by him prior to July 1., 1945, and therefore, he was entitled to compensation from the Government. On September 14, 1948, the State of Andhra Pradesh issued a notice under section 19(1)(a) of Estates Land (Amendment) Act, 1952, calling upon the appellant to show cause why his lease should not be terminated. The respondent 's reply thereto was that the lease had been granted subsequent to July I, 1945, but before July I. 1945. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the right to terminate the lease was created after July I., 1945 and therefore the termination of the lease could only be done under the second proviso to section 20 (1) which provides for compensation payable in respect of the right created after the notified date but before the notified day, if it is in the public interest to do so. Held, that the rights created after August 1, 1946, were only voidable at the instance of the Government and not on the basis of the second Proviso. The third proviso was intended to be operative only with a view to avoid the same. It did not extend to cases where the right had been created before July1, 1945 but before that date. The second proviso was meant to be effective only if it was in the Public interest to continue the lease and not otherwise. The right created before the specified date could only have been terminated by the State after July1. 1945 and not thereafter.
